transcript.preview: Sand rode the wind as it whipped over the desert dunes, pelting against the Courier’s thick coat. Looking out through his helmet, the orange mountain ranges in the distance crept closer as they moved
transcript.fullText: Sand rode the wind as it whipped over the desert dunes, pelting against the Courier’s thick coat. Looking out through his helmet, the orange mountain ranges in the distance crept closer as they moved across the horizon. “One foot in front of the other, eh Marco?” the courier asked, patting a hand on his horse. A metallic clank echoed throughout his steed’s body, quickly drowned out by the steady whirring of the gears inside. Marco’s head lifted, mechanical eyes making contact with the couriers as it nodded in agreement. “Attaboy,” the courier smiled, adjusting the straps of his pack. Behind him were bags of varying sizes, filled with packages and supplies he had been charged with delivering to a remote city out in the desert. For the past two weeks, the Courier and his steed trekked through this barren landscape after landing at the capital city's spaceport. Despite his best efforts to find a transport service, the fares were higher than his total payout would be upon delivery. One taxi man said something about “scavvers” and “raiders” that were harassing the townspeople living at his destination. Letting out a deep sigh, the courier lifted his wrist and wiped sand from the screen of his technobracer. It came to life at his touch, displaying the map as well as his helpful friend, a red arrow that pointed him toward his destination. Zooming out, he was nearing the end of the mapped-out area and entering uncharted territory. When plotting his course to the delivery point, the courier intentionally avoided the main route in order to skirt around any possible trouble. ___ Looking out ahead, he saw the mountain range that separated him from his destination. His fingers danced over the surface of his bracer, inputting the commands for a short-range scan of the area. Through the lens of his helmet, he watched as a blue pulse of energy emitted from his arm, radiating from his position and out over the mountains. Within seconds, the map began filling in with topographical data, detailing large to middle-sized objects on his side of the mountain. With a few more inputs, the red arrow displayed once more, this time pointing in a different direction. “AUTO-PATH HAS FOUND A MORE EFFICIENT ROUTE,” a robotic voice echoed through his metal helmet, “WOULD YOU LIKE TO CHANGE YOUR COURSE?” A text prompt appeared over the map, showing the two trails and displaying their distance and expected arrival time. The new route was shorter by hours but led over the mountains. The courier knew that without having map data on the other side, the descent might not be as easy as his bracer made it seem. “What do you think Marco?” he asked, pointing towards the new path, “Should we try that way?” The mechanical horse looked back and forth between the two, almost as if it was weighing the options. After a few seconds, it raised its front left leg and tapped the sandy ground twice, shaking its head in the direction of the mountain. “You sure?” the courier asked with a chuckle, “We don’t know what's on the other side yet.” Marco lifted his head, the hydraulics that controlled his neck hissed slightly under the strain of the heat and sand, then nodded. “That settles it then,” The two changed course, following the red arrow on the Courier’s technobracer. *** Hours passed as they fought against the incline of the mountain as well as the rough terrain of loose rocks and sand. The new path snaked up, cutting through until it crested over the top of the range. As they neared the top, the Courier dismounted, securing the cargo from his back onto the saddle to lighten his load. Overhead the sun was at its zenith, giving him no shade or protection from its rays. He could feel the sweat evaporating in his helmet and checked his bracer. HELMET TEMPERATURE RATING BELOW ENVIRONMENTAL STANDARDS - UPGRADE REQUIRED “Well that’s not going to happen any time soon,” the Courier laughed, reaching up to his head and removing the metal helmet. His curly brown hair dripped with sweat, which fell and was absorbed into the thirsty ground below. Taking a deep breath, the Courier could almost taste the sweetness of small round fruits that were ripening on the native cacti nearby. “Woah,” he said, putting out a hand to stop his horse, “Let's take a little break.” They moved over to a small patch of the fragrant plants. The Courier plucked one of the orange orbs and held it in front of his bracer. Scanner nodes lit, sending an array of blue lasers out to inspect the fruit in his hand. Once it was complete, a detailed explanation of the fruit was displayed, which was promptly skipped to find the more important information. SAFE FOR HUMAN CONSUMPTION “Well there you have it,” the Courier said, peeling the thick orange membrane off and inspecting the insides. A yellow fleshy ball lay beneath the skin, filled with thick strands of organic material that held the structure together. Jamming his finger into one end, he pulled it apart until he had two halves and popped one into his mouth. Yellow juice dripped down his chin as he chewed. He closed his eyes as he savored the sweet flavor of organic food for the first time in several days. ___ “You’ve gotta try this,” he said, offering up the other half to his horse. Marco approached, opening his mouth and licking it with a thick pink artificial tongue. It tested the flavor several times before taking the offered fruit from its partner. The two sat beneath the sun, looking back on the path they had traveled over the past few days from their high vantage point. There was no trace of their journey save for the memories of it, the wind displacing the sand and obscuring their tracks. Both chewed for a long moment, taking the silence in stride as they rested. Several minutes and alien fruits later, the Courier lifted his arm and input the commands for another scan. “We’re close enough to the top, the scan should be able to cover the other side from this height.” ___ Without his helmet, he couldn’t see the process, but he could feel the energy shift around him as his bracer sent out its signals. It completed, filling in the map and allowing for a more accurate route to be displayed. The courier zoomed in on the new topographical data, interested in seeing how steep the descent would be when something else caught his eye. Three yellow dots were blinking on the other side of the mountain, and they were closing in on his position. “Shit!” he cursed, standing and donning his helmet. Inside, a notification blinked on the visor. CAUTION - CARGO PINGED BY UNKNOWN SOURCE The Courier reached down to his belt and removed his pistol, making sure to check the small digital display that showed its current charge. Luckily it was full, but he could feel a pit in his stomach growing as adrenaline pumped through his system. ___ “We’ve got company Marco,” the Courier said to his partner, “I need you to be the distraction,” The horse shook its head, letting out a loud electronic whinny of disapproval. “We don’t have time to argue, you just stay here and I’ll try to get the drop on them.” Without another word, the Courier ran up the ridge, checking his technobracer every few seconds to see how close the enemies were. He came to a stop just below the crest of the mountain and hid behind one of the large red rocks, hiding him from anyone coming from the other side. Only a few seconds passed before he could hear the sounds of footsteps displacing rocks as they moved toward him. Taking in a deep breath, he raised his pistol and readied himself. “Who comes this far off the main path?” he heard a young man’s voice ask. ___ “Shhh… keep your voice down, we’re getting close,” another, more gruff voice answered, “but whoever they are, they must have thought we weren’t covering this side of the mountain. The Courier cursed himself internally and felt the tension building as he waited for them to walk past him. Unfortunately, they didn’t. “Hold up here,” the older man said from very close by, “let's scope this out, I’ve got a bad feeling.” Pressing his back up against the rock, the Courier looked up and saw the barrel of a makeshift rifle hovering over his head, pointed down in Marco’s direction. His heartbeat doubled as he tried to keep his breathing quiet, and he froze to listen in on their conversation. “I see… A horse?” the younger raider said, puzzled, “who brings a horse out into the desert?” ___ The two men chuckled above his head, causing the rock to vibrate as sound carried through it. “Do you see anything else? Like a person?” The Courier slowly snaked his way to the left of the large rock and crouched down before sneaking up towards the raiders. He held his breath and waited for one of them to talk before making any sudden moves. “Nope, just the horse… Maybe they’re taking a piss behind a rock or something?” “Maybe…” the older raider said, bringing his gloved hand to his face and thinking for a moment. Without warning, a blue bolt of electricity shot into the back of the pondering raider, sending arcs of energy through his nervous system. He convulsed for several seconds, which drew the attention of his younger partner, who was now frozen in fear. ___ The Courier pressed the barrel of his pistol on the raider’s skull, as well as a single knee on his back to pin him to the rock. “Where's your other friend?” the courier asked, deepening his voice in an attempt to sound more threatening. The raider hesitated, shivering as he watched his friend finally finish convulsing. “Talk!” “I don’t know!” he screamed, his voice echoing down the side of the mountain, “he told us he would be watching our backs and…” BOOM A loud shot rang out from nearby, quickly followed by a rain of rocky debris as the high-caliber bullet turned the rock near the Courier’s knee into powder. The shock of the blast caused him to pull the trigger, sending the full effect of his weapon into the skull of the raider. ___ The Courier rolled to the side, dropping back down behind the rock and catching his breath for several seconds before peeking over the edge once more. He could see the raider still writhing, blue electricity arcing across his body as it reset his nervous system. Narrowing his eyes, the visor zoomed in on the rocks in the distance, scanning for any sign of movement. A glint of light from the east caught his attention, causing the hairs on his neck to stand on end as his intuition kicked in. He ducked behind cover just before another shot rang out, raining more debris down on his head as the ballistic round struck the stone where his face had been. Knowing that it would take the raider another few seconds to reload, he lifted his head once more and fixed his vision on the location of the glint. Sure enough, he found the target and watched as the raider struggled to unjam his rifle. ___ The Courier let out a whistle, catching the attention of his mechanical partner, whose head swung in his direction. He pointed to the rock where the raider was taking shelter, mouthing a command. “Go get him!” the courier whispered. Marco snorted loudly, causing it to echo lightly down the side of the mountain just before the horse began sprinting full speed toward its target. The distinct sound of a metal casing clanked on the rocky ground beneath the raider, followed by a muffled curse as the heavy hoofbeats approached. Taking a deep breath, the courier waited until he heard the shot before rushing the enemy. When it finally came, his steed let out an electronic cry. The courier left the safety of cover and ran with his pistol drawn to finish the fight. ___ Before he could get there, however, he watched as the raider’s body was flung several feet into the air, landing with a crunch that sent shivers down his spine. He came to a stop next to his horse, whose metal exterior had been punctured and was leaking a viscous green fluid. “He really got you, huh boy?” the Courier asked, moving in close and inspecting the wound. Marco took a step back, shaking his head several times. “Let me look at it, you big baby,” Closing the gap, he opened a metal hatch and began the repairs. After only a few seconds of looking around, he reached his fingers into the chassis and turned a small knob. The stream of leaking fluid slowed to a drip, and the courier removed his hand, closing the hatch before wiping his hands on his trousers. ___ “You’re lucky as hell, you know that?” It just nicked your coolant line, you’ll run a little hot until we can get it fixed, but we’re not far from town now. The courier looked over his shoulder and down the other side of the mountain, where a small settlement hugged the edge of a vibrant river that cut through the desert. All manner of foliage and tropical trees lined the banks, and he could see small dots moving to and from the town. He took a step toward the final raider and watched his chest for several seconds, looking for movement. His chest rose and fell, though his breaths were shallow and ragged, he was still alive. “Let’s make our delivery and get you looked at,” the courier said to his partner, patting him gently on the head. *** Cool water trickled down his throat as the courier sipped from his newly filled canteen, sending a wave of relief as the locals peered in his direction. He followed the river, with the only sounds being the stream of flowing water, Marco's hoofbeats, and the soft groans from the bound raiders being dragged behind them. The courier watched as the townspeople gathered around the bridge, their faces lighting up with excitement at the mere sight of him. Taking another sip, the courier wiped the corners of his mouth and waved to them. Displayed on the screen of his bracer were the wanted notices of each of the three raiders, with rewards that were enough to get them through the next few seasons with ease. A smile formed on the courier's face, and he patted the side of his horse as they neared closer to their destination.

transcript.fullText: Campfires crackled beneath the stars, stoked by a cool wind blowing from the east. The rebel encampment was blanketed by the shadow of a nearby mountain, blocking the bright silver moonlight. Footsteps accompanied the sounds of the dying flames as the captain pushed through the flaps of the largest tent. “Is every one asleep?” the gruff voice of an older man sounded from the corner. The face accompanying the question was scarred and pock-marked from years of battling both men and sickness. Furry gray eyebrows scrunched closer together as the amber eyes of the old man waited impatiently for an answer. “Of course not, they’re all scared to death,” the captain said, walking over to a makeshift wooden table where the battle plans were currently being looked over. “How's it coming along, sire?” A red-robed figure stood over the map, tracing his gloved fingers over the surface. Each time he did, a small orange rune appeared, shimmering as if on fire. Not breaking his concentration, the robed man lifted a single finger, asking for silence as he finished his task. Once the final mark had been made, he took a step back from the table and examined his work. Running his fingers between the curly brown locks of hair, the mage visualized the formations of the battle until the runes on the map came to life. Each one projected a fiery image of two different armies, one marked with the distinct armor of the King’s guard while the other was clad in worn makeshift armor that marked the rebellion. “I think I’ve figured it out,” the robed figure mumbled as he circled the table, taking in the battlefield from all angles. The captain stood and watched as the leader of their rebellion carefully plotted out their final assault on the king. Looking over to the old man, the two locked eyes for a long moment, silently communicating both their worry and excitement. “I don’t think you have much to worry about sire,” the captain reassured, moving closer to the table and leaning in close to inspect the magical images of the armies. “Your strategies have gotten us this far, all we need is one more victory to take the crown, your crown.” Lifting his eyes from the table, the mage met his captain's gaze, searching as deep as he could for the truth behind his words. Sensing only honesty, his shoulders slumped slightly and he allowed himself to lean on the table. Letting out a deep sigh, the mage lifted a gloved hand to his temple and did his best to rub away the headache that he had been fighting for the past few hours. “It's getting late, young master,” the gruff voice from the corner chimed in, “You’d best try and get some sleep. We need you in top form tomorrow.” “He’s right sire,” the captain chimed in, moving closer and placing a hand on the mage’s shoulder, “We’ll look over the plans and familiarize ourselves, then we can go over them together in the morning.” Looking back and forth between his two closest advisors, the mage nodded his head in agreement before stretching his arms out above his head. “I guess you’re right,” he yawned, feeling the siren’s call of sleep lull over his body at the thought. “Goodnight, see you both in the morning.” The mage walked towards the exit, lifting the worn yellow flap and emerging into the cool night. He took several steps before he heard the sound of voices speaking in low tones behind him, causing him to stop and listen. “Do you think we’ll live to see another sunset?” the old man asked. The mage's heart slowed as worry rippled through his body. Taking a deep breath, he tuned his ears into the conversation, waiting for the captain to answer. “With him in charge…” the captain paused, “I doubt that there's anything we can’t do.” Despite the bitter cold wind blowing through the camp, the mage felt a warm sense of relief wash over him at his friend's words. Looking up to the stars, he prayed to the gods for strength as he traced constellations in the air with his orange magic. *** Across the battlefield, the King’s guard shimmered in the morning light as their golden armor reflected the sun. Behind them the high white walls of the city were marked with archers, each one with an arrow in hand, ready to let loose their barrage on command. A raven circled over the King as he sat upon his white horse, watching the troops fall into place as the battle neared its beginning stages. Dull eyes followed the bird as it flew lower, perching on a nearby wall and squawking as it cleaned its feathers. “An omen?” his majesty asked dully, turning his head over to the blue-robed wizard next to his side. The ancient caster lifted his head from the scroll he was studying and examined the creature that was idling nearby. Scratching the chin hidden beneath his long white beard, the wizard’s mind was too preoccupied with the battle plans to properly investigate the raven. He shook his head, once again focusing his attention back to the plans. “Doubtful, your highness,” he said passively, “I believe in true magic, not in superstitions,” Accepting his advisor’s answer, the king looked back out to the field ahead and took in the view. The rebels had pushed their way through his kingdom’s defenses in a short few weeks, though his highly trained soldiers had obviously proved effective enough to cull their numbers. As he sized up the competition, he could feel a pit in his stomach that betrayed the words of encouragement from his most trusted council members. “We have sight of their leader, sir,” a young voice chimed in, pulling him out of his thoughts. The king looked down to the soldier, who had an ornate golden spyglass extended out to him. Taking it into his hands, his majesty followed the pointed finger of the soldier and looked through the scope. “Which one is he?” the king asked, scanning the back line of the rebel forces until he stopped at a group of three men mounted on horses that looked as if they hadn’t eaten in days. “Our sources say he’s the one in red,” Taking a closer look, his majesty stared at the young man in red mage's robes that was looking down at his own parchment of battle plans. “He's young, and a mage,” the king noted. “Too bad he’s not a cleric,” the wizard chuckled “Why’s that?” the aged monarch questioned, raising an eyebrow. “Because he’s going to need a miracle to save himself and his men from the mines we’ve planted in the field.” A sharp look of concern flashed over the king’s face, followed quickly by a question. “Our men know to avoid the mines?” The wizard waved a hand in dismissal. “Of course, they’ve been instructed to avoid the areas that have been dug up on the field and try to force the enemy into them.” Letting out a sigh of relief, the king allowed himself to relax. “Good,” he said, “let's make sure that everyone is in position, its almost time.” With his final words uttered, the raven let out another squawk and took flight once more. Across the battlefield, the red-robed mage blinked several times to sever the magical connection to his raven familiar. His vision cleared and focused back on the battle map he had been pretending to look at. “What did you see?” his captain asked from his right. The red-robed mage made eye contact with his friend and smiled. “I saw the future,” he joked. “And? Do we win?” The mage nodded his head, letting the smile that had formed on his face fade into pure focus as his mind adjusted his strategy. *** “Get behind me, your majesty!” the wizard shouted as he began conjuring a wall of protective magic. “I wouldn’t do that!” the red-robed mage shouted back as he lobbed a small ball of flame into the air above the enemy caster. The ball grew several times its size on the short trip to its destination, reaching the ceiling of the throne room before detonating a pillar of flame that engulfed the wizard. The king watched as the outline of his magical advisor turned to dust as the inferno singed his material body from existence. By the time the flames subsided, there was little more than ash left, along with a large hole burning through the ancient ceiling of his castle. Looking out into the throneroom, the king watched as the red-robed mage made quick work of his royal guardsmen. He could feel his heartbeat throughout his body and tried to fight off the dread that had been setting in ever since his forces had failed to hold off the rebels earlier that morning. Retreating back to the throne that sat at the far end of the room, the king looked up to the stained glass window that was casting its multicolored light across the bloodied floor. The sounds of battle faded away as he tracked his royal lineage through the images that were set in the glass. When his eyes finally rested on his own image, telling the story of his many triumphs of war, he let out a deep sigh. “Are you ready to surrender, or do you want to fight till the end?” a young voice called out from a few feet behind him. The king turned, locking eyes with the red mage. His enemy's eyes filled with flames, the burning desire to conquer at all costs. The very same eyes he likely had when he was the same age, leading war campaigns across the neighboring kingdoms. Taking a deep breath, the king steeled his resolve and shifted his feet into an aggressive stance as he raised his sword. “To the death,” he answered, charging forward. The red mage smiled, raising his wooden staff and taking aim at the king’s chest. Within seconds, all that was left of the old monarch was the partially melted crown that clattered to the ground. Picking it up with his gloved hand, the mage turned it over in his hands several times before looking back at his men. Battered and beaten in every way, still they stood, having done what was thought impossible by many. The captain and old man exchanged glances, then looked at the red mage and nodded their approval. With a single motion, the mage lowered the hot crown onto his head, feeling the comfortable weight of power settle through his body as he relished in the moment of achievement.

transcript.fullText: The scent of charred timber still clung to my memory, a perverse perfume of success. Her face once so vibrant, now a canvas of ruin, a testament to my absolute control. I had wanted perfection for Gwen, but the cost I was learning was always paid in blood and broken trust. That moment, a chilling crescendo of my adolescent power felt like a lifetime ago. Yet the echoes of those choices reverberated, shaping the very foundation of my empire. A journey that began with a high school tennis court and a girl I deemed worthy of my divine intervention. Her name was Gwen. A simple, almost unremarkable name. Yet in my memory, it's etched with the sheen of ambition and the bitter taste of a lesson learned. We'd shared the same sterile hallways in middle school, but it wasn't until our freshman year of high school that she truly registered on my radar. She possessed a certain athletic grace, a lean, almost predatory beauty that caught my discerning eye, long dark hair that cascaded like a shadow fair skin that seemed to glow and a body honed by discipline. That year, I'd begrudgingly signed up for tennis in gym, a trivial exercise for someone with my particular advantages. I observed her, noted her competitive fire, the way her eyes narrowed with focus the determined set of her jaw. She was clearly experienced a natural. Yet, she couldn't beat me. No one could. Not then, not now. It wasn't because I was some tennis prodigy. It was because the world in its infinite pathetic predictability bent to my will. It still does. I am Victor Cain, though back then I was simply a boy beginning to understand the terrifying, exhilarating scope of my power. My family, a name whispered in circles far above the common herd, had bestowed upon me a gift, or perhaps a curse. the ability to mold reality, to make desires manifest, to bend the will of others without them ever knowing. I could attain anything I wanted, and people would be none the wiser. Their memories subtly altered their choices, guided by my unseen hand. As long as my interest in Gwen persisted, she was destined to be mine, her path inextricably linked to mine. Looking back, a cynical smile always tugs at my lips. Would she have cared for me truly had I not orchestrated every flutter of her heart, every beat of her ambition? A rhetorical question perhaps, but one that underscores the fundamental truth of my existence. Genuine connection is a weakness, a vulnerability I learned to despise in the squalor of my childhood. Despite my initial fascination with her talent, Gwen struggled against other competitive players. A minor flaw easily rectified, but at the time my attention was fragmented. I was still quite young, navigating the treacherous currents of my own nent power, learning the subtle nuances of its application. I could effortlessly command popularity a fleeting, intoxicating burst of validation that quickly grew tiresome. When the adoration became a boore, people would simply drift away. Their minds wiped clean of my recent presence, a convenient erasure of inconvenient attachments. Though I often refer to my abilities as a curse, a dramatic flourish for the benefit of my own internal narrative. The advantages were and remain infinite. It's a solitary kingdom, this power, but a kingdom nonetheless. Gwen in her youthful naivee abandoned tennis the summer before our sophomore year. I recall standing several lockers down from her figning indifference my ears attuned to the hushed conversation she shared with a couple of friends. Her tone though she tried to mask it with casual dismissal betrayed a raw palpable pain. It was a dream discarded traded for the mundane comfort of resignation. a pity. I could feel the familiar twitch in my right hand, the urge to twist Peter's tarnished silver ring, a habit I'd cultivated to channel the restless energy of my manipulations. I'd acquired it after Peter, after he was gone. I told others it was a family heirloom, a lie that gilded my fabricated past. It was her life, of course, and I harbored a fleeting reluctance to meddle. For most of that year, I allowed myself to attempt to forget her to focus on the endless charade of normal life. Perfect grades required no effort from me. Yet, I would occasionally feain diligence pouring over textbooks to maintain the illusion. In gym, victory in sports was a foregone conclusion, but I'd force myself to exert some semblance of effort to appear human. My power offered countless advantages, yes, but life without a challenge, without a new conquest, could be quite dull. It reminded me of the suffocating sameness of the tenement, the constant hunger for something more, something different. This emptiness, this craving was a void I constantly sought to fill a relentless echo of Peter's absence. My thoughts, ever drawn to the unfinished symphony of potential, returned to Gwen near the end of the school year. Her parents owned a regional pizza chain, a surprisingly decent establishment, though by no means a culinary marvel. Money, of course, was never an issue for me even then. The chefs in my family's estate could conjure far more exquisite gastronomic delights. Yet, I'd found myself on a whim, stopping in one day with a couple of friends, still clinging to the fragile facade of a normal existence. And there she was, sweeping the floor, her movements listless, her spirit dimmed. It was a stark reminder of the mediocrity I had sworn to escape the kind of life Peter had been denied. She could be so much more. The thought was a persistent hum in my mind, a challenge to my burgeoning sense of power. I had spent the year deliberately avoiding her, preluding myself from nudging her towards her dreams. A rare lapse in my usual proactive approach. Was staying out of her life truly for the best. The question felt like an insult to my inherent superiority, a betrayal of my own grand design. Peter, in his innocence, would have simply wanted her to be happy. But I, Victor, knew happiness was a fleeting illusion and control a far more satisfying reality. A week later, I informed my parents of my decision to court Gwen. They, in their detached, aristocratic way, offered their tacit approval, their eyes already fixed on grander schemes. And so I made my move. I instructed Chase, my family's imposing, impeccably dressed butler, a man whose loyalty was as absolute as his methods were ruthless, to place an order for several pizzas. A special request, I added, with a subtle smirk, Gwen herself must deliver them. A little over half an hour later, she arrived a vision of youthful uncertainty on my manicured doorstep. I met her at the imposing row iron gate, a carefully constructed tableau of casual encounter. Hey, you're Gwen from school, right? I offered my voice a blend of figned surprise and genuine charm. She blushed a delicate flush that spread across her cheeks as soon as I uttered her name. She liked me that much was clear, but the authenticity of her affection remained even then a point of detached curiosity for me. Like me, she hailed from a wealthy family. Her natural talent shining through a brief illusion of independence. It echoed the lessons I'd learned from the botch deal with that collector in Chicago. how far one must go to ensure compliance. After realizing the full gruesome extent of what I had done, a rare flicker of something akin to remorse stirred within me. I stopped requesting such extreme retaliations. I was reluctant to have Gwen's opponents injured in any overt way, opting instead for more subtle, less traceable interventions. having them stumble or simply swing their rackets the wrong way. Their minds clouded by an unseen influence. My ambition, however, remained undimemed. In the end, it paid off. Gwen, my puppet, my masterpiece, could finally play at the national level her career, a shining monument to my hidden power. But I didn't feel comfortable with what I had done. Not truly. The satisfaction was hollow. a gilded cage. Also, my relationship with Gwen, once a fascinating experiment in control, was becoming more intimate. Yet, it felt increasingly fake, a hollow echo of genuine connection. Did she truly love me? Or was it merely the lingering effect of my manipulations, the subtle strings I'd woven around her heart? I was in a position where I could marry any woman I wanted, live happily with them at will, as the saying goes. As nice as the thought sounded, I kept wondering how things would have played out had I been more of a normal person, a man unbburdened by this relentless need to control. It was a question that nawed at me, a reminder of the boy I once was before Peter's death hardened me into what I am today. I decided to put that to the test. One day, a foolish indulgence. I walked home with Gwen, a rare moment of manufactured normaly. We stopped in a secluded gazebo in a nearby park and I allowed myself to be drawn into the charade of passion. We kissed and for a fleeting moment I almost believed it. I loved her. Or at least I loved the idea of her, the perfect projection of my desires. She was amazing, everything I'd wanted. But I needed to know if it was real. If any part of this was unblenmished by my touch, there's a way to loosen the threads of my control. a subtle unraveling of the spell. I stopped our kissing session, pulling back just enough to stare deep into Gwen's beautiful blue eyes. My own gaze unwavering, searching for a truth I feared. "What's wrong?" she whispered, her brow furrowed with concern. "This doesn't feel right?" I told her, the words tasting like ash in my mouth. "Am I a bad kisser?" she asked, a flicker of insecurity in her eyes. I shook my head a slow, deliberate movement, and then I spoke my real last name, the name almost no one outside of my family and my most trusted servants truly knew. It was a name that carried a certain weight, a certain immunity to my influence. My fears, my deepest insecurities sprang to life as her expression shifted, the confusion deepening a veil lifting from her eyes. "How do you feel now?" I asked, my voice laced with an uneasiness I rarely allowed myself to betray." She shook her head again, a slow, dawning realization washing over her features. "You're right. Something feels off, but I don't know why." The spell was breaking. The strings were fraying. From there, we grew apart, a slow, agonizing drift. We still dated, spent a lot of time together, in and out of school, but the passion, the manufactured intensity was gone. She tried to act like she was still interested, a pathetic attempt at politeness. But it seemed now that she was just trying not to let me down her sense of obligation, a lingering chain. I'd been so supportive of her now national tennis career, a career I had gifted her. And it seemed she felt obligated to stay with me because of it. It was a familiar pattern, this dependency, one I had seen in others, especially Emma, whose quiet resentment I had to constantly manage to prevent a full betrayal. Our relationship, a fragile construct of my own making, had been a lie. And so I broke it off. It was a quiet breakup, devoid of drama, a testament to the emotional distance between us. She acknowledged it, her eyes vacant, and walked away as though it meant nothing to her. It hurt like hell a sharp, unexpected pang of something I refused to name. But I accepted my decision. I had freed her from my spell, and in doing so, perhaps freed a small part of myself. A few years later, the memory of Gwen had faded almost entirely. Since distancing myself from her, I had also begun distancing myself from my family, from the suffocating influence of their power, and from Chase, my loyal amoral shadow. I hate having this ability to manipulate the world around me so easily, this constant gnawing hunger for control. I've hurt people for my own selfish desires, ruined a couple of lives, all in pursuit of a hollow sense of victory. In my family, such actions are considered normal, even lauded. But I don't want to be like them. I don't want to be the monster they created. This feeling, this internal conflict has been a constant companion since that disastrous auction of secrets. When I realized my manipulations were attracting darker forces, forces that knew too much about my past, threatening to unravel my carefully crafted persona. In spite of this burgeoning moral conflict, this unwelcome introspection, I finally returned to my family's nefarious luxury succeeding my late greatgrandfather, a man whose legacy of ruthless power I was now bound to uphold. I found out recently that Gwen's career is faltering, her ambition dimming once more. And I've been offered the opportunity to come to her rescue again to rekindle the flame to become her personal god of fortune. If I want to, she can still become an international champion. If I want her, she can still become my wife, a perfect plant companion. I can undo my confession to her in that gazebo erased the moment of weakness that shattered her illusion. The thought seductive and dangerous has been a constant companion. I've started checking in on her again discreetly. Of course, whether she's out running errands or relaxing at home, I've had the opportunity to spy on her, to observe her, to re-evaluate her potential as a pawn in my grand design. The more I think about her, the more I want her back in my life. I've been feeling rather lonely lately, despite often being in the company of others. A familiar ache that reminds me of the empty gallery. The profound blow where a deal gone wrong stripped me of my illusions of invincibility. My new butler, Sam, a far less enthusiastic presence than Chase seems quite fond of the idea of bringing her back into my life. I want to see Gwen again. I want to help her become the tennis legend she deserves to be a testament to my power, a living monument to my will. I want to reunite her with her high school sweetheart, Victor Kaine. And perhaps this time I'll truly understand the cost.

transcript.fullText: The door swung open, allowing cool air from the streets outside to blow through the cluttered workshop. A pair of green eyes scanned the entrance, finding the main counter empty save for piles of books and scrap metal. The Orc looked over his shoulder down to his two partners, whose eyes were darting across the room as they fought against the urge to snatch up anything that wasn’t nailed down. “Keep yer mits to yourselves, uh?” Krugor snarled, adjusting the leather strip that kept his Warhammer strapped to his back. Shivering, the two goblins shrank in fear as their boss walked deeper into the room. The door closed behind them, muffling the sounds of the busy streets outside, replaced by a rhythmic thumping that reverberated through the shop. “Anyone here?” the Orc called out, the bass of his voice rattling the loose metal fittings nearby. Suddenly, the sound stopped, leaving the room eerily silent for several seconds before a voice called out from deeper into the building. “Be right there!” Krugor looked back at his minions, who were busy plucking shiny pieces of scrap from the piles and placing them in their pockets. They froze at his gaze, then slowly returned their stolen baubles. Footsteps echoed through the workshop accompanied by creaking wood as the Craftsman rounded a corner and stood behind the counter. The human’s olive skin was shimmering with sweat, which he wiped off with a rag before taking a proper look at his customers. His gray eyebrows furrowed, intrigued by his current customers. A soot-covered hand reflexively stroked his goatee, which still had flecks of brown hair mixed in with the white. “What can I do for you, gentlemen?” the Craftsman asked, making sure to maintain eye contact with the Orc. “Names Krugor,” he started, flashing a confident grin, “Krugor, the Hammer.” The Craftsman waited expectantly for the Orc to continue. “We work for Don Moretti…” Krugor added. Looking into the Craftsman’s eyes, he could see that there was no spark of recognition to the names. “Nice to meet you,” the aged human finally answered, keeping his face devoid of emotion as he continued, “What can I do for you?” The orc cleared his throat, feeling a sense of irritation flow through his body. There was no way the man didn’t know who the local criminal boss was, or at least he had never encountered anyone who didn’t. Taking several steps forward, the orc towered over the shopkeeper, looking down at him before speaking. “My boss needs a construct for the fights, and we hear that you are the best artificer this side of the river,” Krugor explained. The human looked up at him, his aging eyes showing no sign of fear. “While I appreciate the compliment, I don’t make automatons for fighting, and my commissions are closed,” the Craftsman said, crossing his arms as he finished. Krugor’s face contorted as he flashed through several emotions all at once. “Haha,” he laughed, “I like your attitude, old man. You’re a brave one, I’ll give you that. As much as I want to cave your face in with my hammer, my boss made sure to send me plenty of gold for you.” The orc reached to his belt, removing a small brown bag with silk drawstrings and tossing it onto the wooden countertop. Despite the orc’s words, the bag didn’t jingle as it landed. “I told you, my commissions are closed at the-” “Just look in the damn bag already,” Krugor growled, pointing his finger at it. The craftsman reached down and lifted the sack, tugging at the opening until the strings loosened. Looking into it, all he could see was blackness. Confused, he reached his hand inside and felt the familiar surface of cool metal. He removed the hand, bringing with it a fistful of gold. Whimpers of excitement sounded from the two goblins, who were quickly silenced by a raised fist from the orc. Gold light reflected on the craftsman’s face as he inspected the coins. They were real gold alright. As he confirmed their authenticity, he turned the bag upside down, conjuring a stream of gold and gems that piled onto the counter from the mouth of the magical bag. Running his fingers through the pile, he picked up an emerald and looked through its perfectly cut and polished surface. As he inspected it, the Orcs face came into view from within the gem, darkening his already green skin as he took in the human’s reaction. “Is that enough gold to open up your commissions?” Krugor asked, his grin showcasing his sharp canines. The craftsman looked back and forth between the Orc and the pile of treasure for a long moment, allowing the sounds of the busy street outside to creep back in as he pondered. “When do you need it by?” the craftsman asked. *** The craftsman wiped sweat from his brow as he finished pouring the molten metal into its mold. Reaching over to the magical bag, he grabbed another handful of gold and dropped it into the crucible, watching the coins melt into liquid as the imperfections manifested as slag on the surface. He repeated this process several times until he was satisfied with the amount of golden wires he had produced. Moving over to the metal frame lying on his workbench, the armor of the automaton reflected the deep purple of its intricate plating, dwarven dark steel. The Craftsman set to work intertwining the wires together in an intricate network, all leading to one central point where a human heart would be. Reaching into the open chest of the automaton, the craftsman attached the final golden wire to a small unlit furnace resting in the center. He unlatched the slotted door and stared deep into the dark void where its power source would be. Taking in a deep breath, the aged human walked into the back room of his cluttered workshop. Down a dimly lit hallway, he walked past his own bedroom and stood in front of a wooden door. His eyes fixed on the faded brass knob, covered with cobwebs that marked the passing of time since he last entered this room. The craftsman reached out, hesitating slightly as his fingers wrapped around the cold metal. He turned it and pushed the door open. A wave of musty air rushed past him, escaping its prison and allowing for a fresh gust to blow dust across the floor. On the wall next to him, a lantern lit with a cool blue light at his presence, illuminating the room with an eerie aqua aura. The craftsman could feel his stomach churning at the sight of the small bed that sat in the corner of the room, still unmade from the last time its owner had rested on it. Taking his first steps, he made his way over to the foot of the bed where he came to a stop in front of a small wooden chest with copper fittings. Rubbing his hand over the top, he wiped away the dust that settled on the carved lettering. Sam, it read. He ran his fingers over the lettering several times until it was completely clean, building up courage before opening the lid. When he was finally ready, he lifted the latch and opened the chest. Inside was mostly untouched by the passage of time, save for the moth-eaten strips of fabric that remained of some clothing. Reaching inside, the craftsman removed several metallic toys, all of which he hadn't seen in decades. He inspected each one, some were obviously his handiwork, masterfully crafted trinkets that moved when wound up. Then there were others, ones that he knew were made by his son. They were rough, cobbled together with spare parts from his workshop. As he stared down at the assortment of trinkets and toys, the craftsman could feel tears beginning to form in the corners of his eyes. Fighting back against them, he swallowed hard and filled his hands with objects from the chest until he could hold no more. When he finally returned to the workshop, he laid out each memento on the table and stared at the lifeless automaton on his table. He stood from his stool and walked to a large metal cabinet, opening it to reveal a collection of mysterious vials and ores that were neatly organized and labeled. His fingers danced between them until they came to a stop in front of a stone cylinder. Ember of Life, read the paper tag attached by a string. Taking it into his hand, the craftsman returned to his workbench and stood over the automaton’s chest. Unscrewing the top of the container, a flash of heat scorched the air, drying it out as the contents were exposed. Once again, his brow was coated in sweat as he carefully emptied the ember into the open furnace. A shriveled mass of black coal rippled with molten orange flames dropped into the automaton, slowly beating as it expanded to fit its new housing. Streams of lava flowed between the cracks in the coal as it finished its transformation into the crude shape of a human heart. Though it beat rhythmically inside its cage, the craftsman could tell that its flame needed to be fed. Reaching over to his lineup of trinkets, he plucked the first one into his hand and cranked the key. Small wings beat as the tiny thopter tried to lift from his hand and fly around the room. Despite his better judgment, he let go, allowing it to take flight making several circles over his head before fluttering back down. He caught it, remembering the first time he had held it with hands that were far less wrinkled. Closing his eyes, he positioned the toy over the open furnace and dropped it in. Flames roared to life as the cloth wings burned and the metal melted, fueling the heart and causing its beating to become stronger. He continued this process until each of the trinkets was fully consumed by the ember, whose flames were pulsing out of the open chest of the automaton. Using a long set of tongs, he closed the door sealing the fiery beating heart in its cage. Wiping away the sweat, he moved over to the head of his creation, whose face was expressionless despite having masterfully sculpted human features. The craftsman placed his hand on the cold metal of the automaton’s forehead and closed his eyes as he began the incantation. A ghostly blue light emitted from his fingers, quickly reaching across the dark purple surface of the dark steel armor until it was fully encased. As the craftsman chanted, flames erupted from the slits in the furnace door, followed shortly after by an intense golden glow that spread through the tangled wires lining the inside of the metallic body. The craftsman could feel the dark steel surface heating as magic flowed through the circuit and up to the head where it would be completed. When it finally did, the metal eyelids of the automaton fluttered for a moment before opening. Inside the sockets were two metal orbs, intricately crafted to resemble human eyes, and both were filled with the same blue glow of the craftsman’s magic. He stared into the blue orbs of the automaton for a long moment, watching as they blinked several times, like someone who had just woken from a deep dream. “Father?” a flat voice reverberated from the construct’s mouth. Unable to hold back any longer, tears streamed down the craftsman's cheeks, splashing on the hot metal surface of the automaton and slowly evaporating. His chest heaved as sobs overtook the air in the craftsman’s lungs. A warm hand reached up and touched his cheek, wiping away a stream of tears from the old man's face. “What's wrong, father?” the automaton asked, a look of child-like concern on its metallic face. *** Bits of rubble rained down on the audience as the automaton’s fist shattered yet another piece of the stone golem’s body. Cheers erupted from the stands despite the injuries that a few of the watchers sustained, it was part of the experience after all. A fluorescent white light illuminated the circular arena, where the two combatants traded blows once more. The dark armor of the craftsman’s construct showed little damage despite the many hits it had taken during the tournament. On either side of the arena, there were two dugouts each containing the team that controlled and supported the constructs. Behind the stone golem, a blue-robed wizard stood and watched in disbelief as his conjured creature was slowly being turned into rubble. Directly across from him, the craftsman watched with crossed arms as his creation parried a strike from the golem and responded with a solid punch to its center mass. The stone cracked, allowing silver light to seep out of the spaces between, leaking out the magical force that kept the creature together. Sam carefully watched the golem’s movements, anticipating another right hook and preparing himself to deflect it. Despite the lack of need to, he blinked reflexively, and in the second where his metallic eyelids had lowered, the golem’s left arm was already mid-swing. His balance was thrown off by the sudden change in tactics, and the attack connected with his face, sending him rocketing back with his feet still firmly planted. The weight of his body was enough to keep him upright, though the shock of the hit shook his metallic body to its core. Blinking several times, Sam refocused his attention on the opponent, realizing that the left hand of the golem had shattered, further disarming the creature. He could feel the air shifting in the room as the crowd cheered. “SAM! SAM! SAM!” He looked back at the craftsman, his father, and waited for a command. “Finish him!” someone shouted. His father nodded. Sam felt his heartbeat pulsing, the magical flames begging to be released. Clenching his fists, the dark steel began to glow as it heated to temperatures that even rock couldn’t withstand. Lowering his stance, Sam pushed off the ground, the sheer force of his jump leaving a crater in the ground as he barreled toward his target. With the arc of his jump, he could see the expression on the wizard's face turn from worry into terror as his fists made contact with the golem. Each punch shattered more of the enemy's body, and what didn’t fall away was melted down into superheated rock that dripped into piles on the floor. Within seconds, the wizard's conjuration was reduced to slag and rubble. The arena was filled with dust, obscuring the final strike and leaving the crowd quiet as they waited to see the damage. When it finally cleared, the audience erupted into cheers as Sam was announced as the winner. He walked back towards his father, who released the breath he had been holding. “Did I do well, Father?” the metallic voice asked. The craftsman looked up at the towering automaton, the sum of his life's work, and smiled. “You did amazing, Sam. I’m just glad you’re okay,” he said, putting his wrinkled hand on his son’s arm. As the crowd died down, and the arena emptied out, three familiar figures approached them. “Wonderful!” Krugor shouted, clapping his meaty hands together as he cleared the distance between them, “The boss is happy, and the crowd got a great show.” The craftsman shifted his vision from the orc to the two goblin lackeys who were excitedly scanning the ground for fallen coins or mistakenly discarded winning tickets from bets. “Thanks,” he responded, crossing his arms and praying that the conversation would end quickly. Krugor moved closer to Sam, who was still a head taller and several inches wider than the hefty orc. He walked around the automaton several times, inspecting him and knocking on the dwarven dark steel armor. “I have to say, you didn’t disappoint, old man. That's some fine craftsmanship, and the results… Well, they speak for themselves,” he said, gesturing to the arena. Sam watched his father’s eyes, feeling the tension in the conversation building. “Well,” Krugor continued, “We’ll take it from here, the boss wants to have a look at Sam himself, maybe put him to work around the house.” “That’s not going to happen,” the craftsman said with a cold tone, “Sam must stay with me, he needs regular maintenance.” Krugor’s face contorted, it was obvious he wasn’t used to being told “no”. “I don’t think you understand, old man, this thing belongs to the boss. He paid for it, so it’s his,” Krugor informed him, sneering at the craftsman and making sure to show his teeth. “I don’t think you understand,” Sam chimed in, grabbing the Orc’s arm and squeezing it. Krugor’s eyes widened in surprise at the automaton’s voice, accompanied by a wince of pain as Sam’s grip tested the durability of his bones. “I’m staying with my father,” Sam finished, staring at the orc and tightening his grip ever so slightly. “I get it!” Krugor shouted, gritting his teeth as he resisted the urge to pull away. Sam released him, leaving the orc to rub his wounded arm gingerly as he sneered at them. “The boss isn’t gonna like this,” he warned. “Tell your boss whatever you have to, but I’m keeping Sam with me,” the Craftsman said. Looking over to Sam, Krugor weighed his options until his resolve faded. He turned around and began walking towards the exit. “I’ll see you at the next fight,” he said, slapping one of the goblins on the back of the head to catch its attention, “you’re not off the hook just yet.” The arena emptied completely, save for the few crew members who were busy cleaning the stands. Sam and his father exchanged a glance, accompanied by smiles that mirrored one another's. “Let's go home,” the craftsman said, extending his hand out to the automaton. Sam took it, and the two walked the empty streets back toward the workshop.

transcript.fullText: This video will explore the necklace, a short story by Gamopas. Matilda dreamed of a rich, luxurious life, wishing for wealth and status. Despite her dreams, she lived a simple life constrained by her modest circumstances. One day, an important invitation arrived for an exclusive event. The invitation was for a grand ball, a chance for Matilda to momentarily enter the society she longed for. However, she realized with despair that she had no appropriate gown for such an event. Her husband, sacrificing his own plans, gave her money he had saved. With the money, she bought a beautiful, elegant gown. Yet, she still felt incomplete because she had no jewels to match her magnificent dress. Matilda decided to borrow a stunning diamond necklace from a wealthy friend. The necklace complimented her look perfectly and sparkled brilliantly. At the ball, Matild was radiant and captivating. She shone among the other guests. Everyone at the ball admired her and she felt truly beautiful and successful. As Matild prepared to return home after the wonderful evening. She made a terrible discovery. The borrowed necklace was gone. They searched everywhere they could think of but found nothing. To avoid admitting the loss, they decided to replace the necklace secretly. The replacement cost them a fortune, plunging them deep into debt. The couple spent 10 arduous years working hard to pay off their enormous debt. Finally, after a decade of struggle and sacrifice, the debt was completely paid. One day, Matild, aged and worn from her life of toil, met her friend again. She confessed to her friend that she had lost the original necklace and replaced it with an expensive one. Her friend was utterly shocked and stared at Matilda, now looking drastically different. Her friend revealed the shocking truth. The original necklace was merely costume jewelry. The story serves as a tragic reminder that vanity and pride can lead to ruinous and unnecessary costs.

"Oh, my dearest." Ellith reached out to take her sister's hand. Her fair hair was caught back in a golden cirlet. The gown of black leeching all color from her skin until she looked like a ghost. The weeks spent in the elven stronghold after her marriage had made her pale, and the shock of their parents' death only accentuated it. "Will you be?" her voice trailed away. "I'll be well," Alina said, trying to be brave. Her elder sister was worried, as her parents would have been if it had been someone else's death. And Alina did not want anyone to worry over her. It was her parents who deserved sympathy, not she. She was alive and they unexpectedly a wave of anger swamped her. How could they have been so careless as to go riding together near the Freel River at this time of year? The banks were treacherous, the waters rapid and swollen with snow melt, and her parents had brought no one with them, no one at all. For all their years of telling Elith and Alina to be careful, to safeguard themselves as heirs to the throne, their parents had not shown the same caution. What is it?" Elle asked, coming to stand beside her sister. With a start, Elina realized that she had gone to the little altar at the side of the room, and that she was staring at the portraits of her parents, placed there by a friend to help her pay her respects. In the immediate aftermath of their death, she had hardly stirred from her bed for days, thinking that Elith must return and fix this. Elith would know what to do. Elina was only the younger daughter. It was only when Ellith arrived home once more, accompanied by her elven husband, that Elina realized the Cordier's words were true. Elith had seated all claim to the human throne. She would not be able to fix anything. It was up to Alina to lead the country through this shock, a fact that had been made even more brutally clear by the coronation worked into the funeral. "It has always been thus," Ellith said as she put the final touches on Alena's gown. It's barbaric, Alina said simply. A coronation should be a celebration. A coronation needs a death. For a moment, they were just sisters again, bickering. And then they remembered what they were bickering about, and both their faces fell. I can't do this, Alina had pleaded, and Ell took her by the shoulders. You will be a kind queen, a wise queen. I promise you that you can do this. But the panic had not receded as they spoke the final prayers for her parents. And it had not receded as Alina was led to the throne. When the priests settled the heavy crown over her brow, she felt only the rising shity that this must be a dream. "I can't do this," she said again. She looked up at her sister. "Eleith, you must stay. We<unk>ll find a way for you to stay. You'll be queen." "I can't be queen," Ellith said gently. You'll be queen in all but name. They'll accept you. You'll tell me what to do. Alina. Elith turned and took her sister's hands in her own. You are more capable than you know. Do you remember our lessons when we were children? You were always cleverer than me. You thought it so unfair that I would take the throne instead of you. And it was. You knew more about our land and its history than I did. And you always understood trade. A shudder recalled what Alina remembered was Elliot's least favorite topic. Follow your heart, dearest. Take time to think alone, and you will make wise decisions. I wish you could stay. Tears filled Alina's eyes. So do I, dearest, but it is perhaps best that I will not be here. A throne with two heirs is unstable. And you have, oh Alina, tell me you have someone to confide in. at Alena's rofal smile, her sister's gaze sharpened. What is it? Well, it's promise not to be mad. I promise. Elith went to one of the armchairs near the fire and gestured for Alina to take the other, waiting for her sister to sit before she did herself. It was just like Ellie to remember royal etiquette now of all times. You remember Jamoth? Alina asked. It was a rhetorical question. No one could forget Jamoth. As the sole human noble with elven blood, he was one of the most achingly beautiful men Alina had ever seen in her life. Elliot's husband, Savin, was the man's only rival in looks. Jamoth's hair was white blonde, his skin carrying the faintest cast of blue, and his eyes were as piercing and deep as sapphires. And of course, Elith would remember him for another reason as well. Before her marriage to Savin, an alliance forged in desperation against the dragon incursions. Elellith had been betrothed to Jamoth. The two of them, fair and blue-eyed, would have made an almost twin-like pair, and an exceedingly beautiful one at that. "You are," Elliot's brow furrowed, but to Alena's relief, the woman appeared more amused than anything. "You are betrothed to Jamoth." "Oh, no," Alina assured her. No, not that. But he is quite a good adviser. He and I speak often. Yes, he was always very wise, Ellith said, chewing her lip. She frowned. I hope he is not upset that he and I. No, Elina said, smiling. That match was made by neither of you. And frankly, you're both too serious for it to work. Ellie laughed at that and Alina smiled. She had always had an excellent sense of humor, but one that slipped quickly beneath seriousness and urgency. It was a wonder that Savin, as quiet as he was, had brought her to life as he had, but in their quiet camaraderie, the two of them shared amusement as well as love. Alina swallowed, looking away. She did not envy her sister, going to live in a foreign court, being torn from everything she loved so abruptly. But Elifith, if she had nothing else, had love. Against all odds, she and Savin had made a love match, and their companionship filled Alina with jealousy. She had never particularly cared for the idea of marriage. Finding men to be handsome enough, but hardly engaging, only now, now when she must rule, when she must guide a nation, she very much wished she had someone at her side that she might return to at the day's end instead of this empty chamber. "What is it?" Ellith asked and Alina sighed, leaning her crowned head back on the chair. I wish I wish I had what you have. Ellith looked down, her face grave. I know, Elina told her. I know there's no reason to expect it. Before you married, I never would have looked for anything more than a good alliance and simple kindness. I know how royal marriages are made. I never even felt I needed someone. Be careful, Ellie told her, raising those sapphire eyes to stare at her sister. Alina, you are grieving and you will be vulnerable to those who claim to have all the answers. There will be people who will try to manipulate you, try to make you believe you cannot live without them. I know, Molina said, nettled. I am not a fool. Not in the slightest, dearest, but you are human and you are alone. Are you telling me to be wary of Jamoth? Alina asked, her voice very small. I don't think so. All I ask, little sister, is that you listen to your heart. It has never led you astray yet, has it? Remember when we saw the fairies that one day out near the river? I wanted to chase them, but you pulled me back and tore my dress. And you were right. They were leading us to a fairy circle, and we would never have gotten home again. Promise me. Promise me that no matter how bad it gets, how lonely you feel, how sure of themselves others seem to be, you will not let them rule this country instead of you. I will, I will try. But something in Elliot's urgency scared her. What is it? What do you fear? I Ellith stood pacing, her arms wrapped around herself. Elina, I think I am going mad sometimes, but others it seems clear as day. Mother and father would never have been so careless as to ride at the river without a guard. They would never have ridden there at all. You and I both know it. Oh gods. Alina stood. You can't think. I don't know what to think. Elliot's voice rose and she turned away. It is madness that speaks to me. It is grief. But Elina, please be careful. You were always cleverer than me. Be wise now. When a knock sounded at the door, they both jumped, but it was only Savin sticking his black head around the door. His eyes flicked between them, taking in Elliot's tempest of emotion and Alena's rising fear, but he said nothing about it, only slid into the room. Sister-in-law, he said gravely to Alina, your majesty, I fear I must call Elith away. Alina nodded. Before she had wondered how she could bear to be alone with few friends. Now at the thought of Elith leaving, her wondering had turned to a pit of cold despair. She must not go. She must stay and give Elena counsel. But Elith was needed. Ellith had been sent to her own court alone as well, and she had found something beautiful there. Elina smiled wly at the sight of her sister arm-in- arm with Savin. It was impossible to begrudge them the happiness they clearly shared. Be wise, her sister's words echoed in her head as Alina climbed the battlements and watched them ride away on the long road out of Terrestra. Follow your heart. The advice should make her feel hope. So why did she feel as if she was so terribly alone? Chapter 2. Promises have been made, your majesty, one of the counselors protested. His black robes flapped around him in the breeze from the windows. No, they haven't," Alina pointed out. "Not by me." In any case, there was an uncomfortable silence, and she tried her hardest not to look uncertain as she stared the counselors down. They looked at one another, men and women with old, pinched faces, and the sort of sneer that said they thought Alina was young and impressionable. The fact that the snears were beginning to turn into looks of weariness filled Alina with equal parts satisfaction and trepidation. They should learn not to underestimate her, she thought firmly. They were her counselors and they advised her, but she was their queen and she made the decisions. Surely they had never questioned her father and mother as they questioned her. But your majesty, one of them said now, her tone suddenly ingratiating. Surely you must agree that selling our grain within our borders is the best plan of action. The farmers agree. If the farmers agree, then there should be no trouble with my lifting the trade embargos, Alina pointed out coolly. But it troubles me that our farmers would rather sell within the country for much lower prices than trade with neighboring kingdoms. She tried to refrain from sighing and rubbing at her forehead. It was a beautiful day outside, and she wished she were out riding with Jamoth instead of stuck in this room arguing with the people who were supposed to support her. Have regional relations grown tense? There is some resentment between the ice elves and terrestra. Yes. I've never heard mention of it. Elina met the counselor's eyes steadily. No doubt your ah yes, your father would not have wanted to worry you. My father and mother, Elina said, trying not to grip the arms of the chair too obviously were always more interested in trade than they were in war. Was it just her imagination or did dislike skitter across the faces of her counselors? Your parents, one of them began, and another shushed him. He gave what was ostensibly a smile, but looked more like a grimace. I see, Alina said, looking around at all of them. Well, thank you for your counsel. I shall think on this. And should we tell the troops to march to the western border? One of the counselors asked smoothly. First you mention trade, then some resentment, then ask me about sending our soldiers. What is it that is happening on the western border? Nothing you need concern yourself with, your majesty. If I'm sending my troops, Alina snapped. I will indeed be concerned. There was a stony silence. Your majesty is wise to approach the decision with such gravity, one of them said finally, bowing low so that Alina could not see his face. We are certain that you will make the correct decision. Thank you, Alina said with as much warmth as she could muster. Something told her that this assurance was far from sincere. Now, if you will excuse me, I must tour the outlying holdings. Your majesty, there is one more matter. A woman spoke up from the corner of the room. Yes, please let her not sound like a petulant child. Alina wanted only to flee, but she knew she must not let them think she was frivolous or lazy. The matter of your majesty's marriage, the counselor said. Ah. Alina smiled. This she would stay for a friend, a confidant, someone she could trust to hold Terrestra's interests in as high a stead as she did. Counselors were all well and good, but her mother had once told her that only those who wore the crown could truly understand the weight of it. She was glad to see now that her council wanted her married. I will count on all of you to submit your recommendations to me. Then surely you all have valuable insights regarding the eligible noblemen of our kingdom. She had meant it to soothe them, for she knew that the choice of a consort was often a fraught endeavor, pitting regional and family alliances against one another. She expected her counselors to leap forward with their suggestions, denigrating each other's choices, but to her surprise, the council was remarkably reserved. "One such gentleman will arrive at court shortly," the woman said, smiling. "Gareth of Vestin, he has come to pay his respects to your majesty on your ascension to the throne. Better he had come to her coronation to pay his respects to her parents' reign." But Elina did not say that. I will rely upon you to look at his credentials and character and arrange a meeting, she said, favoring the woman with a smile. One must always show the greatest respect for a counselor's opinion, and the rest of you must submit your recommendations to me as well. You are all dismissed. Blessings upon your majesty. But their chorus was more subdued than she would have expected, calm and entirely without the animated conflict that often accompanied their exit from her presence. Alina watched them go, frowning, and then shook her head and stroed purposefully out onto the battlements. The council chambers were situated for the best view of the soul road leading into the castle, so that the counselors might assess any invading force at a glance. But it had been years since Terrestra went to war. And in any case, Alina could hardly think of such matters today. The weather was perfect, the late spring air holding the promise of summer's heat, and Alina had been looking forward to the day's ride all week. She smiled as she descended the steep stairs to the courtyard, nodding to pay her respects to the soldiers who climbed past her with crisp salutes and murmured blessings. When she was in the council chamber, surrounded by reports of problems and discontent, she worried that she was a very poor ruler indeed. But when she saw her subjects, she noticed that they smiled at her without reserve. Perhaps she thought she should ask them what they thought of war with the ice elves. All thoughts disappeared, however, when she saw Jamoth waiting. His white blonde hair had been drawn back into an ornate braid, another nod to his elven heritage, and his clothes, though simply cut, were of the finest deep blue silks and velvets, making his eyes shine brightly in his beautiful face. "You look very fine today," she said with a smile, noting that the pale blue of her own gown was complimented by his attire. "Your majesty is kind," he told her, bowing. "And I do not wish to shame her as I ride through the farms with her." Alina laughed and let him swing her up into the saddle of her horse, a rone marare whose coat had been brushed until it gleamed. It is I who always have dust on my hem and my hair escaping its braid. I should think I would shame you. Never, he assured her. You are the queen, and to your subjects you shine as brightly as the sun. It was the oversweet flattery of courtly love, the sort of flirtation that every courtier engaged in, and Alina had never put much stalk by it. But when Jamoth spoke, no matter the nonsensical words, she heard true kindness in his tone. Tell me, she said as they set off, is it true that there is war brewing in the west? Or Jameth looked over at her, his brow furrowed. I have heard no such rumors. Neither had I, and yet my council tells me to send troops. Can it possibly be so bad? I shouldn't think so, Elena said, examining the earliest spring planting and waving to the farmers. She looked over at Jamoth and frowned. It seems to me that if it were serious enough to send troops, I would already know, and if not, sending troops can hardly improve things. And more to the point, where are these troops coming from? He asked, frowning back. Aren't most of ours still training at Alpha? I hadn't even thought of that. Alina rubbed her forehead, then recalled that she was in plain sight of her subjects. There was a silence so long that she looked over and found him staring away from her. At length, he said simply, "Oh, yes. Their first candidate is arriving soon, I hear." Gareth of Veston. I'm not sure I know him. Has he been to court before? Is he terribly old? Gareth of Veston. You know him? Alina asked eagerly. I Jamoth now looked profoundly troubled. We trained together for some years. Sword fighting history, that sort of thing. You don't like him, Elena observed. It's not Well, I haven't seen him since he was 15. The lords of Veston rarely venture out of their stronghold. But there have always been rumors, you see. They say every once in a while that Veston was once its own country, conquered in the name of Terrestra, and that as kings in their own right, they should have equal claim to the throne. What? Alina drew her horse up and stared at him. And my counselors want me to marry this man. He was only a boy when he said such things, Jameth assured her. Perhaps he is different now. Perhaps. Alina shook her head, then brightened. Perhaps they wish to do away with the bad feelings of other generations. They want Veston to know that it is valued and it would give them the troops they need. Jamoth murmured. Veston controls an army nearly the size of yours. I Alina. He looked over at her then blushed. Your majesty I apologize your majesty. He is but one suitor. My laughter froze in my throat. "Did anyone else see that?" I asked, pointing to behind that door. "They didn't even look." My mom waved me off. "Stop being silly," she said, her voice light, but her eyes didn't meet mine. My sister chuckled nervously, but she stayed glued to her phone. I stared harder, my heart pounding. The hand was gone. Maybe I was imagining things. Minutes later, the lights flickered. "Must be the storm," Dad said, getting up to check the circuit box. But before he could leave the room, the electricity cut out completely, plunging us into pitch black. "Stay here," he instructed. But his voice had a trimmer he couldn't hide. That's when we all saw it. Opening the door and stepping out, faintly illuminated by the moonlight, was the giant hand. It spread wide, its long, skeletal fingers tapping the floor as though testing its strength. The room fell silent. None of us could speak. None of us could move. The hand moved down, disappearing beneath the floor itself. and he was in the middle among us screaming with a small head compared to his hands and a body with holes resting on our living room's floor. I don't remember much of what happened next. Screaming, the sound of breaking furniture, the deafening thud of something massive moving in the dark. When I woke up, the world felt wrong. Even the trees at the end of the street stood still, their leaves quiet as though they too were listening to the silence. The whole night felt as if it had slowed to meet you. At the very end of this lane stood the house. Been here longer than the stories about it, long enough that the wood in its beams had darkened to a deep, steady brown, long enough for its tiled roof to have glistened under more seasons than anyone could count. Its upper windows were small and round like watchful eyes. The glass thick and faintly wavy with age. Tonight those eyes glowed faintly, holding a warmth that felt more like a welcome than a light. The front steps were narrow but firm under your feet. When you crossed the threshold, the night seemed to pause and hold itself behind you. Your shoes found the wood of the hallway floor, smooth in some spots, gently uneven in others, marked by the footsteps of countless nights before this one. The hallway was narrow but not tight. A quiet passage lined with walls the color of honey in the lamplight. Only one lamp burned here, a brass one resting on a small side table. Its circle of glow reached halfway to the walls, letting the edges of the hall dissolve into soft shadow. Somewhere beyond that dimness, a sound found your ear. A creek from above. The wood was smooth, its edges rounded from years of use, its surface cool under your palm. You began to climb. Each step greeted you with a different note.
