transcript.preview: When you grow up in a developing country like India, as I did, you instantly learn to get more value from limited resources and find creative ways to reuse what you already have. Take Mansukh Prajapat
transcript.fullText: When you grow up in a developing country like India, as I did, you instantly learn to get more value from limited resources and find creative ways to reuse what you already have. Take Mansukh Prajapati, a potter in India. He has created a fridge made entirely of clay that consumes no electricity. He can keep fruits and vegetables fresh for many days. That's a cool invention, literally. In Africa, if you run out of your cell phone battery, don't panic. You will find some resourceful entrepreneurs who can recharge your cell phone using bicycles. And since we are in South America, let's go to Lima in Peru, a region with high humidity that receives only one inch of rainfall each year. An engineering college in Lima designed a giant advertising billboard that absorbs air humidity and converts it into purified water, generating over 90 liters of water every day. The Peruvians are amazing. They can literally create water out of thin air. For the past seven years, I have met and studied hundreds of entrepreneurs in India, China, Africa and South America, and they keep amazing me. Many of them did not go to school. They don't invent stuff in big R&D labs. The street is the lab. Why do they do that? Because they don't have the kind of basic resources we take for granted, like capital and energy, and basic services like healthcare and education are also scarce in those regions. When external resources are scarce, you have to go within yourself to tap the most abundant resource, human ingenuity, and use that ingenuity to find clever ways to solve problems with limited resources. In India, we call it Jugaad. Jugaad is a Hindi word that means an improvised fix, a clever solution born in adversity. Jugaad solutions are not sophisticated or perfect, but they create more value at lower cost. For me, the entrepreneurs who will create Jugaad solutions are like alchemists. They can magically transform adversity into opportunity, and turn something of less value into something of high value. In other words, they mastered the art of doing more with less, which is the essence of frugal innovation. Frugal innovation is the ability to create more economic and social value using fewer resources. Frugal innovation is not about making do; it's about making things better. Now I want to show you how, across emerging markets, entrepreneurs and companies are adopting frugal innovation on a larger scale to cost-effectively deliver healthcare and energy to billions of people who may have little income but very high aspirations. Let's first go to China, where the country's largest I.T. service provider, Neusoft, has developed a telemedicine solution to help doctors in cities remotely treat old and poor patients in Chinese villages. This solution is based on simple-to-use medical devices that less qualified health workers like nurses can use in rural clinics. China desperately needs these frugal medical solutions because by 2050 it will be home to over half a billion senior citizens. Now let's go to Kenya, a country where half the population uses M-Pesa, a mobile payment solution. This is a great solution for the African continent because 80 percent of Africans don't have a bank account, but what is exciting is that M-Pesa is now becoming the source of other disruptive business models in sectors like energy. Take M-KOPA, the home solar solution that comes literally in a box that has a solar rooftop panel, three LED lights, a solar radio, and a cell phone charger. The whole kit, though, costs 200 dollars, which is too expensive for most Kenyans, and this is where mobile telephony can make the solution more affordable. Today, you can buy this kit by making an initial deposit of just 35 dollars, and then pay off the rest by making a daily micro-payment of 45 cents using your mobile phone. Once you've made 365 micro-payments, the system is unlocked, and you own the product and you start receiving clean, free electricity. This is an amazing solution for Kenya, where 70 percent of people live off the grid. This shows that with frugal innovation what matters is that you take what is most abundant, mobile connectivity, to deal with what is scarce, which is energy. With frugal innovation, the global South is actually catching up and in some cases even leap-frogging the North. Instead of building expensive hospitals, China is using telemedicine to cost-effectively treat millions of patients, and Africa, instead of building banks and electricity grids, is going straight to mobile payments and distributed clean energy. Frugal innovation is diametrically opposed to the way we innovate in the North. I live in Silicon Valley, where we keep chasing the next big technology thing. Think of the iPhone 5, 6, then 7, 8. Companies in the West spend billions of dollars investing in R&D, and use tons of natural resources to create ever more complex products, to differentiate their brands from competition, and they charge customers more money for new features. So the conventional business model in the West is more for more. But sadly, this more for more model is running out of gas, for three reasons: First, a big portion of customers in the West because of the diminishing purchasing power, can no longer afford these expensive products. Second, we are running out of natural water and oil. In California, where I live, water scarcity is becoming a big problem. And third, most importantly, because of the growing income disparity between the rich and the middle class in the West, there is a big disconnect between existing products and services and basic needs of customers. Do you know that today, there are over 70 million Americans today who are underbanked, because existing banking services are not designed to address their basic needs. The prolonged economic crisis in the West is making people think that they are about to lose the high standard of living and face deprivation. I believe that the only way we can sustain growth and prosperity in the West is if we learn to do more with less. The good news is, that's starting to happen. Several Western companies are now adopting frugal innovation to create affordable products for Western consumers. Let me give you two examples. When I first saw this building, I told myself it's some kind of postmodern house. Actually, it's a small manufacturing plant set up by Grameen Danone, a joint venture between Grameen Bank of Muhammad Yunus and the food multinational Danone to make high-quality yogurt in Bangladesh. This factory is 10 percent the size of existing Danone factories and cost much less to build. I guess you can call it a low-fat factory. Now this factory, unlike Western factories that are highly automated, relies a lot on manual processes in order to generate jobs for local communities. Danone was so inspired by this model that combines economic efficiency and social sustainability, they are planning to roll it out in other parts of the world as well. Now, when you see this example, you might be thinking, "Well, frugal innovation is low tech." Actually, no. Frugal innovation is also about making high tech more affordable and more accessible to more people. Let me give you an example. In China, the R&D engineers of Siemens Healthcare have designed a C.T. scanner that is easy enough to be used by less qualified health workers, like nurses and technicians. This device can scan more patients on a daily basis, and yet consumes less energy, which is great for hospitals, but it's also great for patients because it reduces the cost of treatment by 30 percent and radiation dosage by up to 60 percent. This solution was initially designed for the Chinese market, but now it's selling like hotcakes in the U.S. and Europe, where hospitals are pressured to deliver quality care at lower cost. But the frugal innovation revolution in the West is actually led by creative entrepreneurs who are coming up with amazing solutions to address basic needs in the U.S. and Europe. Let me quickly give you three examples of startups that personally inspire me. The first one happens to be launched by my neighbor in Silicon Valley. It's called gThrive. They make these wireless sensors designed like plastic rulers that farmers can stick in different parts of the field and start collecting detailed information like soil conditions. This dynamic data allows farmers to optimize use of water energy while improving quality of the products and the yields, which is a great solution for California, which faces major water shortage. It pays for itself within one year. Second example is Be-Bound, also in Silicon Valley, that enables you to connect to the Internet even in no-bandwidth areas where there's no wi-fi or 3G or 4G. How do they do that? They simply use SMS, a basic technology, but that happens to be the most reliable and most widely available around the world. Three billion people today with cell phones can't access the Internet. This solution can connect them to the Internet in a frugal way. And in France, there is a startup calle Compte Nickel, It allows thousands of people to walk into a Mom and Pop store and in just five minutes activate the service that gives them two products: an international bank account number and an international debit card. They charge a flat annual maintenance fee of just 20 Euros. That means you can do all banking transactions -- send and receive money, pay with your debit card -- all with no additional charge. This is what I call low-cost banking without the bank. Amazingly, 75 percent of the customers using this service are the middle-class French who can't afford high banking fees. Now, I talked about frugal innovation, initially pioneered in the South, now being adopted in the North. Ultimately, we would like to see developed countries and developing countries come together and co-create frugal solutions that benefit the entire humanity. The exciting news is that's starting to happen. Let's go to Nairobi to find that out. Nairobi has horrendous traffic jams. When I first saw them, I thought, "Holy cow." Literally, because you have to dodge cows as well when you drive in Nairobi. To ease the situation, the engineers at the IBM lab in Kenya are piloting a solution called Megaffic, which initially was designed by the Japanese engineers. Unlike in the West, Megaffic doesn't rely on roadside sensors, which are very expensive to install in Nairobi. transcript.fullText: I would like to begin my presentation to you with a proposal. A proposal of a new Adinkra symbol. Now, to all those who do not know what an Adinkra symbol is, they are ancient symbols carved by the Akans, an ethnic group in Ghana. They gained their attraction and stood the test of time by their ability to convey complex thoughts and philosophical ideas through seemingly simple symbols. Let's take the Sankofa for example. This signifies learning from the past. The bird's posture illustrates the balance between looking back and moving forward. Where Sankofa literally translates from Twi to "Go back and get it." acquiring and learning from experiences of the past. Now, my Adinkra symbol is the Intsira seed. The Intsira seed represents creativity stemmed from a human spark. Its design would entail a small seed icon with an inner spiral representing experience. This would then be surrounded by irregular halos representing unexpected connections. It would then be dotted in constellations representing individuality. All in all, this symbol would signify that creativity stems from lived experiences. Now, before any questions are asked or any ideas of outreach are formulated on how I, a 20-year-old biomedical science student, could possibly create an Adinkra symbol. This was made entirely out of AI. Of course, it seems preposterous. The capacity of AI to recreate a deep-seated aspect of our Akan culture. When in the past, elders would have journeyed, convened, and deliberated, and discussed these ideas at length. They would have observed the natural and connected to theoretical ideas, and created symbols much like the Sankofa. Where this long creative process and melding of ideas was simplified to a simple prompt in ChatGPT asking for a few new Adinkra symbols, and I simply chose my favorite. Of course, it doesn't reduce its ingenuity or its ability, much like the elders of the past, to condense complex thoughts and philosophical ideas. But, it changes how we feel about it. And that is how AI affects art. It would be naive of me to discuss AI without addressing its numerous benefits to society. AI is being democratized, and its uses in many industries are being uncovered as the days go by. The benefits of AI are boundless. According to PwC, AI has the ability to contribute an astounding $15.7 trillion to the global economy by 2030. According to the Cancer Research Institute, AI has far-reaching impact in early cancer detection. Even in education, AI has the capacity to increase teachers' efficiency, giving them the ability to tailor lessons to each child's unique needs, in turn, increasing accessibility. What are impacts of AI in the creative industry are a little bit more complex. AI has the ability, no undoubtedly, to increase creativity through its enormous capabilities unconfined by the constraints of the human mind. But it diminishes core properties of what it means to create. Ironically, Gemini AI defines art as the expression of human skill and imagination in many forms. So, how then can AI create art? Let's look at art like this, in simple demand and supply. The limited supply of art is what has originally incited its demand. The time, the effort, and the intellectual capacity that goes into making meaningful art has made it rare and incredibly difficult to reproduce. Art's impact is driven by its ability to evoke emotion, to connect individuals through the sharing of lived experiences. Because the value that an artist gives his art is deeply intrinsic, and so is its attributed meaning. So, the fact that I used ChatGPT to make my Adinkra symbol didn't make it any less clever, but its value depreciated to you because of the respect that you attribute to human ingenuity. But does this mean that AI, the creative process can be simplified to the process that it takes to create it? No. But its value is dependent on you. And generally, as human beings and the social creatures that we are, we respect creativity and human ingenuity. And in the current AI climate, human ingenuity is highly valued and adds astounding value to our work as I hope I've been able to successfully demonstrate to you today. Now, we are nowhere near the full capabilities of AI where it would be able to seamlessly create on our behalf without a little push of human creativity. Where the description of my Adinkra symbol was very impressive, the image generated is quite disappointing. But, not for long. In a few years, AI's creative capacity will be a marvel and nearly undetectable. And in a market soon to be saturated with AI art, you will be highly valued. So, I ask us to be mindful of our mental investments in our creations. Do not lose the human ingenuity birth in the creative process to the efficiency of AI. To use AI as a tool to expand our creativity, not to create on our behalf. Thank you very much.

transcript.fullText: The story begins with me, Bryce Shapiro. At 34, I was a police officer in Millbrook Falls, Montana, a small town near the Canadian border with a population of around 4,000. Life here was usually uneventful, but 3 weeks ago, on October 17th, everything changed. My partner, Damon Cabrera, and I responded to a 911 call that ended with Damon dead and me undergoing a psychiatric evaluation. No one believes my account, not the captain, not the investigators, and certainly not Damon's widow. They think I lost my mind, that the trauma of witnessing my best friend's murder shattered my reality. The psychiatrist has labeled me with acute stress disorder and wants to prescribe medication and therapy three times a week. But what he refuses to accept is that something inhuman took Damon's life. I was there, and I'll spend the rest of my life seeking the truth, no matter the cost. Let me take you back to that fateful night. It started like any other shift. My chest ached from healing scars, my hands trembled from the adrenaline crash, and my clothes reeked of smoke and burnt flesh. Yet, I felt something I hadn't felt in weeks, purpose. Instead of going home, I drove straight to the police station. Captain Kuroki was immersed in paperwork when I knocked. His surprise shifted to concern. Bryce, you look terrible. What happened? I found it, I replied. The thing that killed Damon. I found it, and I killed it. Kuroki set down his pen slowly. Bryce, there's a body, sort of remains, at the old Hendrix Mill. You should send a team to document everything. What did you do? My job, the job you wouldn't let me do. I showed him the photos I'd taken, the creature before, during the burning, and after reduced to ash. He stared at the images, his face paling. Jesus Christ, he breathed. What is that thing? Exactly what I told you, not human, not animal, something else. Something that's been killing people in this region for 300 years. I pulled out my research, historical accounts, murder patterns, journal entries, all of it. It's real, all of it. And there are more. The creature warned me, others like it are still out there, still hunting. Kiroki studied the evidence for a long time, then turned his gaze toward me. You killed this creature. Yes. Illegally, using stolen military gear while on leave. Yes. I should arrest you, permanently suspend you, maybe even charge you with multiple violations. Probably. He paused, then closed the folder and returned it to me. I didn't see this, he said. You were never here. We never had this conversation. Captain. I believe you, Bryce. I really do. But if I put this in a report, you'll be committed, and whatever killed Damon will remain an unknown assailant. Is that what you want? No. Then take this evidence and keep it to yourself. Keep hunting, but do it discreetly, off the books. And please, no more military equipment. He stood, extending his hand. Damon would be proud of you. I hope you know that. I shook his hand. Thank you, Captain. Don't thank me. Just be cautious. If more of those things exist, you'll need help, resources, information. I'll find it. As I turned to leave, I paused at the door. There's a name, Helsing. A family of hunters who have fought these things for generations. If I can connect with them, I might not have to do this alone. Kiroki nodded. Good luck. I went home and slept for 16 hours straight in blissful darkness. When I woke, I brewed coffee and sat at my kitchen table with Van Helsing's card in my laptop. The phone number was disconnected, but there had to be other ways to find them. Other Helsings, other hunters. I began my search, not for the creatures this time, but for those who fought them. After 3 days of digging, I found a reference in a niche European forum about folklore. Someone asking about countermeasures against anthropophagus entities. Most responses were jokes, but one stood out, clinical, detailed, signed simply VH. I messaged the user explaining who I was and what I'd done. 3 hours later, I got a reply. "Meet me at the Railroad Diner, Helena, Montana, Friday, 2:00 00 p.m. Come alone. Bring proof." I stared at the message, weighing the possibilities. It could be a trap, or it could be my chance for connection, knowledge, and purpose. I typed back, "I'll be there." Friday dawned cold and clear. I drove 2 hours to Helena, armed with my research folder and photos from Hendrick's Mill. The Railroad Diner was a small, mostly empty spot on the outskirts of town at 2:00 00 p.m. I entered, scanning the room. In a back booth sat a man in his 60s, gray hair, weathered face, eyes that had seen too much. He sipped his coffee and read a newspaper, but I could tell he noticed me the moment I walked in. "Van Helsing?" I approached. He looked up, studied me, then gestured to the seat across from him. "Bryce Shapiro." He stated, not asking. "How did you?" "I've been tracking the incidents at Hickory Ridge Road and the kill at Hendrick's Mill. Impressive work for a first-timer." He set down his newspaper. "Most who encounter these creatures don't survive. Those who do spend their lives convincing themselves it wasn't real. You're different. I killed the one who murdered my partner. Yes, I saw the remains. Well done. He took a sip of coffee, but know this, killing one doesn't end the threat. There are dozens, possibly hundreds across the continent, all ancient and feeding. The creature told me before it died. Did it try to bargain, offer information for mercy? Yes. And you refused? Yes. Hellsing smiled slightly. Good. They're liars. Everything they say is designed to manipulate. The moment you show mercy is when they strike. He slid a folder across the table. This is everything my family has compiled over generations. Confirmed activity locations, effective methods, weapon specifications, historical patterns. I opened the folder, dozens of pages, photographs of creatures similar to the one I had killed. There's more than one species. More than one strain. All are technically the same, but evolved differently based on their feeding grounds. The one you killed was a heart eater. There are also blood drinkers, bone crushers, soul stealers. Different methods, same result. They feed on human life. How do I find them? You don't, not initially. You study, learn, and prepare. Going after these things unprepared is a gamble. You got lucky once. Luck doesn't last. Then teach me. Hellsing regarded me thoughtfully, then nodded. My family has been doing this for over 300 years. We have resources, knowledge, and contacts. We can teach you to be a proper hunter, but it's not a life. It's an existence. You'll lose everything else, relationships, normalcy, safety. Once you start down this path, there's no turning back. I thought of Damon, of his heart in that creature's claws, and the woman on Hickory Ridge Road, about 300 years of victims screaming. "I'm already on this path," I replied. "I just need to know where it leads." Helsing smiled, a genuine smile this time. "Then welcome to the hunt, Mr. Shapiro. Let's get you properly trained." He raised his coffee cup in a toast. "To the ones we've lost and to the ones we'll save." I clinked my cup against his. "To Damon." "To Damon," Helsing echoed. For the first time in 3 weeks, I felt something other than grief and rage. I felt hope. The creatures had hunted humans for centuries. Now, finally, we were going to hunt them back. The end.

A bone deep chill that had nothing to do with the night air crept up his spine. Following the letters instructions, Adweight made his way to the westernmost room. His flashlight beam cut through the gloom, dancing over dustcovered furniture and faded portraits that seemed to watch his every move. He ran his hand along the cold stone wall. There it was, a hollow sound. With trembling hands, he worked a loose brick free. Adwight's heart pounded in his chest as he opened it. The first line sent a shiver down his spine. If you're reading this, I might not be alive anymore. It was Vikram Seth's diary. Page by page, it revealed a tale of betrayal. Vikram wrote of his suspicions about his wife, Nana, and their loyal servant. Ragu, they're hiding something. One entry read, "Last night, I saw them meeting a stranger in the basement. My money, my entire fortune is being siphoned abroad under my own name. The final entry was a gut punch. I have all the evidence I need to expose them. Vikram had written his handwriting growing frantic. But tonight, Nina gave me a glass of milk. It had a strange bitter taste. I feel so sleepy. But I have a terrible feeling I won't wake up again. Vikram Sethi hadn't taken his own life. He had been murdered. Suddenly, a floorboard creaked behind him and weight spun around, his hand instinctively going for his weapon. Standing in the doorway, wreathed in shadows, was Ragu, the servant. His face was a mask of sorrow and fear. You shouldn't have come here, Ragu whispered, his voice. Some things are better left buried. Let the dead rest. Ragu then held out a weathered envelope. This was Vikram's last letter. He explained adit shaking toito pen called. It was the exact same letter he had received earlier that night. The same words, the same handwriting. It was impossible. This meant the letter that brought him here was sent by the ghost of Vikram Sethi. At that exact moment, a deafening crack of thunder shook the Havi. The lights flickered and died. When they came back on, Ragu was gone, vanished. At wait, turned back to the wall, and there, where the diary had been, words were glowing with a faint ethereal light. The truth is out now. I can rest. As Adwait walked out of the ancient mansion, leaving the darkness behind, he glanced back one last time. In the window of the western room, a single small lamp had lit itself, its warm glow, a lonely vigil in the night. Was it truly the work of a restless spirit seeking justice? Or just an elaborate game born from a guilty conscience? Add weight didn't have the answer, but he knew one thing for sure. The Rasher Havily had finally given up its secret. What do you think? Was it a ghost or was there a more human explanation? Let me know your theories in the comments below. transcript.fullText: This video is based on the short story After 20 Years by O'Henry. It was a cold night on a quiet street. A policeman walked his beat, keeping watch over the area. A man stood in a doorway, his cigar unlit. He waited for a friend, a man named Jimmy. They had promised to meet again 20 years after they said goodbye. It was 20 years later at the same place where they had parted ways. The man told the policeman about his friend. "Jimmy was my best friend," he continued. We grew up here like brothers, the man explained. But I went west to make my fortune, he added. Jimmy stayed here. He didn't want to leave New York. The man finished his story. Tonight we meet again. The policeman walked on and minutes passed for the waiting man. Soon footsteps came closer. A second man stopped and the waiting man asked, "Bob?" The other man, who was a policeman, asked, "Jimmy?" The two men shook hands, glad to see each other after so many years. As they walked down the street, Bob bragged about his fortune in the West. The two men, Bob and the second man, walked down the street together. Under a bright electric light, the second man stopped and looked closely at Bob. The man said, "You're not Jimmy. Jimmy never was this tall." The second man then said, "I'm a detective and you're under arrest." He explained that Jimmy recognized Bob from a wanted poster. Jimmy couldn't arrest his old friend himself, so he sent the detective. The detective handed Bob a note from Jimmy. Bob read the note slowly, his dreams broken. The note said Jimmy was the first policeman he talked to, but he couldn't do the arrest.

transcript.fullText: In the heart of Chicago, where the L trains rattle overhead and the glow of street lights barely cuts through the smog, the city hums with secrets. Most folks talk about the monsters out in the wild. Bears in Yellowstone, cougars in the Rockies, but the real terrors, they're right here, slinking through the alleys, hiding under overpasses, watching from the shadows of abandoned lots. For every hiker lost in the backwoods, three vanish on these streets. And not all of them are mugged or kidnapped. Some meet things that don't belong in this world. Ask the people who live on the margins, the homeless guy muttering on Michigan Avenue, the woman pushing a cart down Clark Street. They'll tell you about tongues that snatch bodies into sewers, kids with eyes too old for their faces, shadows that choke you with tar. Most call them crazy, but they're not. They've seen the truth, and it's getting worse. This is the story of Amelia Meager, a girl whose name was on every TV screen in the city. 16, blonde, blue-eyed, the kind of face that stops traffic when it's plastered on a missing poster. She disappeared from a loop street one Tuesday night right outside a Starbucks buzzing with late night commuters. No trace, no witnesses, just gone. Her parents begged on the evening news, her picture haunted billboards and Chicago held its breath. A week dragged by, hope fading like a cigarette's ember. It was a muggy August night when Mike Carter, a bartender at a dive bar off Wabash, stumbled into the dark heart of this nightmare. Mike was 24, cocky with a buzz from too many whisies and a bruised ego after striking out with a girl at closing time. The streets were quiet, the kind of quiet that makes your skin crawl, like the city's holding its breath. He cut through a shortcut under the I90 overpass. The concrete looming above like a tombstone. The air smelled of piss and diesel, and the only sound was the distant screech of a train. Then a voice, soft, trembling, a woman's. Help me. It came from the shadows under the overpass where the street lights didn't reach. Mike stopped dead. his heart kicking up a notch. At 2:00 a.m., you don't answer random calls in Chicago's underbelly. But this voice, it was scared, desperate, and Mike, half drunk and half horny, couldn't resist playing hero. "Who's there?" he called, peering into the dark. The overpass swallowed his voice, the echo twisting into something hollow. Nothing moved, but the air felt heavier, like it was pressing down on him. "I'm lost," the voice answered closer. "Now it was off, though, too flat, like someone reading a script they didn't understand." Mike's gut churned, but he stepped closer, his sneakers crunching on broken glass. The shadows seemed to pulse, alive with something he couldn't name. "Where are you at?" he said, his Chicago accent thick, his eyes straining. A faint rustle answered, "Not footsteps, but something dragging slow and deliberate, like a sack pulled across concrete." His pulse hammered, but he didn't back down. Come out where I can see you." The darkness stirred and a shape took form. A white sundress, dirty and torn, glowed faintly against the black like a ghost in a photograph. The figure was small, fragile, but her face was hidden in shadow. Mike's breath hitched. Something about her felt familiar, like a memory he couldn't grab. "I'm right here," the voice said, now just feet away. The figure drifted forward, the dress swaying as if caught in a breeze. No footsteps, no dragging, just a slow, unnatural glide. Mike's stomach nodded, but he squinted harder, trying to make sense of it. In the dim spill of a distant street light, he saw her. Blonde hair caked with grime, blue eyes wide with panic. Bruises and scabs dotted her face and arms, and her expression was pure terror, like she was screaming inside, but couldn't make a sound. Amelia. Mike's voice cracked. It was her, Amelia Meager, the girl from the news. His mind spun the whiskey haze burning away. "Holy [ __ ] are you Amelia?" "Please help me," she said, her voice a broken whisper. Her hand jerked toward him, the motion stiff like a marionette's. Mike flinched, stepping back. Her jaw moved, chomping up and down, but her lips stayed frozen, sealed in a grimace. It was wrong, like watching a dubbed movie where the words don't match the face. He froze, caught between fear and guilt. This was Amelia, the girl Chicago was tearing itself apart to find. Her parents sobs echoed in his head from the news. He couldn't just walk away, but every nerve screamed to run. The air was thick, suffocating like the darkness was alive watching him. "Okay, kid," he said, forcing calm. "I'm going to get you out of here." He stepped forward, reaching for her hand, his fingers brushing the edge of the shadow. The cold bit into his skin, unnatural, like dipping his hand into a freezer. Just as he was about to grab her, a car sped by on the highway above, its headlights slashing through the dark for a split second. And in that moment, Mike saw hell. Emmelia wasn't standing. Her bare feet hung limp, toes scraping the pavement, chipped nail polish glinting in the light. Thin shimmering threads, silk fine as spiderweb, were wrapped around her wrists, elbows, knees, shoulders. More threads tethered her jaw, pulling it open and shut like a puppets. Her eyes, wide and wet, locked on his, screaming a silent, desperate plea. Mike's gaze snapped upward, following the threads. Clinging to the overpass's underside was a thing, a spider. But no spider belonged in this world. Its body was the size of a pickup truck, legs thick as baseball bats, covered in bristling hairs. Dozens of eyes, black and gleaming, stared down at him, and a low hiss like steam escaping a pipe filled the air. Each leg twitched, tugging the silk, making Amelia's body dance below. Mike stumbled back, a scream clawing at his throat, but dying in his chest. The spider's eyes followed him, unblinking, and the hiss grew louder, vibrating in his bones. Amelia's body jerked, her arms snapping back like a broken toy. Her eyes stayed on him, begging, even as the threads dragged her deeper into the dark, her dress vanishing into the void. The headlights faded and the shadows swallowed everything. Mike ran, his sneakers pounding the pavement, his breath ragged. The city blurred around him. Alleys, street lights, shuttered storefronts. All of it a maze of threats. Every shadow seemed to writhe. Every corner hit a trap. He didn't stop until he crashed through his apartment door in Pilson, slamming it shut and sliding to the floor. or his heart thundering. Amelia Meager was never found. The news kept her face alive for weeks. Her parents' grief a nightly ritual, but the city moved on. Mike didn't. He saw her eyes every time he closed his own. Heard that hiss in the quiet of his room. He started listening to the street people, the ones he used to ignore. They told him things about a man pulled into a storm drain by something with too many arms. A kid who lured a cop into an alley and left only bones. A shadow that wrapped its victims in slime and left nothing behind. Each story was a shard of the same nightmare. Mike changed after that night. He stopped walking alone after dark carried a flashlight stuck to main streets. The city he'd grown up in with its deep dish joints and Cubs games wasn't his anymore. It was a hunting ground and he was prey. He saw Amelia in every flickering shadow, her face a warning etched into his soul. Chicago's monsters are real. They wear human skin, mimic voices, hide in the places you pass every day. The subway platform, the empty lot, the alley behind your favorite bar. They're patient, hungry, and they know you. So keep your eyes sharp, your steps quick. Ignore the whispers and you might end up like Amelia, a puppet broken and screaming in a city that never sleeps but always feeds.

If you've ever felt like a place was watching you, you're not alone. Let me tell you what happened when I stepped into a village that doesn't exist. I wasn't supposed to take that road. The man at the petrol station had warned me, in that off-hand way locals sometimes do, with a smile too wide to mean it, said something like, "That stretch is a ghost." Sat Nav thinks it's there, but it ain't. Might drop you in the lock if you're not careful. I laughed, nodded, and took the road anyway. It was dusk, and the highlands looked like an oil painting soaked in storm water, rolling fog twisted between the trees like pale, shifting fingers. My rental car groaned as it crawled up the incline, tires slipping on moss-slick gravel. The GPS spun in place until it blinked out entirely. I don't know how long I was driving, half an hour, maybe more. The road narrowed into a single muddy track, hemmed in by black pine and gnarled oak. Then, just as I was debating whether to turn around, I saw a sign. It was wooden, hand-carved, leaning at an angle like it had been driven into the ground centuries ago. The name etched into it read, "Greichel." The letters were warped, the kind you see on old gravestones. I had never heard of it. Not on any map. Not on any guidebook, but the fog lifted slightly, and I saw a village nestled in the hollow ahead, no more than a dozen houses, a crumbling stone church, and a single winding path leading deeper into the woods, and for some reason. I kept driving. The village seemed, suspended in time. Everything looked old, but not abandoned, more like it had simply stopped aging. Each roof sagged, but held strong. Stone walls were moss-lined, but uncracked. I parked near a crooked well and stepped out, immediately struck by how silent it was. No wind. No birds. Not even the chirp of insects. Then the fog shifted again, and from one of the houses, a figure emerged. She was small, hunched, wrapped in a gray shawl. She didn't speak right away, just stared at me with eyes the color of peat, finally. In a voice like crumpled paper, she said, "You've come late, but there's still time." I blinked. "I'm sorry." She tilted her head. "You'll be needing a place." The hollow house is empty, for now. I told her I wasn't staying long, just passing through. She nodded, but it felt like she didn't believe me, or didn't care. She led me up a narrow lane line with leaning fences and splitwood gates. We stopped before a cottage set slightly apart from the others, half-swallowed by ivy. It was meant for someone else, but the forest chooses, not us. She handed me a rusted key and turned to leave. I called out to ask her name. She didn't. "Answer." The inside of the cottage smelled like damp stone and old firewood. The windows were fogged from the inside. No electricity, just a hearth and a few oil lamps. On the table sat a small loaf of bread, wrapped in cloth. Beside it, a note. No name. No message. Just a symbol scratched into the paper, a kind of spiral, with branches or antlers curling outward. That night, I tried to sleep, but I kept hearing it. A sound. Low. Steady. Like breathing. At first, I thought it was wind, but the trees outside weren't moving. It wasn't until just before dawn that I realized. The sound was coming from beneath the floorboards. The next morning, I wandered into what I guessed was the village square. An old man sat outside the church, sharpening a blade that looked too old to be practical. I asked him how far the nearest town was, if there was a mechanic, a phone, anything. He stared at me for a long time before answering, "You've come through the fog, then. Best not to go back." Things in the Vale don't like to be disturbed. When I asked him what that meant, he only shrugged. The green remembers, he muttered, "It always remembers." There was a pub, if you could call it that. A low-roofed room behind a sagging door. Inside, three people sat in silence, not drinking, just waiting. The moment I stepped in, they turned to look at me, not in curiosity, but recognition. Like they already knew me, like they had been expecting me. I stayed one more night. Told myself it was just fatigue, just imagination. But the sound came again, stronger now, rhythmic, like a heartbeat echoing through stone. I pressed my ear to the floorboards, and for a moment, I thought I heard my name whispered between the beats. At dawn, I packed my things. I was leaving, or at least. I tried to. The car wouldn't start. Not even a click. I checked the engine. Nothing obvious. Battery was fine. Wires untouched. No corrosion. I walked to the edge of the village to get a signal, but the path just looped. No matter which direction I took, I ended up back at the crooked well. I even marked a tree with a pocket knife. Deep, unmistakable gouges. I walked straight for 20 minutes, and when I stopped, I was looking at the same tree, still bleeding from the cuts. I went back to the cottage. The bread was gone. In its place was a wooden bowl of something warm. Stew or broth. I didn't touch it, but I noticed the note had changed. Same paper. Same antlered spiral. But now, three words were written beneath it. The hollow fills. The villagers stopped pretending after the third day. Not that they were pretending well to begin with, but they no longer nodded politely. No longer offered vague, cryptic phrases. They watched me now, openly, constantly, from windows, from behind doorways. In the edge of the woods, always with that same expression. Like they were waiting for something to happen, or worse. For me to do something I hadn't yet realized I was supposed to do. I tried asking questions, direct ones, but every attempt was met with silence, or that same phrase, over and over. The hollow fills, it became a refrain, like a hymn. Even the children said it, a small girl in a torn red dress whispered it when I passed the church. Two boys drawing circles in the dirt said it without looking up. No one explained what it meant. On the fourth morning, I woke to find the inside of my cottage changed. Not the furniture, but the walls. They were covered in carvings, dozens of them. Like someone had taken a blade to the stone itself. Circles I didn't recognize, interlocking spirals. Branching antlers, wide staring eyes, they hadn't been there the night before. I went to the church, not for prayer, but because it was the only place I hadn't looked inside, it was dark, colder than the outside air. A long altar ran down the center, draped in tattered green cloth. No cross, no saints. Only a single wooden mask mounted above it. The mask was wide and round, carved from black ash wood. It had no mouth, only eyes. Too many eyes, seven of them, arranged like a crown, each one slightly different in size and angle. As I stared, I realized the eyes weren't carved flat. They bulged, slightly, as if something behind the mask was pushing through. There was someone else in the church, a man, maybe in his 30s, dressed in faded green wool. He stood at the far end of the room, whispering, "Not to me." But to the altar itself, I approached cautiously and asked him what this place was, he didn't look at me. Only said, "It remembers the shape of men, but it wears them thin." Then he turned to me, and I saw that he was weeping, but not from his eyes, from the pores of his cheeks. Clear, thin streams like sweat, they ran, in perfect lines down his face, never breaking, never stopping. He smiled and walked past me, murmuring, "Don't resist it. It's easier if you don't." That night, I dreamed I was underground. Beneath the village, beneath the woods, the earth around me pulsed like muscle, and I was being dragged, not by hands, but by roots, they curled around my limbs, gentle at first, then tightening, and just before I woke, I heard a voice, ancient, layered, like many throats speaking at once. We only borrow the skin. You are hollow, and the hollow must be filled. I woke gasping. There was dirt on the floor, not just a little, a trail of it, leading from the door to my bed, small clumps of moss, wet leaves, scraps of bark, something had been inside, and beneath the pillow, a gift, a bundle of animal bones, tied with green twine, arranged in the shape of a person, but with antlers. I should have run, but there was nowhere to run. Every path looped, every direction ended at the same tree, the same stone, the same well. I tried screaming one night, just to see if anything would answer, and something did, from deep in the woods, a long, low howl, not canine, not human, something in between, it echoed for almost a full minute, and when it stopped, I swear I heard movement, like something crawling, slow and deliberate, just outside the reach of the moonlight. I tried 911 again, whispering, "Maplewood Elementary, please. Someone's after us." The operator snapped, "Stop wasting our time." and hung up. I crouched, knife in hand, the fake Ryan's voice looping in my head. Did it know I'd seen the body? I couldn't stay trapped. I needed to find the other kids, figure out what these things were. Then a memory hit, sharp and cold. When I was a student teacher here 10 years back, kids whispered about the old wing. A crumbling annex from the 1920s boarded up after a fire. They said it was cursed that teachers heard voices, saw shapes in the dark. I'd stayed late once grading papers and felt it. A chill like fingers brushing my neck. I'd brushed it off. Now I wasn't so sure. Ryan said the kids were taken to the old wing. Ascending, I slipped out of the closet, gripping the knife. The cafeteria was silent, but the air felt charged, like a storm was coming. I crept to a window peering out. The fields were empty, but the old wing loomed across the campus, its windows boarded, vines choking the brick. A faint hum like a distant swarm, came from that direction. I ran, sticking to shadows, the hum growing louder, buzzing in my bones. The old wing's door was a jar. Splintered wood dangling. Inside the air was damp, smelling of rot. A stairwell led down, glowing faintly blue. I descended. The hum now a pulse vibrating my teeth. At the bottom, a rusted door stood open, blue light spilling out. I stepped inside. The room was massive, its walls slick, pulsing like living flesh. In the center, a machine thrum, cables burrowing into the floor, glowing with that same blue light. The missing kid stood around it, eyes blank, tendrils of light tethering them to the machine. Mrs. Jensen and Mr. Brody, or whatever they were, stood nearby, their faces flickering like static on a screen. Between them was another Ryan, not the dead one or the fake, but a pale, trembling boy. his real self. Miss Harper, the Jensen thing said, its voice a hiss. You shouldn't have come. The Brody thing smiled, teeth too sharp. You're part of it now. I raised the knife, heart pounding. Let them go. They're ours, Jensen said, feeding the signal. The world will hear it soon. I lunged, slashing at the cable. Sparks flew and the kids flinched, some blinking awake. The creatures screamed, a soundlike tearing metal, and charged. I swung again, cutting tendrils, freeing more kids. Ryan, the real Ryan, stumbled forward, grabbing my arm. Run. We bolted up the stairs, the creature's screams echoing. The hum faltered, the blue light dimming. Outside, the kids scattered, some crying, others silent. I kept running, Ryan's hand in mine, until we hit the road. A truck stopped, the driver staring. What's going on? Call the police, I gasped. Now, as he dialed, I looked back. The old wing was dark, silent. But in my head, the hum lingered faint, waiting.

transcript.fullText: Ethan Caldwell was no stranger to digging up the past. A genealogologist from Boise, Idaho, he'd spent the last 10 years piecing together family trees for folks across the states. At 33, Ethan had a knack for finding the unfindable. Birth certificates buried in county archives. Obituaries tucked in forgotten newspapers, names etched on crumbling headstones. His cluttered home office stacked with binders and old maps was his sanctuary. To him, every name was a story, every date a clue. But nothing in his quiet, methodical life could have prepared him for the nightmare waiting in the Swiss Alps. It started with a late night email from Clara Hensley, a wealthy widow from Seattle. Her voice when they spoke was sharp but shaky like she was chasing a ghost. Clara's parents, Anna and Friedrich Mueller, had left a tiny Swiss village called Shatenberg when she was a kid. All she had were their names and a faded memory of a mountain town. She wanted Ethan to uncover their story, her story, and she was willing to pay big. Real big. Ethan ran his usual searches, ancestry databases, church records, immigration logs, nothing. Shatenberg was a black hole. No digital footprint, no paper trail. If he wanted answers, he'd have to go there himself. Clara didn't hesitate, wiring funds for a plane ticket and a rental car before he could blink. Ethan touched down in Geneva on a chilly October morning, the kind that makes your breath catch. He picked up a Jeep from the rental lot, tossed his duffel bag in the back, and hit the road. The Alps were something else. Rugged peaks stabbing the sky, valleys glowing with golden aspens. He cranked up Springsteen on the radio, feeling like an explorer charting new territory. But as he climbed higher, the vibe shifted. The roads got tighter, snaking through switchbacks that hugged cliffs. The air turned cold, heavy with the threat of snow. Then the fog came. Thick, suffocating. It swallowed the road hole. Ethan's headlights barely cut through, and every turn felt like a roll of the dice. One wrong move, and he'd be over the edge, tumbling into the void. His palms sweated on the wheel, his heart thumping like a bass line. He was about to pull over, sleep in the damn jeep if he had to, when the fog thinned just enough to reveal a miracle. A building carved into the mountainside, its neon sign flickering like a beacon. Belvadier in. A gravel lot sat across the road, empty as a graveyard. Ethan pulled in, his tires crunching on loose stones. The inn looked like it hadn't changed since the Great Depression. Peeling paint, sagging eaves, windows dark as dead eyes. He grabbed his backpack and headed inside, the wind biting at his neck. The lobby was a time warp. Creaky wood floors, iron chandeliers coated in dust, a faint smell of mildew. Behind the counter stood an old man, maybe 70, with a face like weathered leather. His eyes flicked up cold and tired. "You speak English?" Ethan asked, stomping the chill from his boots. "Some?" the man grunted, his accent thick as the fog outside. "You want a room?" "Hell yeah," Ethan said relieved. "How much?" 125 Franks cash. The man's voice was flat like he was reading a script. Ethan fished out his wallet, but the man, Klouse, he called himself, held up a gnarled hand. You're the only one here tonight. I own this place. I don't stay after dark. You'll be alone. That okay. Ethan's gut twisted. An empty inn. No staff. Weird as hell, but the fog wasn't giving him options. Sure, man. I'll manage. Claus's stare bored into him. One rule. You stay in your room, door locked all night, no wandering. Swear it. The words landed like a warning shot. Ethan figured Klaus was just paranoid about his property. "Yeah, I swear," he said, forcing a grin. Klaus handed him a key. Old school heavy iron etched with room seven top floor. It felt like something from a horror flick. Ethan trudged up the stairs, each step groaning under his weight. His room was straight out of a museum brass sink, creaky bed, a balcony with a view of the valley's twisting roads. The fog had lifted a bit, and the moonlight painted the switchback silver. Ethan snapped a photo, half wishing he could share it on Instagram. No signal, though, no nothing. Jet lag screwed with his head. By midnight, Ethan was wired, pacing like a caged animal. The silence was deafening. No hum of traffic, no buzz of a TV, just the occasional creek of the old inn settling. Klouse's truck was long gone. Ethan had watched it disappear down the mountain. He was alone. Totally, utterly alone. And that's when the itch hit. The same itch that made him a damn good genealogologist. Curiosity. Klaus's warning echoed in his mind. But come on, what was the harm in a little snooping? Just a quick look around. He grabbed his phone, flicked on the flashlight, and crept into the hall. The inn was a labyrinth of shadows. Every corner hiding dust and decay. Cobwebs draped the walls like funeral shrouds. Ethan tried a door across from his. It wasn't locked, swinging open with a low moan. The room inside was a wreck. Dust an inch thick. Furniture rotting. Air so stale it choked him. He swept his light across the space, catching glints of spiderw webs. At the window he rubbed away grime and peered out. This side faced up the mountain, the road above faintly lit by a full moon. That's when he saw them. 30 figures standing like statues on the road. Each held a candle, the flames steady despite the wind. Their faces were hidden, but their bodies were tense, heads tilted toward the inn. Ethan froze, his breath fogging the glass. Some clutched sythes, the blades gleaming like crescent moons. Others held rusted tools, axes, sickles, a goddamn pitchfork. They weren't moving, just watching, staring right at him. His stomach dropped. He killed the flashlight, plunging the room into black. When he dared look again, the figures were gone. No moving. descending the road, their candles bobbing like willow wisps. Ethan's heart slammed against his ribs. He bolted back to his room, fumbling with the key. The lock clicked just as his phone buzzed. 10:05 a.m. He pressed his ear to the door, straining for sound. Nothing. Then a boom. The inn's front door crashing open. Footsteps thundered below, heavy, too many to count. They climbed the stairs, deliberate, closing in. Ethan's eyes darted around the room. Weapon. He needed a weapon. The glass tumbler by the sink was all he had. He gripped it, backing against the wall, ready to swing. The footsteps stopped outside his door. The knob rattled slow at first, then violent. Fists pounded the wood, hard, rhythmic, like a war drum. The door groaned, splintering at the edges. Ethan's mouth went dry. These weren't pranksters, not locals messing with a tourist. This was something else, something wrong. He lunged for the balcony, the alpine air slapping his face. The railing was slick with frost, but he climbed it hard in his throat, and leaped to the next balcony over. His boots hit metal with a clang, and he ducked low, praying they hadn't heard. Inside his room, chaos erupted. Wood cracked as the door gave way. Furniture scraped, fabric tore, glass shattered, his backpack, his laptop destroyed. The worst part, not a single voice, no shouts, no whispers, just the sound of ruin, cold and mechanical. Ethan huddled on the stranger's balcony. the cold seeping into his bones. He waited, counting breaths, listening as the intruders tore through his room. Hours later, the noises stopped. Footsteps retreated, fading down the stairs. Still, Ethan didn't move. Not until Dawn's gray light crept over the peaks. He climbed back to his room, legs shaking. It was trashed. Bed flipped, clothes shredded, laptops snapped like a twig. His car keys, thank God, were still in his jacket. He didn't stop to think. He ran downstairs past the splintered front door and dove into the Jeep. The engine roared to life, and he peeled out, tires spitting gravel. He drove for hours, not stopping until he hit a city with lights, people, life. In a diner with spotty Wi-Fi, he searched for answers. The Belvadier Inn had been shut down since 78 after a string of vanishings. Locals called it cursed. Shatenberg was worse. A village steeped in whispers of a cult. Some ancient order tied to the mountains. They called them the Watchers, guardians of a secret no outsider could know. Ethan dug deeper, finding a grainy article about Friedrich Mueller, Clara's dad. In 1949, he'd fled Shatenberg, branded a traitor for exposing the village's blood oath. The details were hazy, but Ethan knew one thing. His poking around had woken something up. He emailed Clara, begging her to drop the search. She never replied. Back in Boise, Ethan tried to move on, but the shadows followed. At night, he'd hear footsteps outside his apartment. Slow, deliberate, stopping just shy of his door. One morning, he found a candle on his porch, its wax still warm, a tiny flame flickering in the dawn. Shatenberg wasn't done with him. And deep down, Ethan knew. Neither were the Watchers.

Amy was positive her boss was out to make her life miserable, but she hadn't been able to prove it yet. Every day when she arrived in the office, she got straight to work, always checking her emails and voicemails first and making sure she was on time with all her deadlines second. Every day, her boss, Jack, arrived at 9, glared at her, and proceeded to point out that she had deadlines to meet and she should spend less time drinking coffee and more time working before telling her to go get him coffee. every day. Amy wanted to walk out and tell Jack where to shove his coffee, only to be reminded that she had rent to pay and food to buy. Amy then proceeded to get Jack his coffee, and after getting back to her desk, she checked the classifides to see if there were any jobs out there. Every day, she was disappointed, and after a moment of drowning in misery, she'd get back to work to ensure her clients stayed happy. Karen Enterprises was her newest account while she had gotten a handsome bonus for signing them. And one of the other bookkeepers usually picked up the backups and documentation needed to prepare their financial statements. Those weren't due for another 2 weeks, but on Tuesdays, she also prepared payroll for them, which they emailed to her by 10:00 in the morning. When Amy still hadn't received it by 11, she picked up her phone and dialed the direct line for one of the bookkeepers at Karen Enterprises. Hi, this is Amy. I was just calling to see where Peril was. Hi Amy, we are having some issues with our computers. Would someone be able to pick it up? I was able to print the spreadsheet, but both our email and the fax machine are down. Sure, I'll come get it. I think it's about time I meet you all anyway, so I'll be there in about 20 minutes. Amy hung up the phone and sighed. While it was true she really should meet the bookkeeper she worked with regularly, she also wished the bookkeeper who worked under her at Gloumer and Gloumer didn't have the day off so she could go instead like she usually did. Amy changed her status on the time entry program to indicate where she was going. Switched her phone to out of office and walked out into the sunshine. It was a beautiful day and Amy wished she could stay outside but instead she walked down the street to Karen Enterprises. It was only four blocks and walking was easier. The fact that it got her out of the office longer was an added bonus. "Hi, I'm here to pick up a spreadsheet from Susanna," Amy told the receptionist as soon as she walked in. "She told me you would be coming. You can go right up to the 10th floor." "Thank you," Amy said with a smile before making her way to the elevators. Karen Enterprises was a large corporation employing thousands of employees and with revenues at hundreds of millions of dollars. She only did payroll for the management level salaried employees while the hourly payroll was outsourced and for that she was glad. She looked around in interest and noticed that the walls were granite and the floors of beautiful stone. As soon as she stepped into the elevator, she couldn't help but admire the beautiful woodwork that adorned the walls. It was clear that whoever had designed the building had not spared any expense and paid great attention to detail. "Hi, I'm here to see Susanna," Amy told the next receptionist up on the 10th floor. "Go right on in. She's the third office on your left." The girl smiled back at her, pointing at the doors to her left. Clearly, the receptionist downstairs had called up to announce her arrival. And when she walked into Susanna's office, she was already out of her seat and ready to greet her. It's so nice to finally meet you. I feel that so much is lost when you can't put a face to the name. Here is the spreadsheet before I forget. Also, Mark heard you were coming and asked me to show you up to his office so he can meet you. While he has heard great things about you from other clients you work with, he felt that it was important that he actually met you. Come on, it's one floor up. The ride up was quiet, and the second they stepped out of the elevator, Amy knew they were on the executive floor. Not only were the walls granite, the floors were marble. The chairs in the waiting area were nice, comfortable armchairs, and there were large, expensive looking paintings on the walls. Large wooden doors to either side of the receptionist's desk fit into everything perfectly and yet gave a feeling of exclusivity at being allowed through them. "Hi, Erica. Mark asked me to bring Amy up," Susanna told the receptionist. "Thank you, Susanna. I will let him know she is here." Susanna left and Amy turned to Erica, who was smiling sweetly. "Go ahead and have a seat. I'll let Mr. Karen know you have arrived. Would you like a cup of coffee? That would be amazing. Thank you. Amy sat down on one of the chairs and soon Erica handed her a cup of coffee. Amy couldn't help but notice it was a nice cup, not a cheap paper or foam cup she got at most places she went. She couldn't help but appreciate the proper cup, as paper and foam had a way of making coffee taste different. She didn't have to wait long, and soon Erica was leading her through a hallway to the left until they came to more large wooden doors. Erica opened one of them and gestured for Amy to enter, which she did. The office in front of her was incredibly bright, which she attributed to the fact that the entire wall opposite the door was made out of glass. In the middle of the office was a large glass desk, behind which was a stern-looking man looking at her. The marble flooring continued as did the granite walls and Amy found she truly loved the office and the layout. Good morning. I'm Amy. I'm glad we finally get the chance to meet. I agree. Have a seat. Amy walked towards the chairs in front of the desk and took a seat. Getting her first chance to observe Mark up close. She realized he was a good-looking man if he would just smile instead of look so forbidding. with his green eyes appearing to pierce her soul. His black hair was neatly combed to the side, curling slightly at the end, indicating that it was about time for another haircut to keep it nice and straight. Now that we've met, there is something I would like to discuss. We just received your invoice, and I must say I'm shocked at how high it is. I mean, it is almost double what it would have cost me to simply hire someone, which I wasn't expecting. I understand, but if your bookkeepers would know what they were doing and would get us the information we request in a timely and orderly fashion, we wouldn't spend as much time fixing everything. Our invoice is based on the time spent on your account. I see. You think my bookkeepers don't know what they are doing? It's clear they have some knowledge, but they need someone to supervise them, and they need additional training. Some of the mistakes are so basic. I wonder if they even went to school for accounting. Well, you sure don't mince your words. Are you always this straightforward with your clients? I find that telling the truth works best. You asked why the invoice was high? I'm giving you the reason. And you're not worried about insulting me. I'm sure your boss would not be happy if we took our business elsewhere. Look, I'm only on my third cup of coffee for the day. I need at least six or seven to care what my boss thinks. Mark raised an eyebrow at that statement as it was clear there was no love lost. So, you think we can do better? Yes. If I didn't need my job so much, I'd tell you to simply hire a new CFO who can oversee those bookkeepers and make sure everything is done right. It would save you money and it would save someone else the headache of figuring out what they did. How would you like to be my new CFO? Mark asked as if he had just asked her if she wanted more coffee, not if she wanted a job. What? You can't be serious. Oh, I am. I think we could use someone like you around here. And you've proven that you know the work and are capable of doing it. I have a non-compete clause in my contract. I can't work for you. I'll handle that if you want the job. It comes with a six-figure salary if that helps. Full benefits. You have got to be joking. Six figures and full benefits. Yes. And I can't be harder to work for than that boss of yours. You might not even need six cups of coffee first. Look, I'd love the job simple because I've wanted to switch to corporate accounting anyway, but I can't get out of that clause in my contract. I can't work for anyone who has been our client in the past 2 years. I'll have my lawyers draw up your contract and get you out of the clause in your current one. Why don't you come back after work on Friday and we will have dinner and discuss everything. If asked later, Mark would deny having ever done this, but there was just something about this woman. He wanted to get to know her better, unrelated to work, and he knew the best way to do that would be to have her in the same building every day. Money could do a lot of things, so he knew her contract wasn't an issue, and the dinner was an excuse to see her again. "I think I can do that." "Don't feel bad if you don't succeed," Amy said as she stood up to leave. "I need to get back to work. I will see you on Friday." Walking back to her office, Amy couldn't help but be slightly excited at the prospect of getting out of public accounting, even though she knew she shouldn't get her hopes up. The job would be perfect, and silently she had to admit Mark wouldn't be so bad to work for. If nothing else, he was pleasing to look at while her current boss was mean and looked like a rat. She knew it would be challenging at first to get the bookkeepers to do things the proper way, but once she had policies in place and they knew they could come to her for anything, she had no doubt it would be a wonderful job. The salary wouldn't hurt either, as she had seen what the previous CFO was making. And if she made even half that, she'd be tripling her annual income. Goodbye student loans. Hello, sunny beach vacations. Chapter 2. Friday afternoon was dragging for Amy as she tried not to think about where she was going as soon as she was done. Mark had sent her a note that gave her the name of a restaurant where they'd be having dinner and to let her know a driver would pick her up at 5. While the driver wasn't necessary, she was silently glad as she hated the subway during rush hour and this way she could avoid it. It was just before 5 that she realized the real reason for the driver as her current boss came up to her desk looking almost happy though she wasn't entirely sure. Make sure you take all your belongings with you since this is your last day here. Mark Karen informed me you are starting there on Monday. There are boxes in the supply room if you need one. Amy stared after her boss or former boss in shock as the reality of what he had just said sunk in. She got the job. Mark had been able to get her out of her contract. And this dinner wasn't just to sign her new employment contract. It was also to celebrate. She almost jumped for joy and almost skipped to the supply room to get a box, getting to work on boxing up everything. Several other accountants and bookkeepers came to see what she was doing, and she excitedly told them about her new job, which got her just as many envious looks as it got her congratulations. It was a happy Amy, who instantly felt like a weight had been lifted off her shoulders, who put her box in the trunk of the car at 5:00 on the dot. "I will take the box to your new office after taking you to the restaurant, ma'am," the driver said as they pulled away from the curb. "Thank you. That is very much appreciated. While the drive was definitely more pleasant than the subway, it also took longer as traffic was positively insane. Half the time they weren't moving at all, which is why Amy didn't arrive at the restaurant until 6:00. She smiled when she saw Mark waiting out front for her, and she let him help her out of the car after he opened her door. I hope I didn't keep you waiting. Not at all. I planned for it to take some time for you to get here. Shall we head inside? Amy smiled at him and let him lead her to their table where he pulled out her chair like a true gentleman would before sitting down himself. Considering you are smiling, I take it you already know I was successful. Yes, I do. Thank you truly. I feel lighter somehow. It was clear you were not happy there. I hope you don't mind, but I went ahead and ordered a bottle of champagne to celebrate the happy occasion. I don't mind at all. I finally have something worth celebrating. I am curious how you did it though. Money can do a lot of things, as does knowing your competition. Your employers have some things they don't wish to have become public knowledge, and I gave them some excellent referrals for your replacement, so they won't be without a CPA long. Clearly, they didn't worry about getting good lawyers for those contracts either, as my lawyers pierced right through them. All in all, it was really quite simple. Well, thank you. I look forward to starting on Monday. Excellent. Now, before dinner, let's get the formal reason for this dinner out of the way before we let alcohol influence anything. This is the contract. Let me know if you want to see any changes. I'm willing to negotiate. Amy took the contract and started reading, her eyes nearly popping out of her head as she did. She would be making the same as the previous CFO, which was over half a million a year, full health, dental and vision, 401k, pension, life insurance, and 4 weeks vacation a year. When she got to the paragraph about living arrangements, she almost forgot how to breathe. You have an apartment for me. Our executive officers have housing provided as part of their benefits package. Besides me, there is you and our COO whom you will meet first thing Monday. After that meeting, I will make the formal announcement during our regular Monday morning town hall meeting which is open to all employees. We all live in the same building where I have the penthouse and you and the COO Kevin split the floor below it. It is convenient as we sometimes work late and our chef can easily prepare meals while our housekeeper can easily take care of all our homes. Chef, housekeeper. Yes, I have a chef in my employee and she will also be available to you. Trust me, there will be times when you'll love it, especially when it comes time for the annual audit of the books. Our housekeeper simply keeps everything clean and does your laundry, including taking anything that needs dry clean to the dry cleaner and picking it back up. With three of us, there is always something. And if she goes for one of us, she might as well go for all of us. I believe that good employees should be valued. And I take care of mine to ensure they will want to work hard. All employees get 3 weeks vacation starting out. And even though they are at work less than employees at other corporations, they are also more productive. It's amazing how that works. You will be busy. You will have many days where you'll want to go home and sink down on your couch with a glass of wine. The last thing you'll want to do is worry about cleaning or doing laundry or cooking dinner. Lydia is actually really excited to to finally have a woman to take care of. Is there anything you'd like changed or added? No, it all looks good. Do you have a pen? 5 minutes later, the contract was signed in duplicate and Amy was handed a check much to her confusion. Sign on bonus. Movers will be at your apartment tomorrow to help you pack up and move. The bonus will help with any expenses you might incur. Also, you will receive formal notice of your stock shares by Monday afternoon. Stock shares. Did I miss that? It's standard for an executive. It's incentive for you to help our company do well. If we keep up our stock prices, you benefit from it. It's also why I like the annual audit. It makes sure we aren't doing anything illegal to keep that benefit at a maximum. Now, how about some shrimp cocktails for an appetizer? And just like that, Mark switched away from the business portion of the dinner to the pleasure portion, waving over the waiter, who immediately came to take their order. Amy was glad that Mark ordered for her, as she wasn't sure she could remember how to speak. And when he filled her glass with champagne, she gratefully drank half the glass, causing Mark to chuckle. You do know there is water if you are thirsty. I'm not thirsty. I needed some serious alcohol to make sure I still know how to breathe and swallow and all those normal things humans do. Mark got a slightly strange look on his face at that statement before it went back to his normal smile before he picked up the bottle to refill her glass. Well, then I see we need some more. If you need a minute, might I suggest looking at the menu to decide what you want as your main course? Food? Yes, let's focus on food, Amy said slightly numbly as she started focusing on her menu. She almost felt like she was living a dream and any moment she was going to wake up and she would be back at her crappy job working for someone who hated everyone and everything. When she placed her order and everything was still going on around her, she started to realize that not only was this very real, she also hadn't said a word in almost 20 minutes while Mark simply sat there watching her. All right, this is real. I don't know how. I don't know why, but it's apparently real as I'm still here and you're still here. Good. Now that that's settled, are you going to eat your appetizer? Amy laughed and started eating a piece of shrimp before looking at Mark. You are taking my silence surprisingly well. I recognized that you needed a moment. Apparently, your moment lasts a little longer than that of most other people, but a moment it was. I see. So, nobody knows I start on Monday. Kevin knows, but he's the only one. He is out of town this weekend. Otherwise, you'd meet him tomorrow. Would you like to go see your apartment after dinner? I'll see it tomorrow. I want to get started on packing. I also need to make a list of everywhere I need to change my address and call my mother to inform her. You're a list person. I have lists for everything. Somehow that doesn't surprise me. So, what do you like to do in your free time? I love going out into the mountains and hiking. It sounds strange since I live in the city. And I truly love it here, but when I have the time, I like to escape all the hustle and bustle and go somewhere I won't encounter anyone else. It gives me the opportunity to relax. In the city, I love attending plays, go to movies, or simply spend time with friends. I will admit that it surprises me that you enjoy the outdoors, but I could see why you would. Do most of your friends live in the city? They do. I'm assuming it doesn't matter if I have them at my apartment. That's fine. It's truly your space. You can entertain as much as you'd like. Lydia can help you if you need anything. I don't want you to feel like you'll be constantly watched because you won't be. I work odd hours and I can usually be found at the office even on the weekends. Kevin has a daughter he has every other weekend, so he'll be busy with her on those weekends. He occasionally has her on weekdays as well when her mother needs someone to watch her. So, you'll probably see her around some. How old is she? 12. She is a beautiful little girl. I've watched her grow up over the past few years. She calls me Uncle Mark, and I won't deny I love it.
