transcript.fullText: 23 hours. A co-work production. Author's note. On the night of the 22nd of April, 2026, a young geology student became trapped beside a flash flooded river inside Du Titzclouth Pass in the western Cape of South Africa. He survived thanks to a rescue team that climbed in through rain and dark. The newspapers gave that story half a column. This novella is a fiction built on its bones. Names, families, and inner lives are invented. But the river and the mountain are real. And so is the kind of courage it took to bring him home. 24th April, 2026. Chapter 1. The weather window. Liam Becka checked the rain map on his phone for the fourth time that morning. And for the fourth time, the cold front sat parked off the western coast like a freight train waiting at a signal. The yellow and orange smear over the Atlantic looked enormous on the screen, but the model said landfall on Sunday afternoon, 2 and 1/2 days away. He had a 48 hour window. He was going. The kettle clicked off. He poured boiling water over the instant coffee, stirred in three sugars, and stood at the kitchen sink of the small cottage on Reneeld Street, looking out at the lemon tree his mother had planted the day his father died. The tree was 8 years old now, and had begun finally to bear fruit. Two yellow ovals hung among the dark leaves like little lamps. He thought about picking one for the road, and decided against it. Marina Becca came in from the courtyard wearing the thick cardigan she wore from April through September. Her hair still pinned up from a phone call with a client. She was a financial adviser, careful with everyone's risks but her own sons. She had not slept well last night. Liam had heard her up at 3. The kettle, the cupboard door, the soft stir of a teaspoon. You're really going, she said. It's a window, ma. I told Professor Neoot I'd have the sample set by Tuesday. He can wait. He can, but the river won't. Once the rains start, I won't see those exposures until October. She made the small sound, half breath and half consent, that he had heard a thousand times in his life. It was the sound of a woman who had decided long ago not to be the kind of mother who made her son into a coward. She moved past him to the stove, flicked the gas on under the pan, and reached for the eggs. "Sit," she said. He sat. His pack stood by the front door, lashed and ready, the geology hammer slotted along its spine. Tucked into the lid pocket was the orangecased Garmin in Reach Mini his mother had given him for his last birthday. He had laughed when he opened the box. "Ma, I do day trips." She had held his eyes and said, "Take it anyway." He had carried it on every walk for 10 months and had not yet used it for anything but its weather forecast. Today, before leaving Stellenbos, he had checked the SOS subscription was active. He did not know why he had thought to do this. Over scrambled eggs and toast, he traced the route on his battered topo map with the back of his fork. Up the N1 to the eastern portal of the old Dtoids Cliff Pass. Park at the trail head down the contour path to the second meander of the Molinar's River, where Cape Granite suite intruded the Tigerberg shales in a contact zone he had been describing for his master's thesis. Sample photograph log out by midafter afternoon. Home by supper time. How long? She asked. 5 hours in. Sample for two. 5 out. I'll be back by 7. It's going to be cold. I have the down jacket. I'll keep your dinner. Don't. I'll keep it anyway. He kissed the crown of her head on the way out. He smelled the royos on her breath and the lavender she rubbed into her wrists each morning. and would much later reach for that scent in the dark of a ledge above black water and find it still on his collar where he had pressed his face into her shoulder. He walked to the car under a sky the color of wet slate. The wind was coming over Hilderberg from the southwest, soft yet, but with a freight to it. He told himself he had read the model right. He told himself the front was 36 hours out. He started the car. The petrol gauge sat at 3/4 full. He pulled out of Rhineld Street and turned toward the N1. Behind him in the kitchen window, his mother stood with her cup in both hands and watched the back of his car until it turned the corner. Then she set the cup in the sink, dried her hands on the dish towel, and went to her desk to begin the Friday accounts. She did not know yet that she would not finish them. Chapter 2. First light. The N1 climbs out of the Cape Flats and sweeps east through the Boland farms, vineyards in their autumn russet, rows of vines pruned back to the bone. Liam drove with the window cracked to keep himself sharp. The radio gave him the news at the top of the hour. A mining strike in Rustenberg, a budget speech postponed. Light rain expected on the Cape Peninsula by Sunday morning. Sunday morning, he repeated, thumbs tapping the wheel. plenty of time. Past Worcester, the mountains piled up in front of him, the Hex River ranged to the east, and the dude Toys Cliff to the north, the Molinar's River running between them through a gorge so steep that the engineers in 1949 had simply blasted a road into the cliff above the water. The new tunnel, bored through the heart of the mountain, had taken most of the traffic by the 80s. The old pass remained narrow and serpentine, a place where you could pull over at any number of slate roofed picnic spots and feel the river roar below you. He took the exit for the old pass. The road climbed sharply, switchback twice through a stand of stone pines, and then opened out onto a long contour with the gorge dropping away to his right. He could see 150 m below the Molinars in its clear autumn condition braided through pale riverstones. From up here it looked like a child's drawing of a river. Calm, navigable, almost tame. The trail head sign was bolted to a granite boulder. Wilderness area. No fires. Permit required. He had his permit in his wallet. He locked the car, shouldered the pack, settled the hip belt. The path dropped through Finnboss and Wild olives, traversing the slope in long, lazy zigzags. The smell of the mountain rose around him. Pelagonium buu, the sharp clean aringency of crushed restio. A pair of clipbringer broke from a thicket and bounded along the contour with their odd springing gate. All four hooves landing on a stone the size of a saucer. He stopped to watch them disappear into a fold of the slope, and felt for a moment what the mountain always gave him, the sense that the world was older than him by an unimaginable amount, and patient with him, and indifferent to his small hurries. It took him 80 minutes to reach the riverbed. He paused at the bottom of the path on a wide gravel apron the river had laid down over centuries, and he ate an apple and refilled his bottle from the current. The water was cold enough to ache his teeth. Upstream, the gorge narrowed into a slot perhaps 8 m wide, with cliffs of buff sandstone rising sheer for 20 m above either bank before opening out into the broader bowl. He could see even from here the dark line of the contact he had come to sample. A band of granite shouldering its way through the older rocks like a scar that had never quite healed. He worked his way upstream, hopping from boulder to boulder, the river running shind deep in places, knee deep in others. He took photographs. He swung the hammer, listened to the dull bell of granite under steel, chiseled off neat fist-sized samples, and labeled each in his notebook. The work absorbed him. He did not look up at the sky for a long time. When he did look up at 11, the high Cirrus had thickened into an unbroken sheet of gray, and the wind had shifted to the south. He told himself it was nothing. He took one more sample. Chapter 3. The storm cell. The first warning came from a sound that did not belong. He had been kneeling in the shallows, scraping moss from a piece of contact rock, when he heard a low percussive thump from the southwest, like a heavy book dropped onto a carpeted floor. He paused. The river answered with its own percussion, [clears throat] the small rapid above him chuckling steadily. He held his breath. The thump came again, louder now, and behind it a softer rumble that he felt in his sternum as much as heard. He stood up and looked over his shoulder downstream. Through the V of the gorge, where the cliffs framed the lower valley like the lens of a telescope, he could see a piece of sky he had not noticed before. A blackbellied cloud that had reared up out of nowhere, its top boiling pale into the cirrus, its base trailing a curtain of gray that did not look like rain so much as like something poured. As he watched, a fork of lightning unwound from the curtain to the ground, and the thunder he had heard rolled up the gorge a heartbeat later. He stood very still and ran the numbers. The cell was perhaps 15 km south, moving. He watched it for a slow count of 30, moving northeast at maybe 40 km an hour. That gave him 20 minutes before it was overhead, give or take. 20 minutes was enough. 20 minutes was a hop back across the river. A wedge into a dry overhang. A rainshell zipped to the chin. He started across. The river was slightly higher than it had been an hour ago, he noticed, and slightly more opaque. He frowned. There had been no rain here. He looked upstream and saw nothing alarming. The same braided water, the same pale stones. He shouldered his way up the bank and was reaching for his rainshell when the first drops hit him in the face. They came in great soft splatters the size of a coin, and the rain that followed was not rain at all, but a slle, a cold weight of water that was already a torrent before he could get the shell over his head. He pulled the hood up, his glasses flashed, and went blind. He took them off, wiped them with a finger that was already wet, gave up, and shoved them in his pocket. He looked at his watch. It was 11:42 in the morning. He looked at the river. The river had changed color. It was no longer clear with a faint tea tint. It was gray brown, the color of weak coffee, and it was moving faster, much faster. The small chuckling rapid above him now a steady hiss. As he watched, a stick the size of his forearm shot past at the speed of a throne ball. Some part of him, the careful lecture trained geology student part, said, "Flash flood. This is what flash flood looks like. You are standing in the bottom of a flash flood gorge." Another part of him, older and less polite, said only, "Go up." He went up. He scrambled over the boulders he had been working between, water slooing now off the cliffs above him in white veins, and he made for the path. The path was where he had come down. The path led to the contour. The contour led to his car. The path crossed the river 30 m downstream of where he had been sampling. He saw when he reached it that the path had ceased to exist on his side. The river was already up to the lowest of the orange marker pegs, and the small natural causeway of round stones he had hopped across an hour earlier was now under 50 cm of fast brown water. He could see on the far bank the path winding away up the slope, perfectly normal, perfectly walkable, 15 m away, across a flow he could no longer cross. He looked downstream for a calmer spot. There was none. He looked upstream and saw the slot canyon narrowing, the cliffs stepping in. Above him, the cliff was a vertical face of buff sandstone shelved here and there with narrow ledges of darker rock. One of those ledges, 4 m up, looked deep enough to sit on. He climbed. Chapter 4. Water memory. He climbed badly. His hands shook. His boots soaked. slipped twice on the wet sandstone. His pack pulled him backwards every time he reached high. Halfway to the ledge, his hammer banged against the rock, and the chisel slipped out of its loop, and rang down the cliff into the brown water below. He did not look to see where it had gone. He pulled himself onto the ledge on his belly, slithered round, so his back was to the cliff, and sat with his knees drawn up. He was breathing hard. His glasses were in his pocket. His hair ran with water. His left hand was bleeding from a cut he could not remember making. The ledge was perhaps 2 m long and a meter and a half deep with a slight overhang above it that kept the worst of the rain off his head. Below him the river was rising visibly centimeter by cimeter, pebble line by pebble line. He could see the orange marker peg now half submerged. He could see the gravel apron where he had eaten his apple disappear inch by inch under the brown lift. He thought with a clarity that surprised him I should have turned around at 11. He thought after a moment I should have turned around at 10:00. He thought later still I should not have come. This last he set aside as a man sets aside a tool he cannot use right now. He took stock. He had a backpack with one rainshell on him, one synthetic puff jacket in the lid pocket, dry, one beanie, one pair of liner gloves, one head torch with spare batteries, a liter of water, two energy bars, the remains of the morning sandwiches, his notebook, his hammer, the rock samples, heavy, stupidly heavy, 12 kilos of them, his car keys, his wallet, his cell phone. No signal here. The gorge was a black hole and the orangecased Garmin Enreach Mini his mother had given him for his birthday. He took the InReach out of the lid pocket with hands that had begun, despite the puff jacket he now pulled on under the rainshell, to tremble with cold. He turned it on. It found four satellites in 20 seconds. He had to scroll the menu twice with stiff fingers before he found the SOS option. He paused with his thumb above it. He thought about his mother. He thought about the lemon tree. He thought about the fact that the river had risen another 5 cm while he was looking at the screen. He pressed SOS. The little screen asked him to confirm. He confirmed. The unit began transmitting. A status bar crawled across the screen, sending message, acquiring response. He looked up. The rain was a wall now, drumming on the rock above his head, slooing off the overhang in a clear curtain that landed on the ledge a meter in front of him. Beyond the curtain, the world was a gray blur. He could see no further than the far cliff. He could not see the gorge above or below. The inreach beeped. Message acknowledged. A reply scrolled across the screen in the small gray font. Goss emergency response. Help is being arranged. Stay where you are. Reply with details. He typed slowly with his thumbs. Stuck on ledge above Molina's river. Doit's cliff. Flash flood. Cannot cross. Path on west bank. I am on east bank. 4 m up cliff. Dry but cold. Please advise. He pressed send. It took 28 seconds to confirm. While he waited for the reply, he reached into the lid pocket and took out the one thing he had not cataloged. A small muchfolded photograph he had carried in that pocket for 6 years since his second year at university when he had begun walking alone in the mountains. The photograph showed his father on the summit of Snowberg in the Cedarberg in 2017, 3 months before the heart attack. His father was laughing. His father looked exactly like him. He held the photograph in his lap beneath the curtain of falling water and he waited for the reply. The reply came at 12:14. Wilderness search and rescue. Western Cape coordinator notified. Helicopter assessment underway. Stand by. He pressed the photograph to his lips for a moment, then folded it carefully and put it back. The river rose. Chapter 5. The ledge. By 1:00 in the afternoon, the river had risen 3 m. By 2, it had risen another meter and a half. By 3, the brown coffee color had turned the dark gray of slate, and the noise it made was no longer water against stone, but a single sustained roar pitched somewhere between a freight train and a wind that filled the gorge from cliff to cliff, and made his headache. He sat on the ledge with his back to the cliff and his knees drawn up tight to his chest. He had eaten one of the energy bars. He had drunk half of his water. He had tried twice to stand and stretch his legs and had given up because the ledge was too narrow to take more than one careful step in either direction. His feet had gone numb in his soaked boots. He had pulled the dry beanie down over his ears and the dry liner gloves onto his hands. But his fingers had begun around 2:00 to lose the fine motor control he needed to type on the inReach. Messages had come and gone. Helicopter unable to fly. Cloud-based 200 m. Repeat 200 m. Wind southwest 65 kmh. Cannot operate in gorge. Mountain team being mobilized. ETA 4 to 6 hours. He had typed carefully acknowledged. stable position will conserve battery. He had typed after a while please contact Marina Becca Stellenbos my mother. He had given the number. He had typed then deleted then typed again and finally sent tell her I am dry. Now he was watching the river. The river had lost any resemblance to the thing he had crossed that morning. It had become a dark, muscular slide, lifting branches the size of a man's thigh, and rolling them like toothpicks. A juniper tree that had been growing on the west bank, perhaps 50 m downstream, leaned slowly into the current and was gone in the time it took him to draw breath. Underneath the surface, he could hear occasionally a deep, dull thunk as a boulder shifted on the bed. He thought about boulders shifting on the bed. He thought about the ledge he was sitting on, which was bolted to the cliff by nothing more than the ordinary friction of bedded sandstone and a million years of weather. And he did the small shameful arithmetic of asking whether his ledge could fail. He decided it could not fail. The ledge was old. The water would have to rise another 6 m to reach it. The water was not going to rise another 6 m. He decided this and then he watched the water rise another centimeter and sat very still and tried not to think about the ledge. To not think about the ledge, he made himself think about other things. He ran through the periodic table in his head. He named all the rock types he could remember from firstear prology. He named all the girls he had ever held hands with, which took less time than he had hoped. He named the towns on the road from Cape Town to Johannesburg in order. He named the Beatles albums in order of release. He thought about his mother. He hoped someone had reached her. He hoped she was not alone in the kitchen on Reneld Street. He hoped she had her sister with her. He thought about Anakah Duplexie, whose name had appeared in one of the Geos messages as the rescue coordinator. He pictured her without justification as a woman in her 40s, broad-shouldered with gray at her temples, wearing one of those red wilderness search and rescue soft shells. He pictured her standing in a control room somewhere in Cape Town, looking at a satellite map with his red dot blinking on it. He thought, "Please come." He did not type this. He typed at 3:17. Still here, still dry. Battery 64%. The reply when it came was longer than the previous ones. Liam, this is Anakah. Mountain team is on the road. Six members. We'll reach trail head 1730. Approach down path will take 90 minutes in this rain. We will be at the river opposite you by 1900. Plan is to fix a tool line and pull you across. We have done this many times. Stay where you are. Stay warm. Conserve battery. Reply only every 30 minutes. Anakah. He read the message three times. He typed, "Thank you, Anukica. I will wait." Then he folded his hands over the in reach, pressed it against his sternum, and let himself for the first time cry. Chapter 6. Anakah. Anakah Duplesis was 43 years old, a former paramedic, a mother of two, the volunteer coordinator for the Western Cape Wilderness Search and Rescue, and on Friday afternoons in autumn, a woman who liked to sit at her kitchen table in Pinelands with a cup of strong tea and the Cape Times crossword. The crossword was half done when her phone rang. She looked at the screen, set the pen down, and answered before the second ring. Dup pie Anakah it's Pierre at ge o I have an active SOS in the dude toits cliff single subject 22year-old male stellin Bosch student trapped on a ledge west of the river no east of the river path is west he's dry he's stable he has an inreach coordinates coming through to your tablet now she had her tablet open before he finished the red dot was already on the screen, blinking softly inside the dark blue line of the Molinars. She zoomed in. That's the slot, she said. That's the slot. How long ago? 38 minutes. He's been responsive throughout. I have a transcript. Send it. What's the weather? Cold front arrived 2 days early. Cloud base 200 m. Wind 60 out of the southwest. Rain. I have you down for 46 mm in the last hour at the due twitzcliff gauge. She closed her eyes for a moment. 46 mm an hour over the catchment of the Molinars meant the river was going to do exactly what it was doing now and worse before it was better. She knew this gorge. She had pulled a body out of it in 2018. A hiker who had not been carrying an inreach helicopter grounded. All right, I'm calling the team. Keep him talking. Tell him I'm on the line. He gave me his mother's number. Marina Becca Stellan Bosch. I'll handle her, too. She rang off and stood up. The kitchen was very quiet. Outside, the wind had begun to turn the seed heads of the Pampers grass. Her husband Yan was in Johannesburg until Sunday. Her older son was at university. Her younger son was at rugby practice and would walk himself home. She had perhaps 3 hours before she needed to be at the trail head in Dutitgluff. She needed to use those 3 hours well. She made the calls in the order she had made them a 100 times before, the order rehearsed and refined over a decade of these afternoons. Peter Smith first, her senior climber and the man she trusted most in moving water. Peter answered on the second ring and said, "I'm on my way." before she had finished the sentence. Then Annalie, her ropes led. Then Carol, her medic. Then the two younger climbers, Civ and Tumi, both fit, both unflapable. Then the truck, Eugene with the kit truck, who would meet them at the trail head with the rope bags and the dry suits and the flood lights. Six in the team, plus herself, plus Eugene at base. She walked through the house as she made the calls, gathering her own kit out of the cupboard in the hall. helmet, headlamp, personal harness, dry bag with thermals, gloves, a chocolate bar, the small steel flask of black coffee she always took. Her phone vibrated against her ear with an incoming call and she took it, said hold, and finished briefing to me. Then she switched to the other call. Mrs. Becca, yes, Mrs. Becca, this is Anakah Duplexie from Wilderness Search and Rescue. Your son Liam is safe. He is dry. He is on a ledge above the river in Due Toys Cliff Pass. He activated an emergency beacon. He is in regular contact with us. We have a team of six going in to bring him out tonight. I want you to know all of this before I tell you anything else. There was a silence on the line. Then a voice, very quiet, very controlled said, "Tell me everything." She told her everything. the flash flood, the gorge, the ledge, the fact that they could not fly, the fact that they would walk in, the fact that they would be at the river opposite him by 7:00 and across to him by, she chose her number carefully, by 10:00. She did not promise. She told her what they were going to try to do. You should come to the trail head, she said. Bring a thermos. Bring dry clothes for him. Bring someone to drive you home. The road is the old pass. Park at the marker that says wilderness area. There will be a man called Eugene in a yellow jacket. He will look after you. Will he be there when I arrive? Marina asked. Eugene? Yes. By 6. My son, will he be there when I arrive? Anakah paused only a fraction of a second. Not when you arrive. Tonight. We will bring him to you tonight. She heard the breath go out of the woman on the other end of the line and recognized the sound. She had made it herself eight years before when a doctor had told her about a lump that had turned out, as it happened, to be nothing. "All right," said Marina Becca. "All right," Anakah rang off. She stood for a moment in her hallway with her kid at her feet. She thought as she always thought at this stage, "Please let me do this right." Then she picked up the bag, put her boots on, and went out to her backy. Chapter 7. The cell phone tree. Marina Becca sat at her desk for perhaps a minute after she put the phone down. The rain had not yet reached Stelenbos, but the sky over the Hilderberg had gone the color of a bruise, and the lemon tree in the courtyard was tossing its branches in a wind that had not been there at lunchtime. She did not cry. She had decided 8 years ago in a hospital corridor in Cape Town with her hand on the cold steel of a door handle that she would not cry until she knew there was something to cry about. She had held to this. she would hold to it now. She rang her sister Lebet. I need you, she said. What's happened? Liam is stuck in a gorge and do Toys Cliff. Flash flood. He is safe, but they have to walk him out tonight. I'm driving up. I need you to come with me. I'll be there in 15 minutes. Bring a flask. I'll bring two. She rang Professor Nwood, Liam's supervisor, because Liam would have wanted her to. Marina. He's stuck in the due twice clue. He's safe. He activated the beacon. They're going in for him. A long pause. Then I told him not to go alone. He went anyway. He's going to be [clears throat] all right. I'll come. You don't need to come. I'll come anyway. She rang her mother in Johannesburg who did not need to know, but who would never forgive her if she found out from the news. Her mother was 81 and had buried two husbands and a son and would not be thrown by this. Her mother said, "I am praying as we speak." And rang off without further comment, which was as much love as she had ever expressed. Marina went to her son's room. She had not been in it for a week. The bed was made after a fashion. The desk was a graveyard of geology textbooks, sample bags. A labeled rock she had been told was a piece of bassalt from Lotho. On the wall above the desk was the photograph of Liam's father on the summit of Sneberg. Liam had had a copy of the same photograph framed for himself when he turned 20. He carried the original in his backpack she knew because he had told her once and she had pretended not to mind. She took down the framed photograph. She held it for a moment in both hands. Bring him home," she said to nobody in particular. "Bring him home, Andre. You bring our boy home." She set the frame back on the wall. Then she went into the kitchen and made cheese sandwiches and a flask of soup and packed Liam's spare fleece, his second pair of boots, two pairs of dry socks, his old sleeping bag, and the woolen blanket from the back of the couch. She filled a second flask with the robers he liked. She put it all in a canvas bag. Lee's bed arrived in 20 minutes, not 15, because the wind on the N2 had been brutal. She came through the door without knocking and held Marina for a long time without saying anything, which was the thing Marina needed. Then they got into Marina's car, which was newer than Lebetts and more reliable, and they drove east on the N1 into the rain. The rain reached them at Due Toys Cloff Mountain, the wipers going at full speed and the road shining black with water. Marina drove carefully. Leisbet kept up a soft running commentary about anything and everything. The rugby score, a new restaurant in Franchook, a piece of gossip from her own work, none of it important, and all of it threaded through with the kind of love that knows when silence is the crulest thing. Tell me about Liam, said Lebet after a while. What about him? Anything. The first thing that comes. Marina drove a kilometer before she answered. Then she said he used to go out with Andre's every Saturday morning before he could walk properly. Andre would carry him in that backpack. They would go up Stellenbos Mountain. [clears throat] Andre told me once when he came back, he is going to be one of those boys who needs the mountains. I said, "We will deal with that when we come to it." And now you're dealing with it. Now I am dealing with it. They reached the trail head at 20 to 6:00 in the evening. The light was already dim. Six rescue vehicles were parked along the verge with their hazard lights on. A man in a yellow high visibility jacket came forward as they pulled in. He was perhaps 60, white bearded with the kind of face that had spent years assessing the worst news a stranger could bring. Mrs. Becca. Yes, I'm Eugene. Anakah asked me to look after you. Come and sit in the truck. I'll put the kettle on. Merina got out of the car. The rain hit her face cold and full. She stood for a moment looking up the road into the cloud into the place where her son was. Somewhere she could not see, on a ledge above water she could not imagine. The wind blew the wet hair from her cheek. Her sister took her hand. "Come, sweetie," said Lebert. "Come on inside." They went inside. Chapter 8. Nightfall. On the ledge, it was already dusk by 5. The cloud had lowered until the gorge above him was a corridor of white blindness with the dark cliffs sliding up into it on either side. The river had stopped rising finally at about 20 5, leveling off some 4 m above its morning bed. It still ran with its single sustained roar. It still carried trees. It still occasionally clunked with the sound of moving stone, but it had stopped rising, and he sat on the ledge with that small fact warming him like a coal. His feet had passed beyond pain into a steady absence. He could not feel his toes inside his boots. He had taken the boots off twice and rubbed his feet vigorously inside the dry socks, and put the boots back on, and felt no different. He had eaten the last energy bar. He had eaten the half-melted cheese sandwich which had been crushed in the lid pocket. He had drunk the last of his water and refilled the bottle with caution from the curtain of clean rainwater that fell off the overhang. The water tasted of rock and of cold. The inreach had become his world. He had checked himself twice when he caught his thumb hovering over the button to type some unnecessary thing. Conserve battery, Anakah had said. He had let the screen go dark and he had stared at it and he had not pressed it. The screen was on now because a message had just come in. Team at trail head six in Eugene at base with your mother and your aunt. They are warm. Peter Smith leading rope team. ETA River edge 1900. Hold. Anakah. He typed with thick fingers. Holding. Mother safe? The reply came in 2 minutes. Mother strong. Aunt with her drinking tea. Asks if you have the down jacket on. He smiled in the dark. He typed, "Tell her yes. Thanks." A. He let the screen go dark. He had been on the ledge now for 6 and 1/2 hours. He had cried twice. He had said a sort of prayer once which had embarrassed him, although there was nobody to hear it. He had spoken aloud to his father three times, once an apology, once to ask a question he could not now remember, and once simply to say his name. He had thought about what would happen if the inreach died. He had thought about what would happen if the river rose again. He had thought briefly about what would happen if the rescue took longer than tonight, if it took into tomorrow, if he had to stay here for another night without food, and with the wet that was creeping up his legs. He had set those thoughts aside. He had decided to use his battery, his strength, his attention only on what was now. Now was He was dry under the overhang. Now was the river was no longer rising. now was people were coming for him. He thought people are coming for me. He thought six people are walking down a wet mountain at this moment to come for me. He thought about that for a long time. A man called Peter Smith was leading the rope team. He pictured Peter Smith. He pictured a tall man with a beard and a yellow helmet and the steady eyes you would want on a rope opposite you. He pictured Peter slipping on the wet path and recovering with the easy footwork of someone who had been doing this for decades. He pictured Peter standing on the bank opposite him in the dark in the rain and looking across the river at him and saying, "All right, mate. Let's get you out." He decided he was going to like Peter Smith. He reached for the head torch, which he had not yet used. He turned it on at the lowest setting. The beam, even at low, blazed into the curtain of falling water in front of him and made everything beyond it black. He turned the torch off again. He would save the torch. It was full dark by quart 6. He put on the spare beanie he had not yet used, the wool one his mother had knitted him for his 18th birthday, in the colors of the Stellen Bosch rugby team. He pulled the hood of the rainshell up over the beanie. He drew the dry pair of socks he had been saving onto his feet inside the wet boots, which made the boots tighter and warmer. He talked to himself. He said, "It's going to be all right, Liam. It's going to be all right. They are coming for you. You did the right thing. Mom knows you are alive. They are coming for you. You did the right thing." He said this for some time. At 7:00 he saw through the curtain of water and the curtain of darkness beyond it a small bobbing point of light on the far bank. His breath caught. The point of light was joined by another, then a third, then a fourth. He pressed the inreach. He typed with stiff fingers and a heart that had begun ridiculously to lift. I see your lights. The reply came in 40 seconds. We see your ledge. Hold position. We are setting up. He let the in reach drop into his lap and he watched the lights moving on the far bank. The links had lifted from Istlat at 4:15, had reached the eastern portal of the pass at 435, and had attempted to descend into the gorge from the north at 438. The pilot was Commander Marius Angelre. He had 18 years on rocraft, four of them in mountain flying. He was a careful man and an unscentimental one. He had not spoken to his crew on the descent except to call out altitudes. At 200 m above the river, he had lost the horizon to cloud. At 150, he had picked up a downdraft on the south side that pushed him sideways 12 m in 2 seconds, which his co-pilot read out as 11.8 in the bored tone of a man committing himself to memory for the inevitable inquiry. At 120, he had aborted. He had pulled up out of the gorge with his teeth set and had circled at 400 m looking down into the white. Returning to base, he had unhooked his microphone for a moment after that and said to the inside of his own helmet in African's fone meong ekisyama. Forgive me, young man. I am sorry. Then he had hooked the microphone back up and turned the links for Cape Town. In the truck at the trail head, Anakah had let her breath out slowly, opened her eyes, said, "Right, and turned to Peter Smith. We walk it. We walk it, Peter had said. He was a big man, broad in the shoulder, with gray already in his beard at 48. He had run mountain rescues in Western Cape since he was 22. He had pulled bodies out of the Cedarberg, the Hottton Tots Holland, the Hex River. He had pulled live people out of the Drackensburg in conditions that had aged him 5 years in a night. He had lived through all of it with a patience that came partly from temperament and partly from training and partly from the simple fact that he had decided as a young man that he was going to spend his life saving other people from the consequences of their own enthusiasms. And you could not do that for as long as he had done it without a steady hand. Packlist Anakah had said he had read it. Two static lines, one dynamic. Tyrion kit, dry suit, harness, helmet for the subject, stretcher in case, medic kit, flood lights, battery packs, six headlamps, six personal harnesses, six radios, six VHF spares, food and water for the team for 12 hours. Move, she had said. They had moved. Six bodies in red and orange soft shells out of the truck and onto the path with rope bags on their backs. The path already a stream by half 5. Civ at the front because she was the youngest and the fastest. Tumi behind her with the rope bags. Carol the medic in the middle. Annalie with the rigging kit. Peter at the back hurting everyone through the worst of the descents. His big hands resting once on Civ's shoulder when she slipped on a contour and saying nothing more than steady. Anakah had stayed at the truck because the rules said you did not put both your most senior climber and your coordinator on the same team in the same gorge. She had hated this rule for 10 years and had obeyed it for 10 years. Now she stood at the door of the truck with her radio in her hand and her eyes on the satellite map and the small red dot of Liam Becker's beacon. and she had watched the six green dots of her team's locator beacons begin painfully slowly to inch down the contour line. In the back of the truck, Marina Becca sat with her flask of Roy Boss in both hands. She had not drunk any of it. Beside her, Lebet had quietly taken Eugene's work tablet onto her lap and zoomed in on the satellite map. She had pointed at the red dot. "That's him," she said. "That's our boy." Marina nodded. They're going down for him. Look, those are the green dots. 1 2 3 4 5 6. They're going down for him. Yes, said Marina. He activated the beacon. Ma, said Leisbet. He thought to do it. He was clever enough and brave enough to do it. Yes, said Marina. She took finally a sip of the tea. Chapter 10. The climbing the path down to the Molinars in fair weather is rated as moderate. In the cold front of 22nd April 2026, falling rain at 46 mm an hour with a southwesterly gusting to 70. It was something else. Steve Mmbu, 26 years old and the daughter of a bazer attorney, led down the first switchback at a pace that was as fast as it could safely be and no faster. She had her headlamp on the brightest setting and the rain coming through its beam like a million white needles. Her boots punched into mud that had not been there at 3. Her ropes bag, 22 kilos, sat high and tight on her back, her own small thermos of water and her own headlamp battery clipped to the strap at her chest. Peter had come forward at this point. He had stood with Civ on the lip of the cliff and looked at the water for 10 seconds, the rain hammering on the brim of his helmet. Round, he had said. They had gone round, which had cost them 20 minutes. They had moved back along the contour for 200 meters until the cliff narrowed enough to span with a fallen yellowwood, and Peter had stepped onto the log first, walking it with the calm of a man crossing a bench. They had followed one at a time, with hands on the fixed line he had run across as he went. 20 minutes lost was 20 minutes lost. Anakah had said nothing on the radio because there was nothing useful to say. By 6, they had reached the broad terrace 20 m above the river. The river was no longer the river of the morning. The river was a slate colored monster running fast enough to throw a horizontal spray off the standing waves, and the noise of it had the quality of a sustained mechanical scream that swallowed everything else. They had to use their radios to communicate over a distance of less than 10 m. Civ was the first to put her headlamp across the river and pick out the ledge. The ledge was a horizontal seam in the buff sandstone, perhaps 4 m above the present water level and 70 m downstream. On the ledge in the white throw of her beam, she saw a small huddled figure in a yellow rainshell sitting with knees drawn up. The figure raised one hand. Civ raised hers. She turned to Peter. "There," she said. Peter looked across, swept his beam over the ledge, took it in for 10 seconds. "He's all right," he said, half to her and half to himself. "He's all right," he turned to Annalie. "Tyoleon, anchors here, here, here." he pointed with his torch beam two boulders the size of cars and a third anchor he wanted them to set with chocks in a long crack on the cliff above. I want to back up on each anchor. I want three lines, one static, one dynamic, one tag. We will pull him in a pzle harness on the dynamic with a break on the static. Carol, you set up under that overhang there right above the high water line and you have him in the warming bag inside 90 seconds of arriving. Civ, you and Tumi are with me in the water. Annalie runs the lines. Questions? There were no questions. They built the anchors in the dark and the rain in 50 minutes. The third anchor, the chocks in the cliff crack, took the longest. It was running at a speed he estimated by standard guesswork at 5 to 7 m a second. No, there was a second method. You could fire a line across. Peter had a Plumea line gun in his pack, a small CO2 powered launcher that fired a polyropylene messenger over distances of up to 50 m. Then you are going to put the harness on and we are going to bring you across. Understood. Understood. Good lad. Peter looked up at Steve and Tumi. He nodded. Steve let out a long slow breath she had not noticed she was holding. They began to feed the static line across. Chapter 11. The crossing. Peter had been calm but exact. Three blows to seat, two to test. Liam had hammered with hands that did not feel like his own, and the peton had rung true on the third blow. The bag bumped over the river surface twice, kicking up little bursts of spray, and once a piece of timber the length of his arm skipped over the line and made him flinch. He reeled the bag onto his ledge. He opened it with shaking fingers. Inside was a Pzel seat harness, a chest harness, a screw gate carabiner the size of his fist, a small headlamp already fitted with batteries, and a folded piece of paper. He unfolded the paper in neat block capitals in waterproof pen. It said, "Sit harness, feet through loops, pull up, tighten buckles, chest harness, arms through, clip to sit, carabiner onto blay loop, screw shut, call ready. We will clip you to the dynamic line. When you feel tension, stand, step off, keep feet high, trust the line. You are going to be fine. He read the paper twice. He laughed once, which made him cough. He tore the paper in half, folded the halves, put them in his chest pocket. He was going to keep them. He put the harness on. The buckles fought his fingers. He won. He clipped the carabiner to the blay loop and screwed it shut. He picked up the inreach. He typed, "Harness on. Ready." The reply came in 12 seconds. Standby for tension. The line in his hands went slack for a moment and then he felt it lift. Take weight. Become a living thing across the gorge. Peter's voice came over the radio. Liam, we have the dynamic line clipped to your harness via the Terolon. The static is live. The break is on. When I count three, you stand up and step off the ledge into the air. You will swing. You will not fall. The line will hold you and we will pull you across. Keep your feet high. Look at me. Don't look down. Do you hear me? I hear you. Stand up. He stood up. His legs nearly gave way. He had not stood properly in 7 hours. He pressed his back to the cliff and pushed himself upright by inches, the harness biting into his thighs, the weight of him taken half by his own legs and half by the line he was clipped to. Good. Now step off. He looked across through the curtain of falling water and the dark and the spray of the river. He saw on the far bank a row of headlamps, four of them. The lights bobbed and steadied as the wearers turned to look at him. In the center of the row, one beam was steady on his face, blazing into his eyes. He raised a hand to shield them. "Sorry," said Peter's voice in his ear. "Siv his face there, better." All right, Liam, step off. He stepped off. For one long instant, he was a man falling. Then the line caught him, and he was a man swinging. He swung out over the river, the harness biting harder, his feet held high, as he had been told, and the world inverted into a roar of water and rain and air, and he made a small involuntary noise. And then he was being pulled, pulled steadily through the air, and the headlamps on the far bank grew larger and brighter, and he could see now that the central headlamp belonged to a tall man with a beard, whose face was lit from below by the reflected light of his own torch, and who, as Liam came in, reached out with both hands, and took him by the chest harness, and swung him onto the bank like a man bringing in a fish. Got him," said the tall man. "Got him," Steve echoed, and her arms went round Liam from the other side, taking weight he had not known he still had. He was on the ground. He was on solid ground. He was sitting on wet earth and there were people around him and one of them was unscrewing the carabiner at his waist and another of them was peeling the wet rainshell off his shoulders and another Carol was kneeling in front of him with a thermometer in one hand and a foil bag in the other saying, "All right, mate. Look at me. What's your name?" Liam. Liam what? Liam Becca. Where are we? Do tots clof. Good. Last meal. Cheese sandwich. 2:00 maybe. Good. We're going to put you in the warming bag now. Don't fight us. I won't fight you. They put him in the warming bag, peeled off his wet boots, wrapped his feet in drywool, slid his arms into a dry fleece. Civ held him under one shoulder. Tumi held him under the other. Peter stood above him with the rain running off the brim of his helmet, looking down at him with the kind of expression Liam had only ever seen on his father. "You did everything right, Liam," said Peter. "You stayed where you were. You used the beacon. You kept yourself dry. You did everything right." "Thank you," said Liam. "Thank you. Thank you." Peter put one big hand on his head briefly for a second only and then turned away and began to give orders for the climb out. Up at the truck on the satellite map, the small red dot that had blinked on Anakah Duples's screen for nearly 9 hours blinked twice more in its old position and then jumped abruptly 8 m west across the line of the river onto the green dots of her team. Anakah stood up so fast she hit her head on the truck roof. "Marina," she said. "Marina, they've got him." In the back of the truck, Marina Becka put her face into her sister's shoulder for the first time that day and made the sound she had been keeping in for 9 hours. Leisbet held her. Outside in the rain, Eugene took off his yellow jacket and pumped his fist once at the sky. Chapter 12. 23 hours. The climb out took 5 hours because they would not move Liam fast and because the path had become in places a stream they had to wait up. They put him in the middle of the team with Civ in front and Peter behind and they roped him short to Carol on his right who could feel through the line every time he stumbled. They stopped twice to feed him broth from a flask. They stopped once to change his socks. The wind dropped sometime after midnight, and the rain settled into a steady cold drizzle that was worse in some ways than the downpour because there was no urgency to it, only the long patient soaking of bone. They reached the trail head at 5 minutes 2 on the morning of Saturday, 25th April, 2026. They had been on the mountain for 8 and 1/2 hours. Liam had been on the mountain for 20 hours by then. The flash flood had begun by Liam's [clears throat] first sample of the riverbed at 17 minutes to 12 on Friday morning. It had now been 23 hours. In the back of Eugene's truck, Marina Becca had finally fallen asleep at midnight, her head on her sister's shoulder. Lebet had not slept. Lebet had been watching the windscreen. Leisbet saw the headlamps come up out of the rodendrrons at the top of the path. She counted them. Six. And one in the middle, lower, supported on either side. That was not a rescuer. She shook Marina awake. "They're here," she said. "Marina, they are here." Marina was out of the truck before she was fully awake. She stumbled in the mud and Leisbet caught her elbow. They went forward together into the throw of Eugene's flood light. And then they were running. And then they were not running because Liam had stopped at the edge of the light and was simply standing there in his foil blanket and his two big borrowed fleece and his bare scalp where the wool beanie had been pushed up off his ears and he was looking at his mother and she was looking at him and neither of them seemed able to take the last 6 m. It was Peter in the end who put one big hand on Liam's back and pushed him forward. "Go on, lad," he said very quietly. Liam went on. They held each other in the rain for a long time. Marina did not say anything. Liam did not say anything. Peter and Steve and Tumi and Carol and Annalie stood back in a quiet semicircle and looked at the ground or at the sky or at each other. with the kind of professional and respectful patience of people who had been here many times before. Anakah Duplesis came forward eventually and touched Marina's elbow. Mrs. Becca, she said, we need to take him to Worcester for an assessment. Standard. He's in good shape, but we don't take chances with cold like this. Yes, said Marina. Yes, of course. You can ride with him. Yes, Lebet. I'll bring the car. Eugene will lead you in. Merina turned to Anuka. She wanted for one wild second to hold her too, to put her arms around this red jacketed stranger and say something enormous. Instead, she said, "Thank you," which was not enormous enough and was the only word she had. "You're welcome," said Anakah Duplesi, who had heard it many times and meant something different each time. "You are very welcome, Marina." They drove down the pass in convoy at 20 km an hour. Eugene leading in the kit truck. Anakah behind him, the two ambulances next. Marina and Liam in the second ambulance. Lebbit bringing up the rear in Marina's car. The rain was thinning now, and to the east over the Hex River Mountains, a gray false dawn had begun to feel its way along the horizon. In the ambulance, Liam slept with his head against his mother's shoulder. She did not move for the entire 40-minute drive. She watched the side of his face in the dim red light of the ambulance interior and counted his breaths. She did not cry. She had decided long ago that she would not cry until she knew there was something to cry about. She decided now that this was not a thing to cry about. This was a thing she would carry instead for the rest of her life in the pocket where she kept the lemon tree and the photograph on Sneberg and the long quiet evenings on Rhinereld Street with her son at the kitchen table doing his homework. At Worcester Provincial Hospital, they wheeled him into a warm white room and a doctor with kind eyes pronounced him after an hour of examination to be alive, mildly hypothermic, mildly dehydrated. A small contusion on the left palm, a blister on the right heel, otherwise alive. Marina took Anakah Duples's hand at the door of the hospital before Anakah left. She looked into the rescuer's face for a long moment. "He told me," she said in one of the messages that he could see your lights coming down the mountain and that you were the most beautiful thing he had ever seen. Anakah smiled slowly. He said that to me too. I want you to know, said Marina, what you did. I do know, said Anakah. Go and sit with your boy, Marina. Marina went and sat with her boy. Epilogue. October. In the second week of October, when the spring rains had stopped and the Western Cape had moved into the dry blue weather of early summer, Liam Becker went back to the due to Cliff Pass alone. He drove the same road. He parked at the same trail head. He walked the same path down through the finos and the wild olives. The pelgonium and the buu were in bloom. A pair of clipbringer broke from a thicket and bounded along the contour with their odd springing gate. He stood and watched them disappear into a fold of the slope and felt again what the mountain always gave him. He reached the river at 9 in the morning. The Molinars was clear and shallow and braided through pale stones. It moved at the speed of a slow walk. He stood on the gravel apron where he had eaten his apple 6 months earlier, and he looked across at the cliff opposite, and he found, after a moment, the dark seam of his ledge. It looked smaller then. He remembered it looked entirely ordinary. He took off his pack and sat down on a flat rock beside the river. He took out a small gray pebble he had carried with him from theneberg 3 weeks earlier on a trip he had made with his mother. He had told her what he wanted to do with the pebble. She had nodded and given him the pebble and asked him to bring back a stone from the molaz in exchange. He waited into the river up to his knees. The water was cold, but only the ordinary cold of a clear mountain river. He bent and placed theneberg pebble carefully on top of a flat granite cobble in the middle of the current. He looked at it for a moment. He did not say anything aloud because there was no need. He picked up a small piece of pale Molinar's riverstone, smooth and oval, the size and weight of a robin's egg. He put it in his pocket. He climbed out, dried his legs with a towel, put his boots back on, shouldered his pack. On the way up the path, he passed the place where 6 months earlier he had been crouched on the ledge looking down at the brown water. He paused. He looked across. He thought about Peter Smith, who had retired from Active Rescue 2 months ago and now ran trainings out of an office in Belleville. He thought about Anakah Duplexi, who had emailed him on his birthday last month. He thought about Steven Fmbu, who had become somehow a friend, and who had taught him in three weekends since June how to swim a moving line. He thought about Carol and Tumi and Annalie and Eugene in his yellow jacket. He thought about the unnamed woman at GEOS, who had taken his first SOS. He thought about the pilot of the links, whose name he had since learned, and to whom he had written a letter of thanks that had been replied to with a short dignified note in Africans. He thought about his father. He climbed up the path through the finos and the wild olives in the bright October sun, and at the top, when he reached his car, he sat for a long time on the bonnet, and looked back down into the gorge. Then he drove home to Stellenbosh where his mother had cooked oxtail and was waiting for him on the stoop with a glass of pinotage and the Cape Times crossword half. He sat down opposite her. He put the small piece of riverstone on the table between them. She looked at it. She looked at him. 12 down, she said. Eight letters devoted. Faithful, he said. She wrote it in. Bring the wine closer," she said. He brought the wine closer. Outside in the courtyard, the lemon tree carried four yellow lamps in its dark leaves, and the wind came soft over the Helderberg from the southwest with no freight in it at all. End. 23 hours is a work of fiction. The D Toys Cloff Pass and the Molinar's River are real, as is the Wilderness Search and Rescue Western Cape, whose volunteers go out in conditions like these many times a year, and to whom the author owes a quiet and continuing debt of gratitude. All characters in this nolla are imagined. Any resemblance to actual rescuers, students, parents, or pilots is the result of the author's admiration for them, not of biography.

transcript.fullText: You ever walk into a house and feel it watching you? Not just creaky floors or drafty windows, but something deeper. Like the walls themselves are alive, holding secrets they're dying to spill. That's what happened to Sarah and Ethan when they inherited Willow House. A dream home, they thought. A fresh start. But some houses don't let you start over. Some houses want you to stay forever. Sarah and Ethan were city kids burned out by rent hikes and 80hour work weeks. So when Sarah's great uncle passed and left them Willow House, a sprawling Victorian mansion in the middle of nowhere, Maine, they saw it as a miracle. Three stories of carved oak, stained glass, and history. The kind of place you'd see on a postcard, surrounded by gnarled willows that looked like they'd been clawing at the sky for centuries. The lawer said it had been empty for years, but it was theirs, free and clear. They packed up their tiny apartment, quit their jobs, and drove north, chasing a quieter life. Their first night in Willow House was October 31st, Halloween, because of course it was. The air was crisp, the moon a sickle slicing through the clouds. They laughed about it, joking about ghosts as they hauled boxes inside. The house was grand but warm, peeling wallpaper, dusty chandeliers, and a faint smell of mildew. Ethan, ever the optimist, called it character. Sarah wasn't so sure. Something about the place felt heavy, like the air was thicker inside than out. They were unpacking in the master bedroom when Sarah heard it first. A whisper. Not words, not yet. Just a soft, rhythmic murmur like wind trapped in a pipe. She froze, her hand on a stack of sweaters. Ethan, you hear that? He was halfway under the bed, wrestling with a loose floorboard. Just the house settling, he said, voice muffled. Old places talk. Sarah nodded, but her skin prickled. The sound wasn't coming from the pipes. It was coming from the walls. By the third night, the whispers weren't just noise. They were words. Fragments at first stay. Mine forever, slipping through the plaster-like smoke. Sarah woke up at 3:00 a.m. heart pounding, convinced she'd heard her name. Ethan slept through it, snoring softly. She shook him awake, but the whispers stopped the moment his eyes opened. "You're stressed," he said, pulling her close. "New place, new noises. It's nothing." "But Sarah saw the flicker in his eyes." He'd heard something, too. They tried to ignore it. They painted over the faded wallpaper, scrubbed the floors, and blasted music to drown out the quiet. But the whispers grew bolder. They followed Sarah to the kitchen. Ethan to the attic. One night, while Ethan was fixing a leaky faucet, the walls hissed. "She's not yours." He dropped his wrench, face pale. "Okay," he admitted. That wasn't the wind. They called a contractor thinking maybe it was bad insulation or air vents playing tricks. The guy walked through, tapped the walls, and shrugged. "Solid as a rock," he said. "No pipes rattling, no drafts. You sure it's not mice?" Sarah wanted to scream. "Mice don't whisper your name. Mice don't know your fears." That night, the wall spoke again. "He'll leave you." Sarah clutched Ethan's hand, but he was staring at the ceiling, eyes wide. "It said my name, too," he whispered. Desperate, they dug into the house's history. The town library was a musty archive of yellowed records. Willow House, built in 1873, had a grim past. Its first owner, Elias Willow, vanished after his wife died in childbirth. The next family, the Grayson's, lost three kids to accidents in the house. In the 1920s, a recluse named Margaret lived there alone until she didn't. Her body was found in the cellar. No cause of death. Every owner after either fled or disappeared. The librarian, an old woman with trembling hands, leaned close. "That house doesn't like company," she said. "It keeps what it loves. Back at Willow House, things got worse. The whispers weren't just words. Now they were personal. After the library, Sarah couldn't shake the librarian's warning. That night, while Ethan slept, she crept to the attic, flashlight trembling in her hand. The air was thick with cobwebs and the scent of decay. Amid the cluttered trunks, broken chairs, a cracked mirror, she spotted a leatherbound diary wedged behind a beam. The name Margaret was etched in fading ink on the cover. The same Margaret from the records, the recluse who died in the cellar. The pages were yellow, the handwriting shaky. Margaret's entries began innocently notes about the house's beauty, the willow's grace. But by page 10, the tone shifted. The walls speak, she wrote. At first, it was comfort voices of my lost family. But now they demand. They know my sins. Sarah's stomach churned. Margaret described sleepless nights, the walls pulsing like a heartbeat, faces pressing through the plaster, begging her to join them. One entry read, "I tried to leave, but the roots, they pulled me back. The house loves me too much. Ethan found Sarah hours later, hunched over the diary, eyes wide. Listen to this, she whispered, reading aloud. October 12th, 1923. They showed me my death. A knife, my own hand. I can't fight it. Ethan grabbed the book, skimming ahead. The final page was smeared with what looked like blood. I go to the cellar tonight. The house promises peace. A crude sketch showed a mass of roots, faces screaming from the walls. transcript.fullText: The neon haze of New York City's Time Square buzzed like a fever dream, its lights bleeding into the night sky. Jake, a wiry guy in his late 20s from Chicago, hauled his beat up suitcase through the crowded streets, the wheels scraping against the pavement. His dream trip to the Big Apple, a whirlwind two weeks of hitting every landmark from the Statue of Liberty to the dive bars of Brooklyn, had left him running on fumes. His legs achd from days of pounding the concrete, and his eyes burned with the kind of tiredness that sleep could barely touch. It was well past midnight, and all he wanted was to crash at the capsule hotel he'd booked on a whim. a quirky spot tucked away in the heart of Manhattan. But the night, as Jake was about to learn, had a darker plan in store. The capsule hotel looked like something out of a sci-fi flick, its glass front glowing faintly against the city's chaos. Inside the lobby was stark, white walls, a lone fern in a pot, and a night clerk who barely looked up from her phone. She handed Jake a wristband stamped with capsule 616 and a key for a locker that was way too small for his oversted bag. He mumbled a thanks, his voice rough from exhaustion, and headed to the showers. The lukewarm water did nothing for the knots in his shoulders, but it was a start. All he could think about was crawling into that pod and passing out. The capsule room was eerie, like stepping into a morg designed by Apple. Rows of sleek coffin-like pods stacked floor to ceiling, each one glowing faintly with a soft blue light. It was quiet, saved for the low hum of the AC, but the air felt heavy like it was holding its breath. Jake found capsule 616 slid open the door and crawled inside. The space was tight, just enough room to lie down or sit up with a thin mattress and a control panel of buttons he didn't bother to figure out. He kicked off his sneakers, pulled the sliding door shut, and watched a faint green light flicker on outside, marking the pod as occupied. His head hit the pillow, and the world faded to black. Sleep came fast, a heavy, dreamless pull. But it didn't last. Maybe 10 minutes passed before a sound clawed him back to consciousness. A voice low and steady, seeping through the pod's thin walls. It was a woman, he thought, her words tumbling out in a relentless stream, no pauses, no breaths. Jake lay there, eyes halfopen in the dark, trying to make sense of it. Was she on the phone practicing a speech? The language wasn't English. Too guttural, too fast, with hard rolling Rs that didn't sound like Spanish or anything he'd heard in the city. German maybe, or something older, stranger. The longer he listened, the more it unnerved him like the voice wasn't meant for anyone to hear. Jake groaned, dragging a hand over his face. He was wiped out. Days of walking 10 hours straight, hauling his suitcase through subway stations, skipping meals to squeeze in one more museum. His body begged for rest. But that voice wouldn't quit. It went on for what felt like forever, a half hour at least, each word blending into the next until it was less a voice and more a force pressing against his skull. He tried shoving the pillow over his ears, but it was no use. Every time he started to drift, the voice sharpened, yanking him awake like a hook. Irritation simmering, Jake fumbled in the dark until his fingers found the control panel. a faint click and the pod glowed with a dim sickly light. He spotted a dial labeled white noise and cranked it up. A storm roared to life, rain hammering, thunder rolling loud enough to drown out the voice. It was still there, faint, like a whisper under the waves, but Jake could deal with that. He let out a shaky breath, dimmed the light, and sank back into the mattress. the storm wrapping around him like a shield. But the shield didn't hold. 10 minutes later, a new sound tore through the rain. A whale, sharp and piercing like an air raid siren gone feral. It wasn't part of the white noise. It was coming from the pod next door. Jake's eyes snapped open, his pulse spiking. The whale twisted, rising and falling. A sound so raw it made his skin prickle. It wasn't human, not entirely. Beneath it, the voice kept going. That same unbroken stream of words now layered with the whale in a way that felt wrong, like two signals crossing in a bad dream. His mind scrambled for answers. Was she hurt? Crazy? But the voice hadn't stopped. Not for a second. And the whale was too steady, too deliberate. It was 2:00 a.m. and Jake's nerves were fraying like old rope. He'd had enough. His body was a lead weight. His brain fogged with exhaustion, but anger burned through the haze. Whoever this was, they knew damn well how thin these walls were. They knew they were keeping everyone awake. "Shut the hell up!" he yelled, slamming his fist against the wall. The impact stung his knuckles, but it felt good. A spark of control in the chaos. Silence fell heavy and sudden. The whale stopped. The voice cut off. Jake's breath caught, his ears ringing in the quiet. He waited, fists clenched, expecting something, anything. Then the wall exploded. A bone rattling thud shook the pod. The wall bending inward with the force of the blow. Another hit, then another, each one louder, harder, like someone was throwing their whole body against it. The pod creaked, the plastic groaning under the assault. The voice came back, no longer a murmur, but a scream, jagged and unhinged, cutting through the storm like a blade. Jake scrambled back, his back slamming against the opposite wall, his heart pounding so hard he thought it might burst. The blows kept coming, relentless, rhythmic, the wall buckling with each one. He pressed a hand to it, feeling the vibrations ripple through his palm. It wasn't just shaking. It was giving like it might cave in. "What the fuck?" Jake shouted, but the scream swallowed his voice. The words were still gibberish, a torrent of sound that felt like it was crawling inside his head. The air in the pod was stifling the walls too close. The storm now just a faint hum beneath the chaos. Another blow hit so hard it knocked his phone off the tiny shelf, the screen flashing as it hit the mattress. Jake's hands shook as he grabbed for the door handle. He had to get out, find the clerk, get to another floor, anywhere but here. He yanked the door open and stumbled out, his bare feet slapping the cold floor. The green occupied light blinked off. The banging stopped. The scream died. The silence was worse. thick, unnatural, like the room was watching him. Jake froze, his breath hitching. His eyes flicked to the pod next door. The indicator light was off. His stomach twisted, a cold sweat breaking out across his skin. Just a busted light, he told himself. But the lie felt hollow. The silence pressed in, heavy, alive. He shouldn't have done it. He knew he shouldn't, but his hand moved anyway, reaching for the neighboring pod's handle. Every horror movie he'd ever seen screamed at him to run, but his feet wouldn't move. He gripped the handle, his pulse roaring in his ears and slowly slid the door open. The pod was empty. No bag, no shoes, no sign anyone had ever been there. just a bare mattress and a dead control panel staring back at him. Jake's breath came in shallow gasps. He checked the light again, still off. The air felt wrong, colder, like it was clinging to him. He backed away, his eyes darting around the room, half expecting something to lunge from the shadows. Grabbing his sneakers, he bolted for the locker room, leaving his suitcase behind. He spent the night on a bench under the harsh fluorescent lights, every creek of the building making him flinch. Dawn broke, gray and heavy, the city's hum filtering through the walls. Jake dragged himself to the lobby, his wristband clutched in a trembling hand. The clerk was there, her eyes flicking up from her phone, narrowing as she saw him. He tried to explain. his voice cracked and uneven. Last night in 6:16, someone was screaming, banging on the walls, but the pod next to mine, it was empty. The clerk's face stayed blank, but her hands paused, her fingers tightening around the edge of the counter. She took the wristband, turning it over in her hands. Her eyes widened just for a second before she schooled her expression. This says 919," she said, her voice too calm. "You were in the wrong pod." But the way she looked at him, quick, sharp, like she was hiding something, said more than her words. She slipped the wristband into a drawer and locked it. Her movements too deliberate. Jake nodded, too drained to argue. He didn't want to know what she wasn't saying. He checked out, burning through his emergency cash to book a real hotel for the last two nights. As he stepped into the morning light, Time Square's chaos felt distant, like it belonged to someone else. The memory of that empty pod, that scream, the clerk's fleeting look. It clung to him, a cold weight that followed him all the way back to Chicago. New York had been his dream, a city that never sleeps. But Capsule 616 had shown him a darkness that didn't rest either.

The voice was unmistakable. same tone, same speech pattern, but the message carried metadata showing it was transmitted 3 hours into the future. He ran diagnostics. No anomaly, no interference. Kale tried to respond, sending a reply packet through subspace. No return. only more echoes, each slightly more corrupted than the last. In the first recording, he warned himself to turn back. In the next, he sounded terrified. By the fifth transmission, the voice was screaming, not in pain, but in confusion, as if he didn't remember sending the message at all. He tried to reset the ship's core, but the AI responded with a tone he'd never programmed. A faint human breath before speaking. Kale Draven detected. Temporal synchronization failing. Estimated divergence 107%. Then silence except the hum. A low vibration coming from the hull, rhythmic, like a heartbeat. When he placed his hand on the console, it pulsed back. Outside the viewport, the anomaly shimmerred. It was no longer a distant vortex, but a reflection. An image of his own ship hanging opposite him in the void, mirroring every move. Only one difference. The mirrored ship's lights were off, dead. And yet, someone inside was moving. He stared, breath caught in his chest as a figure in the reflection slowly turned. It was him. Same suit, same scar across the cheek. But the eyes hollow, silver white, like frozen glass. He heard the voice again. You shouldn't have followed the signal, Kale. The fold doesn't copy, it remembers. Panic surged. He engaged full reverse thrusters, but the ship didn't move. The reflection did, accelerating towards him instead. The readings went insane.
