transcript.fullText: My name's Ethan Carter, a senior at Lincoln High in Columbus, Ohio. It's March 2020, and the cafeteria clock reads half noon. The air's thick with the smell of greasy pizza and sweat. I'm slumped at a table poking at a soggy slice while my friends Mia and Jake argue about graduation. This new Corona virus is all over the news and people are freaking out that it might cancel our ceremony. I roll my eyes, tossing a crust onto my tray. No way it's hitting us, I say. Mostly to shut them up. It's just some flu in China or whatever. Columbus feels like a bubble. Safe, boring, untouchable. Jake pushes his tray aside, his voice low. Ethan, my dad's a nurse. He says it's already in Ohio. Hospitals are getting slammed. Mia nods, twirling a strand of hair nervously. My mom's buying like a 100 masks. She says it's going to get bad. I lean back, smirking. Your mom's paranoid. We're graduating next week. They're not canceling [ __ ] But their words nag at me like a splinter I can't pull out. The cafeteria's a mess of noise. Kids laughing, trays clattering when the intercom screeches. Principal Harper's voice cuts through sharp and frayed like he's about to lose it. All students, get to your classrooms now. Grab your emergency kits and masks. We've got confirmed cases of a deadly virus spreading fast. I repeat, schools on lockdown. Move. His words land like a bomb. Kids scream, chairs topple, and everyone's running, shoving, tripping over backpacks. My pulse spikes, and I grab my bag, bolting with Mia and Jake toward our home room, class 12A. The hallways are chaos. Lockers slamming, sneakers squeaking, some freshmen crying in a corner. Men in hazmat suits patrol like ghosts, their eyes hidden behind foggy visors. The air feels wrong, heavy like it's pressing down on my chest. We pile into our classroom where Ms. Delgado, our teacher, is already shouting, "Tape the windows. Seal the doors. Masks on. Let's go." Her hands shake, but she's trying to hold it together. We scramble, taping butcher paper over the windows, stuffing towels under the door. Mia's breathing hard through her mask, and Jake's muttering something about his mom. I pull my mask on, the fabric hot and suffocating. The room dims, the paper blocking the sunlight, and we hunker down, waiting. An hour drags by and it's dead quiet. My phone's got no bars. None of us can text our parents. I try to joke, say something about zombie apocalypses, but my voice cracks and nobody laughs. The silence is worse than the noise. Then the intercom buzzes again. It's Harper, but his voice is off. Slow, flat, like he's reading from a script he doesn't understand. Teachers, take off your masks and head outside. Leave one student in charge. You're needed to clean the school ground. Students, stay put. Stay calm. We'll update you soon. The words hang in the air. Wrong. Mia whispers. Why no masks? That's crazy. Jake's eyes are wide. He didn't sound like himself. M. Delgado hesitates, her fingers twitching. I have to go, she says, finally pulling off her mask. Her face is pale, her eyes darting to the door. She turns to Mr. Patel, the aid. You're in charge. She steps out and the door locks behind her with a heavy click. Mr. Patel paces, muttering about protocol. Nobody moves, he says, but he sounds like he's convincing himself. We sit in the dark, the lights off to avoid attention, though from what? I don't know. The school feels alive, like it's breathing, watching. Two hours pass. No updates, no sounds, just our own ragged breathing. My stomach's in knots, and I keep checking my phone even though it's useless. Then it starts a sharp rhythmic noise from the hallway. Tick, tick, tick. Like nails on tile. It's faint at first, but it gets louder, closer, deliberate. My heart's pounding so hard I think it'll burst. We freeze, eyes locked on the door. Through the papered windows, a shadow moves, tall, human- shaped, but wrong. Its head jerks at an angle no neck should allow, and its steps are too smooth, like it's gliding. Mr. Walsh, some idiot, Tyler, the class loudmouth borch, blurts out. The shadow stops. Its head snaps toward our window, a perfect 90° like a machine. My blood turns to ice. The thing raises an arm and there's a tearing sound, wet and sharp like skin splitting. The silhouette shifts and I see writhing shapes where a face should be snaking, twisting things. It slams its arm against the glass, the impact shaking the frame. The ticking turns frantic, joined by a scraping like teeth on wood. It's at the door now, clawing, gnawing. It's going to break in, I hiss, barely audible. Panic erupts. Kids dive for cover under desks behind shelves. I lunge for a locker, squeezing inside and yanking the door shut. The metal's cold, the slats giving me a sliver of a view. Mia's under a table. Jake's crammed in a cabinet. Tyler's still out there fumbling for a spot. The door splinters and the thing steps in. It's Mr. Walsh's body, but it's not him. His head is a horror. Four hollow eyes glowing faintly, a round mouth packed with needle-like teeth. Tentacles spilling out like they're alive. Its arms twitch too long, too thin, and every step makes that tick tick tick. The air reeks of rot like a flooded basement left to fester. It moves slowly, smashing desks, dragging its claws across the chalkboard. I hold my breath, praying it doesn't hear my heart. An hour creeps by. It doesn't leave. It's hunting, methodical, sniffing out every corner. Tyler the [ __ ] thinks it's gone and slips out. He tiptoes toward the door, but the thing's head whips around. He freezes, then sprints for the locker next to mine, slamming it shut. His breathing's loud, gasping. The ticking stops. The thing turns, its tentacles quivering like they can smell him. It's close now. So close I can hear the wet slither of its face. I peek through the slats. My hand shaking. On my tenth glance, I see it clear as day. Its eyes are pits, its mouth a churning void. This isn't a nightmare. It's real. Then it speaks in Mr. Walsh's voice, but twisted like a radio tuned wrong. Hey kid, open the door. Let's talk. The words crawl into my skull, oily and cold. My mind blanks. My body moves on its own. My fingers twitching toward the latch. I scream inside. No, stop. But my hand jerks, unlatching the door. The locker swings open. The thing's right there, its tentacles curling toward me. I try to shout to beg, but my mouth betrays me. Am I next? I say. The word's not mine. Its mouth stretches almost a grin. Next. Next, it hums. A sound like breaking glass. Darkness swallows me whole. I wake on the hallway floor. My body aching. The ticking's gone. The school silent. My hands feel heavy. Wrong like they're not mine. I stumble to a window. The paper ripped away. Outside the courtyards empty. No cops, no hazmat guys, no Miss Delgado. The skies a sickly yellow ash drifting like snow. My reflection stares back, but it's not me. My eyes are sunken, my jaw twitches, and something moves under my skin slithering. I gag, but my throats tight like it's not mine anymore. Footsteps echo. Mia and Jake step out of a classroom, their faces ghost white. Ethan, Mia whispers, her voice breaking. I try to answer to say I'm still here, but a growl comes out instead. Jake grabs Mia's arm, pulling her back. Their fear cuts deeper than the thing inside me. I want to scream, to run to them, but my legs lurch forward, my hands reaching. The ticking starts again, not outside, but in my chest, my bones. The intercom crackles. Harper's voice smooth and inhuman. All students, head to the courtyard. Time to clean house. My lips curl into a smile. Well, I didn't choose. Mia and Jake Bolt, but I know they're trapped. We all are. The thing in me hums warm and hungry. It's not just Walsh or Harper. It's the hazmat guys, the teachers, maybe the whole damn town. And now it's me. I walk to the courtyard, the ticking guiding me. The air's thick with that rotting stench, and shadows move in the corners. Other kids, other teachers, their eyes hollow, their steps ticking. Graduation's dead, but this is worse. This thing's no virus. It's older, deeper, something that's been waiting, and it's spreading one body at a time. I see Mia and Jake in the distance, hiding. But the ticking in me knows where they are. It always knows.

transcript.fullText: I just got back from a mental health camping trip up in the Aderondex. No phone, no laptop, just an old emergency radio and my trusty digital camera. Work had been grinding me down, and honestly, life was starting to feel like a noose tightening around my neck. I needed to get away to hit reset. And for a while, it worked. The woods, the quiet, the crisp air, it was like a shot of life back into my veins. I came home feeling like a new man, like I'd been handed a clean slate to start over. But I didn't just come back new. I came back wrong. Let me take you back. The trip was everything I needed. I set up camp by a glassy lake, pines towering around me, their branches whispering in the breeze. I spent my days fishing, the water so still it felt like a mirror to another world. At night, I'd build a fire, watch the flames dance, and let my mind unravel. I even ran into a few other campers, folks out there for the same reason, trying to find some peace. We swapped stories, shared a few beers. It was normal. It was good. For the first time in years, I could breathe. I snapped a ton of pictures, too. My camera was always out catching the lake at dawn, the glow of the fire, the way the trees seemed to lean in at night. By the end of the week, I had a whole memory card full. When it was time to go, I packed up, said goodbye to the woods, and drove my pickup back to Syracuse that first night in my own bed. Man, it was like sinking into a cloud. No lumpy cot, no sleeping bag, just my mattress and the hum of my house. Next morning, I woke up early, grabbed a coffee, and decided to go through my photos before heading to the office. Figured I'd pick out the best ones, maybe post a few to show I was doing all right. I sat at my kitchen table, camera in hand, and started scrolling. That's when it all went sideways. The first photo was of me with six other people. We were lined up, arms slung around each other, grinning like old friends. My tent was in the background, same spot by the lake, with a few other tents pitched nearby. Except I didn't know these people. Not a single one. Their faces were blurred like they'd whipped their heads away right as the shutter clicked. Not just out of focus, their features were smeared like someone had dragged a finger through wet paint. The woman next to me had her arm around my waist, her fingers digging in, almost possessive, but I didn't know her. I didn't know any of them. My pulse kicked up. I went camping alone. I'd planned it for months, loaded my truck myself, driven 3 hours into the middle of nowhere. So, who the hell were these people? Why was I standing with them like we were buddies? The background, my tent, the lake, the pines was exactly where I'd been. But those other tents, I didn't remember them. Not at all. I tried to shrug it off. Maybe I'd had one too many beers one night and forgot about some hikers who'd set up nearby. Maybe we'd hung out, snapped a photo, and my brain just blanked it. It was a flimsy excuse, but it was all I had to keep the panic from swallowing me whole. I kept scrolling, praying for something that made sense. The next photos were worse. Shots of me fishing, stirring a pot over the fire, kicking back by the lake. Moments I remembered clear as day. But in every single one, there were other people. Strangers with blurred faces standing by the water, sitting around the fire, even lurking in the background of shots I'd sworn I took alone. It was like someone had photoshopped these ghosts into my life. My hands started to sweat. This wasn't right. I moved to the second day's photos. Another group shot, same as the first, but one person was gone. The guy on the far left just erased. The rest were still there, arms around each other, faces smudged, but the space where he'd stood was empty. The timestamp matched the first photo. How does someone vanish like that? The rest of that day's shots were the same moments I knew. Casting my line, tending the fire, but with these blurred strangers mixed in. It felt like I was staring at a different version of my trip. A twisted reality where I hadn't been alone. But that couldn't be real, could it? Third day, another group shot. Another person gone. This time, someone from the middle. The gap was stark, like a rip in the world. Fourth day, another missing. Fifth, another. By the sixth day, it was just me and the woman who'd been glued to my side in the first photo. Her face was still a blur, her arm still locked around my waist. The other tents in the background were shredded now, like they'd been clawed apart in a storm. My tent? Perfect, untouched. And in the trees behind us, I saw something new. shapes barely there, but unmistakable. Figures dangling, their heads twisted at sickening angles. My breath caught. My hands shook so bad I nearly dropped the camera. Who were these people? Where did they go? Why couldn't I remember them? And those shapes in the trees, what were they? I scrolled to the last photo from the final day. Just me standing alone in the clearing, my tent behind me pristine. But in the trees, clearer now, were six figures. Six blurred bodies hanging like broken marionets. Their necks snapped at 90°, their heads lulled, limbs limp, and my hands, both of them were in the frame, empty. If I wasn't holding the camera, who was? I sat there frozen, the camera's screen burning into my eyes. My coffee was stone cold, my watch ticking like a countdown. I checked the time. Hours had slipped away. I was late for work, way late. I shoved the camera into my bag, grabbed my keys, and bolted for my truck. The drive to the office was a haze. Those blurred faces and hanging bodies flashing in my mind. What the hell happened out there? I stumbled into work looking like I'd crawled out of a ditch. Hair a mess, shirt half untucked. My team gave me weird looks, but I brushed them off belining for my office. One of my guys, Tom, caught me in the hall. His face was pale, his voice low, like he was scared to ask. "Where's your wife?" I stopped dead. "My wife?" "Yeah," he said, eyes narrowing. "Her and the rest of the management team. You all went on that retreat together, right? You're the only one back. My stomach twisted. I wasn't married. I went camping alone. But Tom was staring at me like I'd lost my mind. I pushed past him, heart pounding, and got to my desk. There it was, right by my monitor, a framed photo. The same group from the first picture. Seven of us, arms around each other, smiling. My tent, the lake, the pines. Their faces weren't blurred in this one. I knew them. Sarah, head of marketing. Mike, our CFO, Lisa, HR, my management team. But I didn't remember them being there. Not in the woods, not anywhere. I yanked out my camera, hands shaking, and pulled up the first photo. I compared it to the framed one, lining up the bodies, the clothes. It was them. It was us. But how? Why couldn't I remember? I scrolled to the last photo. The six blurred figures in the trees, Sarah, Mike, Lisa, the others, hanging, necks broken, my hands still in the frame, still empty. Who was taking the pictures? I don't know how long I sat there staring at the camera, the framed photo, a puzzle with no edges. My office felt like a coffin, the walls pressing in. Tom's words kept looping. You all went on that retreat together, but I didn't. I went alone. I planned it alone, didn't I? That last photo haunts me. Those figures in the trees, heads twisted like they'd been rung out. The woman's arm around my waist in the first shot like she was claiming me. The shredded tents, the empty space is where people used to be. And the question that's eating me alive. If I wasn't holding the camera, who was? I haven't gone back to work. I can't. Every time I close my eyes, I see those blurred faces, those snapped necks. I hear the wind in the pines whispering things I don't want to understand. I've checked my camera a hundred times, hoping the photos would change. Make sense? They don't. They're still there mocking me. I don't know what happened in those woods. I don't know who those people were or why my mind's wiped them out. I don't know if I'm cracking up or if something else, something worse, followed me home. But I'm not the man I was. I'm not sure I'm a man at all anymore. At night, I hear footsteps in my house. Soft, careful, like someone circling just out of sight. I check the locks, the windows. Nothing. But I feel it. Something watching, waiting. I keep my camera by my bed like it's a shield, but it's useless. Last night, I woke to a sound, a sharp click like a camera shutter. I grabbed my camera, heart hammering, and checked the memory card. A new photo timestamped 3:17 a.m. Me asleep in my bed, face pale in the dark. My hands were under the covers, nowhere near the camera. In the corner of the frame, just visible was a blurred face smiling.

transcript.fullText: The world dissolved into a swirling incandescent agony. A grotesque kaleidoscope of pain that seared through my very being. My face, my carefully sculpted facade, the instrument of my triumphs, was dissolving, melting like cheap wax under a cruel sun. The scent of cedar and amber, usually my signature, was now choked by the acrid stench of burning flesh, a testament to a betrayal so profound it threatened to unravel the very threads of my existence. This wasn't merely pain. It was the obliteration of everything I had painstakingly built. A brutal reminder of the helplessness I had sworn to bury forever. A searing echo of Peter's fading breath in that squalid tenement. My vision, my control, my very identity all gone, replaced by a blinding, blistering inferno. That was the moment the world decided to remind me of the squalor I'd fought so hard to escape. Though the seeds of this particular catastrophe had been sewn weeks earlier, in a moment of audacious hubris, I now almost regretted a calculated gamble, I thought I could control a game I was sure I would win. Let me be clear. I am not some ordinary man blessed with mere conventional good looks. My features, sharp and aristocratic, complimented by a lean, tailored physique, are a weapon, a key to unlock doors others only dream of. When I walk into a room, the air shifts. It always has. This isn't vanity. It's an objective truth. My career, my carefully cultivated connections in the art world, they are merely extensions of my inherent superiority. People, as I've always known, are so utterly predictable. Give them a compliment, a touch of feigned sympathy, a glimpse of vulnerability, and they'll eat from your hand. Pathetic, really, but exquisitly useful. The problem, if you could call it that, was Hannah. My beautiful, utterly insecure Hannah. She was a stunning creature, all golden curls and eyes the color of rich dark chocolate, a living sculpture of what society deems perfection. Yet her fragile ego, a direct consequence of her parents' grotesque neglect, made her a liability. Her father, a man I'd have dismissed as a pathetic failure had he not been such a useful case study, once told her as a child that her acne was disgusting, such a crude, blunt instrument of a man. It was a wound that never healed even as her skin cleared. It festered, transforming into a desperate, insatiable hunger for external validation through her physical appearance. I saw it, of course. I saw it from the very beginning and I understood how to use it. Hannah, with her striking looks never had to buy her own drinks. Men flocked to her drawn by her superficial brilliance. But her fixation with always being the center of attention could at times become corrosive like the infamous Atalini gate. I remember it vividly. A gala dinner, a meticulously tailored chereatalini suit, a new yacht masteraster Rolex gleaming on my wrist, the one with the birectional rotatable bezel and black dial, a subtle declaration of my rising status. The senior partners at the firm, usually so stiff, practically started a battle royale, craning their necks to get a closer look at my acquisitions, my success. Had Hannah stayed home that night, my triumph would have been absolute acknowledged. But no, she had to be there radiating her incipid charm, drawing the gaze away from me, the architect of our ascension. I woke up the next morning to find a fist-sized tear beneath the lapel of that dinner jacket along with two buttons missing. A petty, childish act of sabotage, a direct assault on my image, my very essence. My blood ran cold with rage, a familiar sensation that often accompanied the realization that someone dared to challenge my preeminence. Her hesitation, her barely concealed jealousy reminded me of that collector in Chicago, the one whose secrets I buried in my pocket notebook before he crumbled under the weight of his own pathetic insecurities. I had dealt with lesser minds then, and I would deal with Hannah now. In the months following that incident, my so-called trophy wife insisted on attending every last cocktail party and charity ball, no matter how mundane, draped in the flashiest dresses imaginable, her hair, meticulously styled, luscious, and bouncy. With a champagne flute perpetually in hand, she endlessly, nauseiatingly referred to herself as my trophy wife or the winning lottery ticket that blew into my hand. It was a performance, a crude, desperate pantomime designed to remind everyone, and most annoyingly me, that she was the true spectacle. My blood simmerred. I could feel the eyes on her, the whispers, the way she absorbed the light, leaving me in her shadow. It brought a familiar bitter taste to my mouth, a taste of being overlooked, of being the invisible boy in the crumbling tenement while the world paid attention to something else. I twisted the tarnished silver ring on my right hand, Peter's ring, a silent promise to myself that I would never again be so utterly forgotten, so easily overshadowed. No Hannah would learn her place. She was my accessory, not the other way around. Little by little, these snide remarks, these pathetic attempts to diminish me, ate away at my composure. From the way she talked, you'd think she married a professional Shrek impersonator rather than a man destined for true greatness. The next time she dropped a, "Don't you think you're punching above your weight with me, honey?" quip in front of polite company a pathetic attempt to belittle me to assert her supposed dominance. I smiled, a slow, deliberate curve of my lips that promised both charm and a hidden blade. I raised my whiskey glass, its amber liquid, a warm comfort against the cold calculations forming in my mind. Actually, I said, my voice smooth, perfectly modulated. I reckon we're about even looks wise. The words hung in the air. A perfectly weighted stone dropped into a still pond. A long awkward pause followed, interrupted only by one startled onlooker choking on a shrimp tartlet. The flicker of shock in Hannah's eyes, the subtle clenching of her jaw. It was a victory, small but satisfying. To Hannah's credit, her temper didn't boil over until we got home. The drive was a silent, simmering cauldron of unspoken fury. I could feel her rage radiating from the passenger seat, a palpable heat that pressed against the cedar and amber scent of my cologne. Rather than explode in a spectacular display of humiliation, she just endlessly ranted about how I'd placed us on equal footing physically. 30 minutes of shouting, screaming, and stomping around the house later, with half the furniture sprawled across the floor or broken a crude, destructive tantrum befitting a child. Not a woman I had chosen to elevate, she finally spat, "Fine, we're even. You're the window dressing and the main bread winner in this relationship. Congratulations." With that, the bedroom door slammed shut behind her, a pathetic echo of her impotent fury. Did I already know this encounter was headed to a bleak place? Absolutely. I'd seen the storm gathering the dark clouds of her insecurity, threatening to unleash a deluge. It was almost dawn, though, and I could feel Hannah's raw fury from the far end of the hall, a venomous current. So I spent the night in the guest room, not out of fear, but out of a calculated desire to let her stew, to let the poison of her own inadequacy consume her. Perhaps a little rest would help dissolve that temper. Perhaps she would wake up, realize the foolishness of her outburst, and return to her rightful place as my adoring, decorative partner. This feeling of being cornered of my carefully constructed world threatening to unravel was a familiar echo of that fiasco with the gilded frame. When I nearly lost everything to arrival, I underestimated. I would not make that mistake again. The next morning, from across the breakfast counter, the beautiful woman stared right through me. Her eyes, usually so vibrant, were cold, unseeing. Everything okay? I asked my voice a carefully modulated meekness designed to disarm to invite a return to the status quo. She finished her coffee, tossed the empty cup into the sink with a brittle clatter, and exited the room without a single word. A theatrical exit, I noted, utterly predictable. Over the next few days, a chilling game began. I'd catch her watching me whenever she thought I wasn't paying attention. her gaze of phantom weight on my skin. While in the shower, the bathroom door would shiver open just a little, and I'd quickly turn off the water and shout, "Hello!" Only to be met with silence. In the middle of the night, floorboards would squeak and I'd catch a glimpse of a shadowy figure in the outside hall. But by the time I flicked on the bedside lamp and scrambled to my feet, the quiet house would be snoozing peacefully. It was unnerving, certainly an annoyance, but I refused to believe the obvious truth that I was terrified of my own wife. The very notion was preposterous. I Victor Cain, who could bend the wills of the most hardened collectors, who could outmaneuver rivals with a whisper and a smile, who had survived a childhood that would break lesser men terrified of a woman. It sounded ridiculous. If my associates, the gallery owners and critics I so carefully cultivated caught me tiptoeing past the master bedroom or jumping at my own reflection, they'd have scoffed. You can bench 220 Kane, but you're terrified of your Mrs. Puliss. Such a public display of my vulnerability, even in this private hell, brought back the cold dread of the auction of secrets when I felt those darker forces closing in, sniffing out my past. Emma, bless her naive heart, would never have dared such a direct assault. Though her growing suspicion of my methods was becoming a tiresome inconvenience, a small, persistent gnawing, unlike this roaring inferno. So rather than retreat to a hotel, a humiliating admission of weakness, I marched into our room one night, a lavish bouquet of crimson roses clutched in my hand. My impeccably tailored suit felt like a suit of armor. I stood before her a picture of feigned contrition and announced to Hannah that I couldn't hold a candle to her. I spun a tale, a masterpiece of manipulative flattery. Every time the human beam of sunlight I was privileged enough to call my wife and I stood next to each other. I looked so ugly by comparison onlookers wondered whether my parents might have been related. My words were a balm, a saccharine poison designed to lull her back into complacency, to make her feel superior, to make her drop her guard. Hannah gave me a long, hard stare, her eyes searching before finally slowly pulling back the bed sheets. What was I meant to do? Wait for a damn smoke signal? I hopped straight in, desperate to believe we'd closed the book on that ugly chapter of our marriage. That my cleverness had once again prevailed. When I woke up, the world was a nightmare. My hands and feet were bound to the bedpost by cold, unforgiving metal cuffs. My dearly beloved sat on top of me, a grotesque parody of intimacy, wearing a face mask, her hips straddling my chest. In her gloved hand, there was a glass container filled with clear, viscous liquid. The sight of it sent a primal jolt of fear through me, a chilling echo of the helplessness I felt as a boy watching Peter's breath grow shallow. Hannah's voice, muffled by the mask, was eerily calm, devoid of her usual histrionics. "I've been mulling over what you said," she purred. "And you were right before we are equal." As she unscrewed the lid, a pungent acrate aroma seeped out, singing my nostril hairs, assaulting my senses. "But that got me thinking." She continued, her voice, gaining a terrifying edge. If I'm not the pretty one, what exactly do I bring to this marriage? Nothing. That's what. So, I'm going to knock you down a few pegs, you know, to even things out. The container dangled directly above my skull, slowly tipping forward, inch by terrible, agonizing inch. Along the side, there was a yellow and black illustration of a beaker spilling over a bare hand and eating away at the flesh. Oh, God. A stammering mess, I choked out a feeble Hannah, please. The last thing I saw was her big, bright smile. The smile that had made so many men melt like butter in a hot pan, now twisted into a mask of pure, unadulterated malice. Then, scalding liquid dowsed my eyes, and an invisible battalion of hungry ants, a million tiny burning needles, sunk their mandibles into my skin. The pain was immediate absolute, a blinding inferno that consumed my vision, my identity, my very being. From there, there are only vague, horrifying echoes. Me clawing my way across the room, a guttural scream issuing from my bubbling lips, eye jelly, my precious eyes, the windows to my manipulative soul oozing onto the carpet. Either I broke free from my restraints, or Hannah, in a perverse act of twisted mercy, released me. The world appeared as blobs of swirling color, a nauseating, distorted canvas. And the front of my night shirt kept growing hotter by the second the acid eating through the fabric eating through me. As I ripped it off over my skull, there came a flash of bright light accompanied by her cackling laughter, a sound that would forever haunt my fractured memory. It occurred to me then, through the haze of agony, that Hannah was probably watching this with great amusement, delighted by her husband's disfigurement. What I didn't realize at the time was that she'd also snapped photos documenting my humiliation to WhatsApp to our closest friends. In the morning, they'd wake up, open pictures of me wrestling my shirt over my head, accompanied by the caption, "My ugly man's got that beach bud and chuckle at what they believed was my disgusting Halloween mask." The thought of their laughter, their pity was almost as searing as the acid itself. Disoriented, still burning, I screamed for help through liquefying lips again and again. There came no response. The silence of the house was a mocking echo of my helplessness. My phone wasn't charging on the bedside cabinet. My fingers, raw and trembling, fumbled around on my hands and knees past the carpeted hall, finally uncovering a cold tiled floor. The bathroom. Guided by muscle memory, by the desperate primal instinct for survival, I worked my way over into the bathtub. My hands spider walking up the side. With help from the towel rack, I dragged myself to a standing position, my muscles screaming in protest. The controls for the shower sat at chest height. Still blind with the inferno raging on my face, growing worse with each passing second, I mashed buttons until a blast of perfect icy water hit me in the face, providing momentary blessed relief from the pain, a brief restbite from the consuming fire. It wasn't long before the shower head got yanked from its holster. The jet pelted me and the stomach moved across my torso and around the side of my thighs. As it turned out, Hannah, in her depraved delight, decided to record an Insta story. Water fight with the hideous hubby. Love how we're still so goofy after all these years. My stomach churned, not just from the pain, but from the sheer unadulterated malice of it all. I toppled over the side of the tub, my ribs thuing against the cold, unforgiving floor. A short time later, I found myself in the outer hall, my hand groping for purchase, but finding only air. I went toppling down the stairs. Each sickening thud a fresh insult to my battered body. Disoriented, bruised, bleeding, I found myself trapped in that maze of a house. My own gilded cage turned into a personal hell. This wasn't working. My only chance of summoning help of regaining control was with Hannah's phone. But how to get it from her? She was a monster, a deranged beast. But she was still, in her own twisted way, cunning. With a series of stiff shves, my darling wife wrestled me onto the armchair in the lounge, her delicate voice barely audible through the agonyfilled haze, whispering something about capturing the moment. She eased herself into a seat across my lap, one arm draped across the back of my neck. Oh god, she was taking a selfie. She was actually taking a selfie. She really had lost it. The sheer audacity, the narcissistic depravity of it ignited a spark of cold fury within me, overriding the pain. The second I saw a flashing light, a brief blinding flash, I sprung into action. Later, I was told in the action shot captured by the phone, my face had the consistency of strawberry jelly, and where our cheeks touched melted skin stretched out like the warm cheese on a piece of garlic bread. Still blind, my rage, a guiding force. I lashed out, swiping at Hannah's chest and arms. My hands finding purchase tearing, scratching. The phone went spinning out of her hand, a small, satisfying clatter. She tried to run a pathetic, desperate scramble. But I cut off her escape, knowing if she slipped away, if she vanished into the shadows, I'd be left there to rot, disfigured and helpless, just like Peter. I couldn't save him, but I would save myself. I would never be that weak again. With every ounce of strength left in my mangled body, I rained down blows, hearing bones crunch and teeth shatter. The wet, sickening sounds a perverse kind of music to my ears. My better half fought back, swiping at me, tearing away chunks of flesh so large medics would later tell me huge portions of bone shown through. But I was beyond pain, beyond reason. I was a force of retribution, a narcissistic god exacting vengeance. Hannah collapsed onto the floor, groaning a broken doll. Just from running my fingers across her crumpled features, I could tell she didn't have that more breathtaking than the first day of summer smile anymore. And most of the polish had been wiped off those well-defined cheekbones. A small cold satisfaction settled in my chest. A fleeting moment of triumph amidst the chaos. From there my survival became a desperate game of Marco Polo with the phone which had taken shelter beneath the sofa. My fingers slick with blood and fluid fumbled searching until they brushed against the cold smooth glass. I dragged it out the screen a blurry green button in my ruined vision. I tapped at a desperate prayer to a world that had betrayed me. And then a concerned voice, a lifeline, spoke back at me. I screamed. I screamed until the police officers kicked open the front door, their shouts echoing in the ruined house. Then I lay in the back of an ambulance speeding toward the hospital. The sirens loud in my ears, a paramedic promising everything would be okay, that they'd save my vision. Lies, of course. All lies. 12 weeks I spent in recovery, my face encased with bandages, a prisoner in my own damaged skin. The authorities took Hannah for her own quick pit stop in the emergency room before carting her off to jail where she's currently awaiting trial. From what I hear, the other inmates have taken to calling her the elephant woman. A fitting moniker, wouldn't you agree? She tried to destroy me to strip away my power, my image. But in the end she only destroyed herself. I Victor Kain always prevail.

transcript.fullText: The mask felt like a slab of ice against my face heavy as a tombstone. I tugged it on stone, scraping my skin, and started up the basement stairs of our old Iowa farmhouse. Each step creaked like a warning, but I couldn't stop grinning. I was going to scare the hell out of my wife, Debbie. Found the thing in a battered crate among dad's stuff him the big shot anthropology professor who left us this creaky house in a pile of cash last year. The eyeholes, one slightly lower than the other, made the world tilt. A thin slit for a mouth lined with jagged carved teeth trapped my breath hot and sour. Perfect for a prank. At the top, I nudged the basement door open. Empty living room, but I heard water and a low murmur from the kitchen. Debbie at the sink, probably glued to her true crime podcasts. I kicked off my sneakers. the hardwood cold under my socks and crept forward, heart pounding. The mask suffocated sweat trickling down my neck, but I wore it anyway. The thrill was too sharp. The kitchen doorway loomed shadows pooling. I leaned in there. She was back turned scrubbing a skillet. Her phone blared something about a missing hiker. I took a shallow breath and moved. Three silent steps and I was behind her. I clamped her shoulder. She spun eyes huge and screamed. Before I could laugh, her knee slammed into my crotch. Pain roared up my spine. I crashed into the island, the mask slipping half blinding me. I hit the floor, gasping just as she spun, snatching a butcher knife from the sink blade, glinting as she raised it. Stop. I wheezed, ripping the mask off. Deb, it's me, Bill. She froze. knife still up her face, twisting from terror to rage. "What the actual [ __ ] Bill? Where'd you get that goddamn thing?" I groaned, clutching myself, one hand, waving surrender. "Basement, dad's old junk. Thought I'd mess with you. Just a dumb scare. A scare." She lowered the knife eyes blazing. I almost gutted you, you idiot. That mask is straight out of a slasher flick. She chucked the knife into the sink with a clang and crouched, grabbing the mask. She turned it over fingers brushing the uneven eye holes and sharp teeth. Jesus, it's heavy. Stone maybe looks like it's been buried for centuries. Your dad picked this up on one of his fancy trips dad had spent his life chasing artifacts, dragging home relics from jungles and deserts. I nodded, still wincing. Yeah, probably. Found it with a creepy bone knife in a locked box. Was going to grab the knife, too. But good call I didn't. We should get it checked out, she said, her voice softer but tight. Might be worth a fortune. Nah, I want to keep it, I said, taking the mask. Reminds me of dad. We don't need the cash. Not with his inheritance. Plus, it's kind of badass, right? Like something you'd show off at a party. She shivered, stepping back. It's [ __ ] creepy, Bill. If you're keeping that thing, it stays in your study. I don't want to see it staring at me every damn day. Things went back to normal, or so I thought. I taught anthropology at the local college in Cedar Falls, same place dad had ruled for 30 years. The mask hung on my study wall, the bone knife pinned below it catching lamp light in a way that made my skin crawl. Debbie steered clear of the room, but I couldn't stop staring. Those crooked eyeholes seemed to follow me like they were waiting. I dug through dad's journals in the basement, hoping for answers, but they just rambled about digs in faroff places. Nothing on the mask. Still, it felt like him. A piece of the man I'd looked up to. A month later, I threw a retirement bash for Roger Wentworth, dad's old buddy. The house filled with professor's whiskey glasses clinking under the hum of cicatas. Derek Nielsen, a buddy of mine, slipped in late. Derek wasn't like the rest of us trust fund academics. Grew up dirt poor, lost his dad, young clawed his way to a PhD. We'd bonded over cheap beers, swapping stories about Cedar Falls, though he never talked about his past. I snagged two Bud Lights and met him at the door. Yo, Derek, come check this out. You're going to love it. He popped the cap with his lighter, smirking. All right, man. What's the big deal? I led him to the study and pointed at the mask. Found this in dad's stuff. Pretty wild, huh? His beer hit the floor glass shattering. His face went gray. Eyes locked on the mask like it was a ghost. This some kind of sick joke, he hissed. Dude, what? I stepped back, his fear hitting me like a cold wind. It's just a mask. What's wrong? I got to sit, he mumbled, collapsing into the desk chair. Tell me you didn't know. Tell me this ain't you screwing with me. Know what? My voice cracked. Derek, you're scaring the [ __ ] out of me. I need a drink. Not beer. Something that burns. I bolted to the liquor cabinet. Pulse racing. Debbie was laughing with some profs wife. Where'd you run off to? She asked. Show Derek the mask, I said, pouring a double bourbon. He's freaking out. Told you that thing's bad news, she muttered. Ditch it, Bill. I barely nodded, hurrying back. Derek was still staring at the mask glassy. I shoved the bourbon into his hand. He slammed it back, coughing. Then he started talking, voice low, like the walls were listening. 35 years ago, my dad died. Coroner called it suicide case closed. No autopsy. But my mom, she saw something else. I leaned closer, dread pooling in my gut. What did she see? She came home and found him in the tub. Blood everywhere. A man was there wearing a mask like that. One round face, crooked eyes, double teeth, holding a bone knife, just watching. She passed out, and when she woke, he was gone. She's been locked in a psych ward ever since drawing that mask over and over. I glanced at the mask, my stomach lurching. "You're saying that's the mask? I ain't saying shit," he snapped, pulling out his phone. "I'm calling the cops." The police rolled in that night, their radios crackling as the party fizzled out. Derek showed them faded photocopies of his mom's drawings, and Hawkins, "The masks were dead ringers for mine." They hauled the mask and knife to the station and I let them poke around the basement. I stood there, Debbie, gripping my hand, feeling like the house was holding its breath. Next morning, they came back with a warrant. They dug into the house records and found a renovation from when I was a kid, 95, the year they poured a new concrete slab over the old dirt basement floor. They brought in jackhammers, and the noise shook the house like a heartbeat. Debbie and I watched from the stairs, her nails digging into my arm as they tore up the floor. They found bodies. 11 laid out under the concrete each with initials scratched above them. Men, women, bones brittle and yellowed. The cops kept me back, but they asked about dad, his late nights, his trips. I remembered him slipping in at 2:00 a.m. saying he was prepping lectures. I remembered that locked crate in the basement, the one I'd never questioned. Forensics tied the knife to one victim, a woman with cuts matching its jagged edge. Dererick's dad wasn't in the basement, but they reopened his case, sniffing for murder. My dad, the guy who'd grilled burgers on Sundays and cheered at my little league games, was a killer. A monster who'd used that mask, that knife to carve his way through lives. We packed up and left within days. The house hit the market, but it's still empty. A cursed husk nobody wants. Cedar Falls whispers about the murder house and I can't walk campus without stairs. Derek ghosted me and I get it. I didn't kill anyone, but I'm his son and that's a stain I can't scrub off. It feels like your entire world tilts on its axis for a moment, right? Our breakup wasn't dramatic. No shouting, no big fights, just this quiet, growing silence that eventually became too heavy to bear. She said she needed time, space to find herself. Or maybe she just wanted to know if I still remembered her, if she still held any space in my thoughts. It really makes you wonder, doesn't it? The truth is, we rarely reach out in the quiet of the night when everything is perfect. We reach out when something inside us feels a little broken, hoping that someone who once loved us might still care enough to offer a comforting word or at least acknowledge our presence. It's a vulnerable moment, both for the sender and the receiver. A silent plea in the digital ether. I still remember the last time I saw her. clear as day. She was wearing that gray sweater, the one she always said made her look plain. But to me, she looked like home. We stood there in the rain, pretending the weather was the reason we couldn't speak. They smother, sever, porterize. Not to empower, but to suppress. Not to grow, but to contain, not to heal. hollow. But why would anyone willingly recite such a thing? The man was motionless beneath the waterline. Only his lips broke the surface, slow and parted like a fish, unsure whether to breathe or drown. The chill was deliberate. He had filled the tub with water so cold it bordered on pain, then slid into it like a soldier into a grave. Not for cleansing, not even for comfort, but for control. Cold blunts thought slows breath muffles pain. He stared at the ceiling. Beneath the quiet surface of his mind, something stirred. She couldn't have been older than 12. He remembered her small frame, her wide eyes that refused to cry, and the swollen red on her cheek. He didn't know her name. He hadn't needed it. He had made a phone call. He had waited until someone came, a neighbor maybe, then police. And then she was taken away like a broken thing wrapped in warm blankets. She hadn't spoken, but her eyes had locked with his for one second longer than necessary. She was older now, maybe 20, maybe less. The curve of her jaw was familiar, but it was the faint scar on her forearm that clicked into place like a puzzle piece sliding home. He stared. She noticed. Her eyes met his. A flicker of confusion passed through her expression. "Do I know you?" she asked, polite, hesitant. His eyes dropped to her neck. a crucifix. His mouth opened then closed. [Music] They call it the diving reflex. The body's ancient reaction to cold water. Heart rate drops. Blood moves inward. Muscles loosen. A survival instinct inherited from seals and whales. He used to test it as a boy. At dusk, he would slip into the pool, hold his breath, and sink. Eyes closed, ears humming. The world narrowed to pressure and dark. It wasn't about breath control. It was about reaching the edge where the chest tightens and time slows. There in that stillness, he felt something approach. Not fear, not panic, something quieter. Darkness, not absence, but presence. Not drowning, disappearing. She looked at him again, this time more carefully. I feel like I've met you, she said. He could feel the memory rise like eat in the chest or a name you almost remember. He resisted and then he heard it. Hi Kuwer. Consumed by darkness, it came unbidden. He had first heard it in a video game as a boy, some silver-haired warrior shouting it before a final blow. Back then it sounded cool. Now it felt like truth, a mantra not for power but for erasia. He spoke calmly flat. No, he said you must have me confused with someone else. Oh, she replied sorry. She walked away disappearing into the crowd. He didn't look back. Just one word, a glance too honest, and the air between them might have shifted. Not memory, meaning, not recognition, hope. And from hope, something worse. Not love, but longing. A thread pulled into something it was never meant to be. So he let it pass quietly, deliberately. consumed by darkness. Light does not only illuminate darkness, it gives darkness its shape. If even the gods choose silence, then man too can save by saying nothing. Some silences are not absences. Their cages left open so nothing gets caught.

Annabelle called, raising her hand in the air without looking up from the book she'd been reading. After a few days on campus, she had quickly learned how the first day of any class usually went. Of the four classes she had already attended that week, only one of the professors had actually bothered to show up. Much to Annabelle's annoyance, most chose to send their teaching assistants in their place. Amabel had taken to silently referring to them as not professors after the second time it happened. The majority of the first class was spent taking roll call, followed by the weakest of introductions to the course before the TA dismissed everyone for the day. So far, Amabel hadn't learned a single thing except to bring a book to class so she would have something to do while the not professors called people's names. The first time it happened, Amabel tried to let it go without much thought. But now her irritation was getting the best of her. How could she possibly hit the ground running if the professors weren't even there on the first day? How could she ask them any of the questions she already had? To her, it all seemed incredibly wrong. Still, Annabelle did her best to listen as the teaching assistant for her English literature class began to speak. Now that role is out of the way, he said, "Hi everyone, I'm Tristan. I'm Professor Tucker's teaching assistant. You'll probably see me more often than you'll see him this semester, so get used to me." Tristan smiled at the 20 people in front of him. Annabelle rolled her eyes and looked back down at her book. It wasn't a particularly interesting book, at least not so far. But she found it much more entertaining than whatever Tristan had to say. Plus, she knew she was less likely to blow up at him if she didn't listen quite so intently. After a few seconds of silence, Amabel looked up to find the entire class staring at her as well as Tristan. She didn't say anything, but she closed her book slowly, a flush already creeping up her neck onto her cheeks. I'm sorry, Tristan said to her, his eyes narrowing slightly. Am I interrupting your leisure reading time? No, Annabelle croked. She cleared her throat and added. I'm sorry. Don't apologize to me, Tristan scoffed. You're only wasting your own time. If you don't want to be here, the door is right back there. He gestured behind her toward the exit. Annabelle didn't move or speak. She simply held eye contact with him and tried not to cry from embarrassment. If there was anything she hated more than not being taught properly, it was being called out in front of a classroom full of people. Her cheeks were burning as Tristan continued to stare at her. It wasn't until after Annabelle gave up and looked down at her hands that Tristan cleared his throat and continued on with his introduction. As I was saying, he said, still clearly annoyed. I'm Tristan. This is English literature 336. In this class, we will focus primarily on. Annabelle kept her eyes glued on Tristan as he spoke, but she let her mind drift. She was already so angry with how college life was turning out. When she received her acceptance letter to the University of New York, she'd been so excited she could barely sit still. Neither of her parents wanted her to move so far away. But after a monotonous childhood in the small town of Trent, Texas, Amabel knew she needed to find something new for herself, something different, something big, something great. For months, she dreamed of all the things she would learn. She bought her required books so far in advance that she had read all of them long before she even left Texas. Her friends back home laughed at her. They couldn't understand her. >> Censored >> to learn, but it didn't matter. Ever since she was little, Amabel craved knowledge. She loved to learn new things. It was both a blessing and a curse. It meant she spent her life stuck between blissful intelligence and eager frustration. Nothing irked Amabel more than not being able to figure something out. As a child, she once spent an entire summer teaching herself how to bake the perfect chocolate sule just because she hated not knowing. That same summer, she read War and Peace in its entirety. She was 12 at the time. College was supposed to be the beginning of everything for Annabelle. She was going to throw herself into her schoolwork with a fervor that would have put Albert Einstein to shame. But every time she tried to do just that, something stood in her way. Today, it was Tristan. What she wanted more than anything was for Professor Tucker to walk through the door and announce that he was open to any and all questions. She knew it wouldn't happen though, so she had to settle for Tristan. Tristan, the not professor who didn't even decide her grade. "Okay," he said as he finished his speech. "Any questions?" Annabelle's hand immediately flew into the air. Tristan glanced around the room. His eyes stopped on Amabel for a split second before he continued moving his head, searching for someone. "Anyone else?" "No one," he asked pointedly. "All right, you're free to go. I'll see you next week." Chairs scuffed the floor as Annabelle's classmates stood up to leave, but Amabel sat stubbornly in her seat, her hand still raised above her head. As they filed out of the room, people looked at her with the mused grins on their faces. Some even laughed. Still, Amabel sat determinedly staring at Tristan, waiting for him to look back over at her. It wasn't until the final person had left that he finally did. "What's your name again?" he asked her, looking down at his roll sheet. "Amabel Parker," she answered immediately. "That's right," Tristan set the roll sheet on the desk behind him and slowly walked over to her, "the freshman. What are you doing in a junior level course? Have you even completed the prerequisites? I completed them two years ago, Annabelle answered. In high school, Tristan considered her for a second before asking, "What's your question?" "I have a few, actually." Annabelle lowered her hand and flipped open her notebook to the page titled English Lit. Intro questions. Tristan glanced down at the paper and laughed. Annabelle glared at him. as determined as she had been not to snap. She couldn't keep the anger in toned what? from slipping through her lips. Tristan chuckled again and said, "You're going to be a handful, aren't you?" Amabel and Tristan sat side by side in Professor Tucker's office, their heads bent together reading Amabel's latest paper. "See," Tristan pointed suddenly, "Right here. You cited the wrong article. I know what you were trying to say, but I had to dock at least a couple points for the confusion of sources. Okay, Annabelle nodded. That makes sense, but is one mistake really enough to knock my grade down by half a letter, Annabelle? Tristan laughed. You were the only person in the class to get anything above a C? Why can't you just accept your success and move on? Because an A minus is not success, Annabelle argued. Tristan just stared at her with the same slightly amused expression he always wore when looking at her. It drove her crazy. Stop looking at me like that. I know when you're making fun of me. You think you're subtle, but you're not. I'm not trying to be subtle. Tristan shrugged. I am making fun of you. I don't need to hide that. Well, stop. But it's just so easy. Tristan laughed. Shut up. Amabel snapped. Whoa. Whoa. Tristan raised his hands in a mock defensive pose. Be careful or I may just dock you down another half point. Tell me, have you ever gotten a B? Annabelle opened her mouth, the proud no already on the tip of her. >> Censored, >> but the smug look on Tristan's face made her second guessess herself. She closed her mouth and scowlled at him before she started packing her bag to leave. When it came to Professor Tucker's office hours, she assumed it would be Professor Tucker there waiting for her. To her fury, the only person in the office when she arrived was Tristan. Smug, annoying, knowit all Tristan, who seemed to make it his personal mission to make her life at NYU as miserable as possible. Ever since that very first class, Tristan had singled Amabel out. She was the person he shot all the hard questions at. It wasn't long before Annabelle was convinced he would spend the rest of the semester doing his best to humiliate her. Just as she was about to leave, Amabel turned around, a frown etched deeply on her face. Her eyes were narrowed as she considered Tristan. He was sitting behind Professor Tucker's desk, his feet propped up, reading a book. It was as if she had already left. "Why are you the one handing out grades?" Annabelle asked, pulling Tristan's attention away from his book. "What?" Tristan asked with a frown of his own. You're the teaching assistant, Amabel said. Not the professor. What gives you the authority to assign our grades? Tristan laughed and said, not what? Who? And that who would be Professor Tucker? I just don't think it's right for you to decide our grades. Amabel insisted. You aren't really the professor. Our grades should be decided by him, by Professor Tucker. I completely agree, Tristan said, folding his hands in front of him and staring up at Amabel. She opened her mouth to speak, already poised for a full-blown argument. When she registered what he had just said, her mouth closed and her frown deepened. For the first time since they met, Tristan had rendered her unable to speak. She never imagined he would agree with her on anything ever. Look, Annabelle, I agree with you. Okay, I do. Professor Tucker is a lazy, ineffectual figurehead who doesn't know his head from his ass. He hasn't taught his own classes in years. So, you and I can hate it all we want, but we aren't going to change it. That's just a fact. And frankly, I'm getting great experience, so I'm not going to complain. Well, sure it's great for you, Amabel agreed. But for the students, it sucks. We're having our academic fate decided by someone who's still working toward his own degree. You're just like the rest of us. At that, Tristan laughed again and stood up. He threw his coat over his shoulders and grabbed his bag before walking around the desk to where Annabelle stood. Without giving her a second glance, he pushed the office door open and disappeared into the hallway. Annabelle blinked, not sure what just happened. She could feel the anger bubbling up inside of her as it so often did whenever she interacted with Tristan. Her cheeks were flushed when she stepped through the door behind him. "Where are you going?" Annabelle demanded as Tristan made his way down the hallway. We were in the middle of a conversation. "I'm going to eat," Tristan said without bothering to turn around. "I'm hungry. You can keep yelling at me if you want, but you'll have to come with me." Are you kidding? Annabelle stared at Tristan's retreating figure in shock. She'd never had someone treat her the way Tristan did. Her entire life, she was the smartest person in any room. But now, Tristan set her on edge just by looking at her. He challenged her in ways she simultaneously loved and hated. No matter how hard she tried, she could never get the better of him the way he did with her. It was infuriating. so infuriating that with a frustrated sigh, she hurried after him down the hallway. As they walked through the streets of New York, Annabelle took in the sights for the first time since she'd moved to the city. The only thing she'd seen until then was the inside of her dorm building and her classrooms. As a freshman, most of her classes were in the same buildings, so she didn't have to travel far. She never ventured out into the city. She'd never even ridden the subway before. Her eyes were wide as they made their way down street after street until Tristan suddenly turned to head down the steps that led to a subway station. Amabel went to follow him, but hesitated for just a second at the top of the stairs. She didn't know why she was nervous to ride the subway. The idea didn't scare her at all. Still, she hesitated just long enough for Tristan to notice she was no longer beside him. "What's wrong?" he asked, turning back around to face her. Um, Amabel said, "Nothing. I'm fine." She hurried down the steps to where he was. He frowned at her for a second before shrugging and continuing after her. When they reached the entrance, Amabel looked around for somewhere to buy a pass.
