transcript.fullText: If you've ever wondered where Rald Doll got his ideas from or what his life was like before he became famous, then his two autobiographical books are a must readad. This first one, boy, tales of childhood starts with doll describing his Norwegian heritage and his parents' strong ties to their homeland. Every summer they would travel back to Norway for the holidays and these visits filled him with a love of nature, adventure, and family. But it also made him feel different from the other English boys at school because he only had two weeks off a year to enjoy being Norwegian. Doll's mom and dad both came from large families. He has many siblings, half siblings, aunts, uncles, and cousins. And when he was three, his dad died suddenly from injuries sustained in a car crash, leaving his mother a widow with six children to raise on her own. So, the family relied heavily on the support of grandparents, aunts, and uncles. In fact, one of the recurring themes of the book is mischief. It seems that everywhere doll goes, trouble follows. One of the most famous stories in the book is called the great mouse plot. When doll was nine, he and some friends decided to play a prank on a sweet shop. They found a dead mouse and put it inside a jar of gobstoppers. Then they waited for someone to put their hand in the jar and pull the string attached to the mouse so it would shoot out. And sure enough, the shopkeeper put his hand in, pulled the string, and jumped a foot in the air when the dead mouse shot out of the jar. The look on his face, according to Dah, was worth the entire prank. Another major part of the book is Doll's experience at English boarding schools. He paints a vivid picture of the strict, often cruel teachers and headmasters who ruled with fear and handed out punishments and canings without mercy. war. There are over 100 boys in dolls class, all of whom have to follow a strict set of rules. If you broke the rules, you would get the cane. And if you were caught doing something really bad, you might get put in solitary confinement where you would be locked up in a small room by yourself for days. But despite the harsh punishments, there are still funny and warm moments at school. Doll writes about the camaraderie among the boys and the thrill of school traditions like singing happy birthday to your friends in the middle of the night, playing football with a stolen pig's bladder, and sneaking extra sweets at meal times. A love of sweets and chocolate runs through the whole book. In fact, this is where Doll got the idea for Charlie and the Chocolate Factory. When he was a kid, he used to help out at his dentist uncle's lab where he would test new chocolate bars for Cadbury. This inspired him to create Willy Wonka, who also tests children's chocolate bars to see if they're good enough. Throughout the book, we see Doll develop a taste for sweet treats, especially chocolate, and a deep dislike for mean-spirited adults, especially those in authority. Many of the unpleasant teachers and headmasters in the book have names that start with the letters C, C, K, or B, B, D, D, L, L, P, P, P, P, P. P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P P. I do love that. Of course, it's not all funny games. The book is full of painful moments, too. In one story, Doll has to have an operation on his tonsils when he S7. And even though it's supposed to be a simple procedure, the doctor carries out the operation without giving him any anesthetic. Doll vividly describes the pain and trauma of the event which leaves him with a lifelong fear of doctors and hospitals and he writes about other scary medical experiences throughout the book including a stay in hospital after he's hit by a car. We also learn about Doll's family through stories about his sister Aster who died when he was 10 and his dad died when he was three. We don't really know Doll's dad, but we do hear about his adventurous spirit through stories his mom tells him. As the book progresses, Doll gets older and begins to see the world around him with more complexity. His accounts of strict discipline, injustice, and cruelty at school show us how these experiences gave him a lifelong sympathy for children and a distrust of authority figures. Themes that appear in his later fiction. This is the first book in the series and it ends with Doll finishing his school years and heading off to boarding house. So, there's more to come. I'll definitely be reading the second book, Going Solo, which covers his life as a young man and pilot. And if you want to see more, check out my review of Going Solo. Until next time, thanks for watching and happy reading. Bye.
